Existing reviews primarily organize biological agents by application, architecture, and agentic capability, but do not jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, we map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources, representing 128 unique publications across genomics, single-cell and spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. We therefore argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the FEV framework to evaluate scientific credibility of bioinformatics AI agents by analyzing workflow trajectories rather than just final outputs, finding that execution capabilities have outpaced reproducibility and validation standards across 109 systems.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of biological AI agents focuses too much on fluent responses and benchmark performance without establishing scientific credibility. Existing reviews don't properly operationalize accountability for agent-generated workflows in bioinformatics.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Function-Evidence-Validation (FEV) framework that analyzes workflow trajectories as the primary unit, separating demonstrated operations, traceable support for actions/claims, and use-case-specific validation. They apply FEV to map 109 agentic systems and 28 evaluation resources across bioinformatics domains.
AI.result: Analysis shows planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced faster than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and empirical testing. The study argues for assessing workflow correctness over final-answer correctness alone.
AI.conclusion: FEV provides a practical framework for comparing bioinformatics AI systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable workflows, shifting focus from output quality to workflow integrity.

title: Rethinking EEG-Based Disease Diagnosis: Decoupling Instance Representation Learning from Subject-Level Supervision
summary: EEG-based disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, yet common pipelines segment recordings into short instances, inherit the subject label for every instance, and train instance-level classifiers. This assumes that all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids inherited labels by treating each subject as a bag. However, EEG datasets contain far fewer subjects than instances, which can limit the quality of the representations learned by end-to-end MIL. We propose BridgeMIL, a two-stage framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags. Variance and covariance regularization prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention. Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater performance sensitivity to subject scarcity than to instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved separation between diagnostic classes. Together, these findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

AI.tldr: BridgeMIL is a two-stage framework for EEG disease diagnosis that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision, addressing the limitations of inherited instance labels and improving classification accuracy across multiple EEG datasets.
AI.motivation: Current EEG disease diagnosis pipelines face two main issues: 1) They segment recordings into short instances and assign subject-level disease labels to every instance, assuming all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence, and 2) While Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) treats each subject as a bag to avoid inherited labels, EEG datasets have far fewer subjects than instances, limiting representation quality in end-to-end MIL approaches.
AI.method: BridgeMIL employs a two-stage framework: Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels using two key strategies: temporal alignment of nearby windows and within-subject sub-bag sampling, with variance and covariance regularization to prevent collapse without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the pretrained encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject-level predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention.
AI.result: BridgeMIL achieves the highest mean accuracy in 14 out of 15 dataset-backbone settings across three EEG disease datasets, with an overall mean accuracy of 76.57% (4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline). Analysis reveals substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater sensitivity to subject scarcity than instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved diagnostic class separation.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate the importance of aligning supervision with subject-level prediction objectives while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances. BridgeMIL effectively bridges the gap between instance-level representation learning and subject-level classification, offering a more robust approach for EEG-based disease diagnosis.

title: SkillMentor: LLM Agent Self-Evolution via Learning Blind-Spot Diagnosis
summary: Agent self-evolution has primarily focused on learning how to act, while overlooking an equally important capability: learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches typically assume that failure discovery is given, focusing on how to repair failures once they are identified. We ask whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned. We thus study diagnosis as an agent capability separate from execution, and exclude two alternative sources of progress: executor adaptation and human supervision. Under these constraints, performance cannot improve through executor updates or annotated examples, forcing all improvements to originate from the learned diagnostic capability. We propose SkillMentor, which trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate them into reusable corrective skills. Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%. These results suggest that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability, enabling self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

AI.tldr: SkillMentor learns to automatically diagnose agent blind spots and create corrective skills without updating executor weights or human supervision, improving executor performance by 44.2%.
AI.motivation: Current agent self-evolution focuses only on learning how to act, while overlooking the equally important capability of discovering what an agent doesn't know. Existing approaches assume failure discovery is given and focus on repair, but blind-spot diagnosis itself may be a learnable capability.
AI.method: SkillMentor trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to: 1) generate diagnostic tasks, 2) identify recurrent failure modes, and 3) curate them into reusable corrective skills. The approach isolates diagnosis as a separate capability from execution, excluding executor adaptation and human supervision as sources of progress.
AI.result: Across AppWorld and BFCLv3 environments, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%, demonstrating that blind-spot diagnosis can be learned effectively.
AI.conclusion: Blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability that enables agent self-evolution without requiring updates to executor weights or relying on human-curated data, representing an important advancement in autonomous agent development.

title: Policy Gradient Steering: Interventions from Behavioral Objectives
summary: Activation steering has emerged in large language models as a lightweight alternative for dynamically changing a model's behavior at inference time. However, we show that existing steering methods fail to steer even a simple policy in a two-route gridworld environment. To address this limitation, we propose Policy Gradient Steering (PGS), which formulates steering as a reinforcement learning problem. PGS accumulates gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations to construct a removable task vector. We first demonstrate the calibration and reversibility of PGS in a two-route gridworld environment. Using chess puzzles, we then evaluate independently fitted PGS vectors both in isolation and in combination, finding that compatible tactical objectives accumulate constructively. Finally, in competitive football, we show that PGS can alter specific team behaviors and that its effects transfer across opponents. Together, these results show that policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains.

AI.tldr: PGS reformulates activation steering as a reinforcement learning problem using policy gradients to create temporary, composable behavioral adaptations across diverse domains.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods fail to steer even simple policies in basic environments like a two-route gridworld, highlighting the need for more effective steering approaches that work across diverse decision-making domains.
AI.method: Policy Gradient Steering (PGS) formulates steering as an RL problem, accumulating gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over rollouts or demonstrations to construct removable task vectors that can alter model behavior at inference time.
AI.result: PGS demonstrates calibration and reversibility in gridworld, compatible tactical objectives accumulate constructively in chess puzzles, and football team behaviors transfer across opponents - showing PGS creates temporary, composable behavioral adaptations.
AI.conclusion: Policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains, addressing limitations of existing steering methods.

title: Flat Score, Amplified Failures: How the Error Budget Masks Damage in Quantized LLM Agents
summary: Post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is widely reported to be nearly lossless. We test this claim for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where it now matters most. On $τ^2$-bench, across two open-weight model families in dense and MoE variants and two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights), quantization indeed looks free on the standard metric. No cell shows a score change that survives multiple-comparison correction, and in the cell that carries the largest process damage, equivalence testing bounds the change within $\pm$7.5 points. The process tells a different story. Quantization amplifies the failure the model already exhibits at full precision (tool-name hallucination in telecom, with the same directional trend in retail entity errors) by up to 2.5$\times$ in volume (+17.6 points per task), while creating essentially no new failures. The failure set is the same at every precision (rank correlation $\geq$ 0.94, 0.18% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbs the extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a score gap of 17 points, and it does so only in the one cell where quantization added error volume, exactly as the masking account predicts. A targeted error-repair prompt, run for five telecom models at every precision, removes the damage exactly and only where it lives. Both diagnostics, the per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking budget, come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward.

AI.tldr: Quantization of language models to 4-bit weights appears lossless on standard benchmarks, but actually amplifies specific existing failure patterns in multi-turn tool-calling agents without creating new failures.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to test the widely reported claim that post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is "nearly lossless" for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where accurate performance now matters most for practical applications.
AI.method: The researchers conducted comprehensive testing on the τ²-bench across two open-weight model families (dense and MoE variants) and two domains. They used 8 cells with 456 episodes each at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weight precision levels. They analyzed standard metrics, multiple-comparison correction, equivalence testing, per-channel error rates, and introduced a shrinking error budget diagnostic to reveal hidden quantization effects.
AI.result: Quantization looks "free" on standard metrics but actually amplifies existing failure patterns (like tool-name hallucination in telecom) by up to 2.5× in volume (+17.6 points per task) without creating new failures. The failure set remains consistent across precisions. Standard benchmarks hide this because their ten-error budget absorbs extra failures, but shrinking the budget to two errors exposes a 17-point score gap. A targeted error-repair prompt successfully removes the damage where it exists.
AI.conclusion: While 4-bit quantization appears lossless on standard benchmarks, it actually amplifies specific existing failure patterns in multi-turn tool-calling agents. Researchers should report additional diagnostics (per-channel error rates and success under shrinking error budgets) alongside task reward to reveal these hidden quantization effects that standard metrics mask.

title: Beyond the Bidirectional Promise: Re-evaluating the Robustness of Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) generation by enabling bidirectional context and iterative refinement. However, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored. To address this, we systematically evaluate DLM robustness and calibration against AR baselines, using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. This paired design effectively isolates architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors. We find a nuanced robustness profile: while highly stochastic DLM loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes, they provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, proving that everyday robustness is weight-dependent rather than inherently architectural. Furthermore, DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence, presenting a practical deployment hazard. Most crucially, mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility entirely to a decoder routing failure. Consistent with this diagnosis, we show that surface-level prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines. Ultimately, DLM robustness cannot be patched on; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

AI.tldr: DLMs offer iterative refinement but show concerning reliability issues: they provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, exhibit systematic overconfidence, and suffer from decoder routing failures despite perfectly encoding input corruption.
AI.motivation: Diffusion Language Models present an alternative to autoregressive generation but their robustness under natural noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored, creating deployment risks that need systematic evaluation.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation using two parameter-matched DLM/AR pairs across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses with paired design to isolate architecture-intrinsic properties.
AI.result: DLMs show nuanced robustness: resistant to gradient-based adversarial suffixes due to stochastic loss landscapes but no guaranteed defense against natural noise (weight-dependent). They exhibit systematic overconfidence and mechanistic probing reveals perfect input corruption encoding but decoder routing failures.
AI.conclusion: DLM robustness cannot be patched superficially; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop, as surface-level prompt interventions fail to address decoder routing failures that cause behavioral fragility.

title: APO: Unsupervised Atomic Policy Optimization for 3D Structure Prediction of Atomic Systems
summary: Predicting the 3D structures of atomic systems is fundamental to advancing material science and drug discovery. While flow-matching models (, FlowDPO) have recently shown promise in this domain, their performance relies heavily on alignment with ground-truth coordinates via supervised preference learning. However, obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive, creating a bottleneck for structural modeling in data-scarce regimes. In this work, we propose (Atomic Policy Optimization), a fully unsupervised alignment framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth reference structures. APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments, utilizing a novel dual-reward mechanism: (i) a that reinforces the policy's dominant latent structural modes through eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (ii) a that enforces thermodynamic stability. Our framework enables the model to ``self-correct'' by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups. Extensive benchmarks on crystal and antibody structure prediction demonstrate that APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving a new state-of-the-art in match rates and structural fidelity. Furthermore, we show that APO effectively straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency. Our results suggest that intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching.

AI.tldr: Atomic Policy Optimization (APO) introduces an unsupervised alignment framework for 3D atomic structure prediction that eliminates the need for ground-truth reference structures by using group-relative policy optimization with dual rewards for latent structural modes and thermodynamic stability.
AI.motivation: Current flow-matching models like FlowDPO rely on supervised preference learning with ground-truth coordinates, but obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive, creating a bottleneck for structural modeling in data-scarce regimes.
AI.method: APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments with a novel dual-reward mechanism: (1) a reward reinforcing the policy's dominant latent structural modes through eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (2) a reward enforcing thermodynamic stability, enabling the model to self-correct by identifying physically plausible configurations.
AI.result: Extensive benchmarks on crystal and antibody structure prediction show APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving state-of-the-art match rates and structural fidelity, while effectively straightening probability paths to improve inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic physical consistency serves as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy supervised coordinate matching, enabling effective unsupervised structural prediction without ground-truth references.

title: The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models
summary:
A capability appears in a language model when the last parts of its circuit align in one stochastic attempt, and getting all but one right is worth nothing. We show this no-partial-credit joint alignment is the rate-limiting step of capability formation. Two fingerprints: in a shortcut-free apparatus a five-part circuit missing three waits as long as a three-part circuit missing three (1.19-1.37), so the wait counts missing parts, not size; and on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales, ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in 32 of 32 discriminating cells, where partial credit predicts 50-83% (p = 2e-10), while a random non-part head leaves 100%.
  One rare event whose barrier grows with missing parts yields a rate equation -- sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K), minus destruction -- read three ways, each preregistered with frozen constants. Forward: a capability flat at baseline ignites at a step of our choosing once the mix passes a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below), and while still flat its arrival is datable from its precursor to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward: the delay to learn a withheld capability grows with waiting until, past a critical step, it never ignites -- yet validation loss falls smoothly throughout, so standard monitors are blind to it. We locate the damage (heads commit to the base data) and isolate the cure: re-initializing only the query-key slices restores learnability (6/6) while the value slices do nothing (0/6). We prove the mechanism in a controlled gated-attention model: occupation forces a deadline whose consequences need no mixing assumption. Completed: SGD's noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test, so we install one and anneal, melt and pin circuits on schedule. Scope: conjunction circuits in transformers to 1.4B.

AI.tldr: Capabilities in language models emerge suddenly when all necessary circuit components align simultaneously with no partial credit. This joint alignment is rate-limited, predictable, and can be manipulated to control capability emergence.
AI.motivation: To understand why capabilities in language models appear abruptly rather than gradually, and to identify the rate-limiting factors in capability formation to enable better prediction and control of model development.
AI.method: Analyzes capability emergence using: 1) Circuit ablation experiments showing no partial credit for incomplete circuits, 2) Rate equation modeling based on rare event theory, 3) Controlled manipulation of capability ignition timing, 4) Head-specific interventions on query-key vs value slices, and 5) Validation loss monitoring vs capability emergence tracking.
AI.result: Found strong evidence for no-partial-credit joint alignment: 1) Wait time depends only on missing parts, not circuit size, 2) Ablating one part leaves only 17% capability (vs 50-83% predicted), 3) Can precisely predict capability arrival timing (5% median error), 4) Discovered irreversible learning windows for capabilities, 5) Isolated damage mechanism to query-key slices and developed restoration method.
AI.conclusion: Capability formation in transformers is governed by rate-limited joint alignment with no partial credit, creating narrow learning windows that can be predicted and manipulated. Standard validation metrics miss these critical capability emergence events, requiring specialized monitoring and intervention strategies for effective model development.

title: Bridging Inference-Time Scaling and Episodic Memory with Action-Centric Graphs
summary: Recent advancements in inference-time scaling have significantly unlocked the complex reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models~(LLMs). However, for agents, these approaches suffer from a critical inefficiency, operating in a stateless manner and engaging in redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms largely rely on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, leading to prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, \textit{GAMER}~(Graph-based Action-centric Memory with Episodic Reasoning), that bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory. Our approach models historical reasoning as a dynamic \textit{Action-Centric Graph}. By decoupling the memory mechanism from LLMs, our method can save token/money usage by providing less memory context than memory mechanism baselines. To extract knowledge from the graph effectively, we use a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism to estimate the positive~(suggestion) and negative~(avoidance) value of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During the inference phase, this learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally, so that positive values provide action suggestions, while negative values indicate high-risk actions. By performing efficient searches on the graph, our method significantly improves the efficiency of inference scaling. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that \textit{GAMER} achieves superior performance by \textbf{20.81\%/6.17\%} for success/progress rate compared to vanilla baselines.

AI.tldr: GAMER is a novel framework that combines graph-based episodic memory with temporal difference learning to make agent reasoning more efficient by reducing redundant search processes and saving token usage.
AI.motivation: Existing inference-time scaling approaches for LLM agents are inefficient because they operate statelessly and engage in redundant search processes. Current memory mechanisms rely heavily on LLM reasoning, leading to prohibitive computational costs and token usage.
AI.method: The GAMER framework models historical reasoning as a dynamic Action-Centric Graph, decoupling memory from LLMs. It uses dual-stream Temporal Difference learning to estimate positive (suggestion) and negative (avoidance) values of action nodes based on past successes/failures. During inference, the learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally through efficient graph searches.
AI.result: Experiments show GAMER achieves superior performance with 20.81% improvement in success rate and 6.17% improvement in progress rate compared to vanilla baselines, while saving token/money usage by providing less memory context.
AI.conclusion: GAMER successfully bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory, enabling more efficient agent reasoning through graph-based action-centric memory with episodic reasoning, overcoming the inefficiencies of stateless approaches.

title: Benchmarking the Residual: What Long-Horizon Evaluations Add Beyond Matched Short-Task Performance
summary: Long-horizon benchmarks often show that agents fail more as tasks become longer. This observation is useful for deployment, but it does not by itself explain why failure occurs. More stages create more opportunities for ordinary errors to compound; longer tasks may also contain harder individual decisions or become harder as conversation history, tool outputs, and environment changes accumulate. We use trajectory-induced degradation to mean this last possibility: earlier execution makes later work harder. When the harmful accumulation is specifically the text visible to the model, it is often called context rot. In this position paper, we argue that to claim a "long-horizon failure", benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. We call the log-ratio between this prediction and actual success the horizon residual. The comparison must use the same agent configuration and specify in advance how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets will be chosen. The residual shows that the full rollout differs from the chosen baseline; targeted experiments are still needed to explain why.

AI.tldr: Researchers propose using "horizon residual" - comparing actual long-task success against predictions from short-stage performance - to properly identify long-horizon failures, arguing that current benchmarks don't explain why agents fail on longer tasks.
AI.motivation: Current long-horizon benchmarks show agents fail more as tasks become longer, but this doesn't explain why failures occur. The authors want to distinguish between failures due to error compounding versus "trajectory-induced degradation" (where earlier execution makes later work harder) or "context rot" (harmful text accumulation).
AI.method: Propose comparing actual full-task success against baseline predictions built from short, individual stages. This log-ratio comparison is called the "horizon residual." Requires using same agent configuration and specifying in advance how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets will be chosen.
AI.result: The horizon residual shows whether full rollout differs from the baseline prediction, helping identify true long-horizon failures rather than just observing that agents perform worse on longer tasks.
AI.conclusion: To claim a "long-horizon failure," benchmarks must use the horizon residual approach to distinguish between simple error compounding and trajectory-induced degradation. The residual indicates whether there's a difference from baseline, but targeted experiments are still needed to explain why.

title: Dimensionality and Measurement Precision in HLE's Multiple-Choice Subset
summary: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) is widely used to evaluate frontier language models. HLE organizes its questions into eight subject-domain categories, whose subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no study has assessed whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs, nor whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability. We evaluate 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE ($J = 428$ items) and apply psychometric methods to assess both the dimensionality of the benchmark and the distribution of its measurement precision. Fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, we find convergent evidence that HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's $ω_h = 0.998$, domain labels explain only 3.5\% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's $d = 0.016$), and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with the total score ($r \geq 0.81$). A separate analysis of the test information function reveals that measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above $θ= 0$, where frontier models sit. These findings suggest that HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations and that the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

AI.tldr: HLE benchmark measures a single general reasoning factor rather than distinct domain capabilities, and has limited precision for discriminating top-performing models.
AI.motivation: Despite HLE's widespread use to evaluate frontier language models, there's been no assessment of whether its domain categories correspond to empirically separable latent constructs or whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability.
AI.method: Evaluated 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE (428 items), applying psychometric methods including fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, analyzing dimensionality, and examining the test information function.
AI.result: HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's ω_h = 0.998, domain labels explain only 3.5% of item response variance, domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with total score (r ≥ 0.81), and measurement precision drops sharply above moderate ability levels where frontier models sit.
AI.conclusion: HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations, and the benchmark has limited ability to discriminate among the strongest models, suggesting the need for improved evaluation methods.

title: TIER-MoE: Trust-Informed Expert Routing via Conditional Modality Risk for Multimodal Fusion in Biomedical Classification
summary: The promise of multimodal fusion lies in combining complementary sources of evidence, yet more evidence does not always yield a better prediction. Recent multimodal models have advanced fusion through richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion. However, the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert. To address this limitation, we introduce TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model that defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is learned from out-of-fold predictions generated by models that were not trained on the corresponding sample. TIER-MoE combines the estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity. We evaluate TIER-MoE on four public multimodal biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification. Results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

AI.tldr: TIER-MoE introduces a risk-guided mixture-of-experts model that estimates modality reliability using prediction loss from out-of-fold unimodal predictors, enabling sparse modality-expert routing while maintaining multimodal complementarity.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal fusion models lack the ability to determine whether modalities are unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to specialized experts. Simply assigning influence to modalities doesn't reveal these critical reliability issues, which limits effective multimodal learning.
AI.method: TIER-MoE defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is learned from out-of-fold predictions by models not trained on the corresponding sample. The system combines estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while including an always-active shared path to preserve multimodal complementarity.
AI.result: TIER-MoE outperforms state-of-the-art methods on four public multimodal biomedical datasets (Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, retinal classification) in both predictive performance and probability calibration, showing consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score with strong zero-shot generalization to external cohorts.
AI.conclusion: TIER-MoE effectively addresses the limitation of current multimodal fusion approaches by explicitly modeling modality reliability through risk estimation, leading to superior performance across diverse biomedical applications while maintaining strong generalization capabilities.

title: Leveraging Trajectory Graphs for Pre-Execution Error Diagnosis in Agentic LLM Systems
summary: Large Language Model~(LLM)-based agents have demonstrated exceptional performance across a wide range of complex interactive tasks. However, they often struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks common in domains, such as embodied AI. The complexity and vast action spaces in these settings lead to compounding errors, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory, causing the agent to exhaust its limited step budget on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. To overcome this without costly fine-tuning, we draw inspiration from software debugging, where execution logs are analyzed to preemptively catch errors. We propose \textit{Trajectory Graph Copilot}, a novel framework that acts as a ``copilot'' for LLM agents by diagnosing potential action errors before they are executed. At its core,\textit{Graph Debugger} models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. Functioning as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, our method provides early warnings on potentially flawed actions, prompting the agent to self-correct. This pre-action error diagnosis prevents costly mistakes, significantly enhancing the agent's ability to complete long-horizon tasks successfully. The extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a $14.69\%$ pass ratio improvement on average.

AI.tldr: Trajectory Graph Copilot is a framework that uses graph neural networks to diagnose potential action errors before execution, helping LLM agents avoid compounding errors in long-horizon interactive tasks without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks (like embodied AI) due to compounding errors where single suboptimal actions derail entire trajectories, causing agents to exhaust limited step budgets on inefficient paths.
AI.method: The framework models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network (Graph Debugger) to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure, acting as a proactive diagnostic sandbox to provide early warnings on flawed actions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a 14.69% average improvement in pass ratio for long-horizon tasks.
AI.conclusion: The Trajectory Graph Copilot framework effectively prevents costly mistakes through pre-action error diagnosis, significantly enhancing LLM agents' ability to successfully complete long-horizon interactive tasks without requiring costly fine-tuning.

title: EvoCause: LLM-Guided Evolution of Causal Graphs for Root Cause Analysis
summary: Modern telecommunication, cloud, and microservice systems emit correlated alarm cascades when components fail. Root cause analysis (RCA) aims to identify the small set of alarms that initiate each cascade. A common approach learns a causal graph from observational logs and predicts all zero-in-degree alarms in each incident-induced subgraph. However, the learned graph remains fixed and cannot benefit from expert diagnoses of historical incidents. We close this loop with EvoCause. Expert labels constrain which alarms should be source nodes but do not specify the edge edits needed to satisfy those constraints. EvoCause uses a large language model (LLM) to propose semantically plausible graph edits, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity and retains the best graph on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph alone produces transparent predictions without an LLM call. We also release TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecommunication network containing $485{,}681$ alarm events spanning $194$ alarm types over $5{,}621$ resources. On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with the PC causal discovery algorithm outperforms the unrefined PC baseline, raising Node F1, Case EM, and Graph F1 by $11.59$, $9.40$, and $4.59$ percentage points, respectively, while reducing nSHD by $0.2379$. On TeleRCA, replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers lowers Node F1 and Case EM by $6.12$ and $8.04$ percentage points, respectively, indicating that alarm-name information contributes to graph refinement.

AI.tldr: EvoCause is a framework that integrates LLMs and causal graphs for root cause analysis, using expert labels to iteratively refine causal graphs without requiring test-time LLM calls.
AI.motivation: Existing causal graph approaches for root cause analysis remain static and cannot incorporate expert diagnoses of historical incidents, limiting their ability to improve accuracy over time.
AI.method: EvoCause uses LLMs to propose semantically plausible graph edits based on expert labels, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity. The system retains the best graph on a labeled alignment set, with the refined graph producing transparent predictions at test time without LLM calls.
AI.result: On synthetic data, EvoCause outperforms the unrefined PC baseline by raising Node F1, Case EM, and Graph F1 by 11.59, 9.40, and 4.59 percentage points respectively. On TeleRCA benchmark, removing alarm-name information reduces Node F1 and Case EM by 6.12 and 8.04 percentage points, showing semantic information contributes to graph refinement.
AI.conclusion: EvoCause effectively closes the loop between learned causal graphs and expert diagnoses, improving root cause analysis accuracy while maintaining interpretable, LLM-free predictions at inference time. The importance of semantic alarm information is demonstrated through performance degradation when using anonymous identifiers.

title: VAmoS Bench: Voice Agent Simulation Bench
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Agent implementations: https://github.com/veris-ai/riley-agent
summary: Production voice agents span cascaded, speech-to-speech, and hybrid architectures. Voice-agent benchmarks typically measure component quality and conversational properties such as word error rate, latency, naturalness, and turn-taking. Fewer measure whether the agent handled a phone call correctly on its own. Contact centers refer to this as ``containment'': the share of phone calls the automated system resolves without handing off to a human. On some phone calls the right outcome is refusal or a redirect. To address this gap, we introduce VAmoS Bench, the Voice Agent Simulation Bench. It measures complete voice-agent systems end to end in a stateful customer-support task. The agent is Riley, a credit-card support representative for a fictional bank who can freeze, cancel, replace, or activate a card. Each of 100 scenarios supplies a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. The platform uses each scenario to populate and activate an isolated simulation in which the caller reaches Riley over audio; roughly one-third apply adversarial pressure. The agent can use five tools that execute real SQL against the backend. Each scenario also defines binary assertions. A grader evaluates them against the complete trace of what the caller and agent said and what the agent did, including tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows. This catches an agent that claims to have changed a card without updating the database, as well as one that makes the right database change while disclosing protected information. This first benchmark version focuses on financial services. Its evaluation protocol supports an evolving leaderboard: additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version, while later versions can expand the tasks and scenarios.

AI.tldr: VAmoS Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating complete voice agent systems in customer support tasks, measuring whether they can autonomously handle phone calls without human handoff, with a focus on financial services scenarios.
AI.motivation: Current voice agent benchmarks focus on component quality metrics like word error rate, latency, and naturalness, but don't adequately measure whether the agent can actually handle phone calls correctly on its own. Contact centers refer to this as "containment" - the share of calls resolved without human handoff. There's a gap in evaluating complete voice-agent systems end-to-end in stateful customer support tasks.
AI.method: The VAmoS Bench simulates credit-card support scenarios for a fictional bank, with 100 scenarios featuring simulated callers with private goals. The agent (named Riley) can perform five operations using real SQL tools against a seeded PostgreSQL backend. The platform runs isolated simulations where callers interact with Riley over audio, with one-third applying adversarial pressure. A grader evaluates binary assertions against complete traces of conversations and agent actions (including tool invocations and database changes).
AI.result: The benchmark can detect various failure modes including: agents that claim to perform actions without updating databases, agents that make correct database changes while disclosing protected information, and general containment failures. The evaluation protocol supports an evolving leaderboard where additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version, with future versions expanding tasks and scenarios.
AI.conclusion: VAmoS Bench addresses a critical gap in voice agent evaluation by providing an end-to-end simulation framework that measures whether voice agents can autonomously handle real customer support tasks, with initial focus on financial services. It enables comprehensive assessment of containment capabilities beyond traditional component-level metrics.

title: THGFM: Dual-Branch Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Fusion Model
summary: Temporal heterogeneous graphs offer a natural abstraction for dynamic relational systems in which diverse node and relation types co-exist and evolve over time. Learning on such graphs requires jointly modeling cross-type structural heterogeneity and the temporal dynamics of interactions, yet existing methods still struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically inject time only as additive features outside the attention kernel. We propose \textbf{THGFM}, a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model that addresses both limitations within a unified dual-path architecture. THGFM couples a \textit{Shared-Space Temporal Attention} branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with a \textit{Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention} branch for relation-aware specialization, and integrates them through \textit{Dual-Path Relational--Shared Fusion}, instantiated with \textit{Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion}: a adaptive mechanism that assigns independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates to the shared and specialized branches, allowing both to be amplified or suppressed without zero-sum competition. To directly incorporate relative time into the attention score, THGFM further introduces \textit{Rotary Temporal Attention}, which rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching. THGFM consistently outperforms baseline graph transformer models on academic graphs benchmarks, delivering a $+3.25\%$ six-task mean gain, with peak relative gains of $+12.37\%$ on OAG-CS PV, $+4.87\%$ on PF-$L_2$, and $+1.18\%$ on PF-$L_1$, and $+4.24\%$, $+3.73\%$, and $+4.61\%$ on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP, respectively.

AI.tldr: THGFM is a temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model that uses dual-path architecture with shared-space attention for cross-type transfer and relation-partitioned attention for specialization, incorporating time directly into attention via rotary encoding.
AI.motivation: Existing methods struggle to balance parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization in temporal heterogeneous graphs, and typically treat time as additive features rather than integrating it into the attention mechanism.
AI.method: Dual-path architecture: (1) Shared-Space Temporal Attention for cross-type transfer, (2) Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention for specialization, fused via Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion. Uses Rotary Temporal Attention to directly incorporate relative time into attention scores.
AI.result: Outperforms baseline graph transformers with +3.25% mean gain across six tasks, with peak gains: +12.37% on OAG-CS PV, +4.87% on PF-L2, +1.18% on PF-L1, +4.24% on OGBN-MAG, +3.73% on HTAG-ArXiv, and +4.61% on HTAG-DBLP.
AI.conclusion: THGFM successfully addresses limitations of existing methods by reconciling cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization and directly integrating temporal dynamics into attention mechanisms, achieving state-of-the-art performance on temporal heterogeneous graph benchmarks.

title: Position, Not Provenance: Separating Reasoning Mediation from Sycophancy in Medical Vision-Language Models
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before answering clinical questions, but whether this reasoning causally influences predictions remains unclear. We present CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework that perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute within a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether the resulting prediction follows the edited reasoning. Our framework combines a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence with prefix-forced continuation, together with a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy. We evaluate LLaVA-Med and MedGemma on 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each. Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, while the provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Across both models, removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, whereas laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute. These results show that the mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness and that contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.

AI.tldr: A framework called CoT-Mediate evaluates whether medical vision-language models' chain-of-thought reasoning actually influences their predictions by perturbing clinical attributes in the reasoning and measuring if predictions follow the edits.
AI.motivation: Medical VLMs generate CoT reasoning before answering clinical questions, but it's unclear whether this reasoning causally influences their predictions or is just a form of sycophancy. The paper aims to determine if the generated reasoning actually mediates predictions.
AI.method: CoT-Mediate framework perturbs single clinically meaningful attributes in a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether predictions follow the edited reasoning. Uses dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence with prefix-forced continuation, plus provenance-controlled intervention to separate reasoning mediation from sycophancy.
AI.result: Evaluated LLaVA-Med and MedGemma on 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each. Prefix-forced continuation yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting. Provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, while laterality is least faithfully tracked attribute.
AI.conclusion: The mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness, and contextual position (rather than stated provenance) is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.

title: INCLAIR: Inception-Based Longitudinal Clinical Anomaly Detection with Informed Reasoning
summary: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important but difficult: abnormal evidence is often sparse, patient histories have unequal length, and expert explanations are costly. We propose INCLAIR, a framework that scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. Under stated within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score takes an order-$l$ U-statistic form, yielding a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independently of profile length. The same analysis shows that mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies by a factor set by the anomaly support and profile length, motivating validation-selected top-$k$ pooling. Across three clinical datasets, INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We further validate practical relevance through a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles, comparing INCLAIR's predictions and explanations against domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis. The results show that INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.

AI.tldr: INCLAIR is a framework for detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles that scores observations against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence, and generates natural-language explanations with limited expert supervision.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection in longitudinal clinical profiles is challenging due to sparse abnormal evidence, unequal patient history lengths, and high costs of expert explanations, creating a need for automated yet interpretable detection methods.
AI.method: INCLAIR uses a framework that scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at profile level, generates natural-language explanations, employs U-statistic-based variance decomposition, incomplete-subset approximation for computational efficiency, and validation-selected top-k pooling to handle localized anomalies.
AI.result: INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across three clinical datasets and demonstrates practical relevance through a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles, matching expert assessments supported by DNA analysis.
AI.conclusion: INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision by providing both accurate predictions and explainable natural-language justifications.

title: ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution
summary: We introduce ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. ZUNA1.1 is capable of reconstructing variable length sequences of up to 30s, with an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to reconstructing entire channels. We demonstrate that ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with our earlier ZUNA1 model, while being far more flexible and capable of handling a wide range of reconstruction tasks. ZUNA1.1 continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation, which is ubiquitously deployed in the MNE package. The ZUNA1.1 model is released open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

AI.tldr: ZUNA1.1 is a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder that flexibly reconstructs EEG signals of variable length (up to 30s), arbitrary EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and arbitrary temporal intervals, outperforming previous methods.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG signal reconstruction methods like spherical spline interpolation (commonly used in MNE package) have limitations in flexibility. There's a need for more versatile models that can handle various reconstruction tasks with different EEG channel configurations, temporal intervals, and signal lengths.
AI.method: ZUNA1.1 uses a diffusion autoencoder architecture with 380 million parameters. It's designed to reconstruct variable-length sequences (up to 30 seconds) with arbitrary numbers of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can handle arbitrary temporal intervals within channels as well as entire channel reconstruction.
AI.result: ZUNA1.1 performs at least as well as the earlier ZUNA1 model while being far more flexible. It substantially outperforms standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods like spherical spline interpolation. The model handles a wide range of reconstruction tasks that previous methods couldn't.
AI.conclusion: ZUNA1.1 represents a significant advancement in EEG signal reconstruction by providing unprecedented flexibility while maintaining or improving performance compared to existing methods. The model's open-source release under Apache 2.0 license facilitates broader adoption in neuroscience research.

title: MedLLM: An Open Medical Language Model at the Sub-Billion Scale
summary: Open medical language models have converged on a single scale: every widely used system runs at 7B parameters or more, leaving the sub-billion regime uncharacterized. We present MedLLM, an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained through a fully open three-phase pipeline: general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, a reference-guided medical corpus we release that is selected from general web data by embedding similarity to medical question-answering (QA) data, and preference-aligned fine-tuning combining SFT with direct preference optimization (DPO). Across medical benchmarks, MedLLM shows a pattern visible only at sub-billion scale: medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression but splits by task type. On context-grounded QA it comes within $2.9$pp of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses the instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines; on knowledge-recall QA it stays near the task floor on clinical-vignette MedQA yet significantly exceeds every 7B and sub-7B baseline on MedMCQA, indicating that where recall fails the constraint is model capacity rather than adaptation. This dissociation is masked at 7B, where both capabilities are present, and surfaces only when capacity is scarce.

AI.tldr: MedLLM is a surprisingly capable 0.1B-parameter medical language model that reveals a dissociation between medical QA tasks at sub-billion scale: it performs close to 7B models on context-grounded QA but struggles on knowledge-recall QA due to capacity limits rather than adaptation issues.
AI.motivation: Current open medical language models all operate at 7B+ parameters, leaving the sub-billion parameter regime unexplored. The researchers want to understand how medical competence behaves under extreme model compression and whether different medical tasks respond differently to capacity constraints.
AI.method: Three-phase open training pipeline: 1) General pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, 2) Domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb (a new medical corpus created by selecting web data based on embedding similarity to medical QA data), 3) Preference alignment combining supervised fine-tuning with direct preference optimization (DPO).
AI.result: MedLLM reveals task-specific responses to compression: On context-grounded QA, it performs within 2.9 percentage points of medically adapted 7B models. On knowledge-recall QA, it shows mixed results - performs poorly on MedQA but significantly exceeds all baselines on MedMCQA. This dissociation (context-grounded QA performing well while knowledge recall struggles) only appears at sub-billion scale and is masked at 7B.
AI.conclusion: Medical competence doesn't degrade uniformly under compression but splits by task type. When capacity is limited, context-grounded QA remains strong while knowledge-recall QA becomes constrained by model capacity rather than adaptation quality. This insight is only visible at sub-billion scale and suggests different medical tasks have different capacity requirements.

title: Modeling Decisions in Blockchain Analytics: A Leakage-Aware Evaluation of Tree-Based vs. Sequential Models
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 23rd International Conference on Modeling Decisions for Artificial Intelligence (MDAI 2026)
summary: Sybil bots are Ethereum actors that imitate legitimate users to extract airdrop rewards or influence governance. Recent Sybil detection methods increasingly use deep learning and treat blockchain activity as a quasi-linguistic sequence. However, complex sequence models are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. We ask whether and how organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots differ in the structural complexity of their transaction histories; whether sequential models outperform tree-based tabular models once leakage is reduced; whether transaction order or timing provides the stronger behavioral signal; and whether the resulting models are practical for low-latency deployment. Our approach to leakage-aware Sybil bot detection consists of a Blind-Spot protocol and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. The former eliminates shortcuts associated with high-signal contracts, whereas the latter models wallets using rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. We evaluate this approach on Ethereum actor classification by comparing Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines. We contribute a framework for leakage-aware Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. Our results demonstrate that, under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while providing lower latency and estimated energy use.

AI.tldr: TL;DR: Sybil bot detection on Ethereum faces challenges with computational expense and label leakage. The paper introduces a leakage-aware framework with Blind-Spot protocol and Transaction Grammar, showing that tree-based XGBoost outperforms complex sequence models when leakage is eliminated.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address two key problems in Ethereum Sybil bot detection: 1) Complex deep learning sequence models are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and 2) Their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts.
AI.method: The method consists of two main components: 1) A Blind-Spot protocol that eliminates shortcuts from high-signal contracts to prevent label leakage, and 2) A Transaction Grammar representation that models wallet behavior using rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. The approach compares Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines.
AI.result: Under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while providing lower latency and estimated energy use. The research shows that once leakage is reduced, tree-based tabular models actually beat sequential models.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a framework for leakage-aware Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation. It demonstrates that simpler tree-based models (XGBoost) are more practical and effective than complex sequence models for real-time Sybil bot detection when label leakage is properly addressed.

title: A dataset of rated conceptual arguments
summary: Large language models have improved rapidly on tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics and programming. Much less is known about their ability to reason about what we call conceptual questions: questions for which no ground truth is realistically accessible and no widely accepted resolution methodology exists, but on which progress can still be made by debating arguments. Most philosophical questions are of this kind, as are central components of questions in AI safety, decision theory, and social choice. Our approach is based on the view that while bottom-line conclusions on such questions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated far more reliably. We therefore introduce a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts, spanning topics from AI safety and decision theory to ethics and politics, with 1,458 ratings by six expert raters along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. We propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of models. Performance tracks general capability rankings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on conceptual/philosophical reasoning by assessing their ability to critique arguments on topics like AI safety, ethics, and decision theory where no ground truth exists.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations focus on tasks with verifiable answers (math, programming), but little is known about their ability to reason about conceptual questions where no ground truth exists but arguments can be debated. This is important for philosophical questions, AI safety, decision theory, and social choice.
AI.method: Create a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts across AI safety, ethics, politics, etc. Collect 1,458 expert ratings along dimensions like centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. Propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of LLMs.
AI.result: Performance of models on this conceptual reasoning benchmark tracks general capability rankings, suggesting that current LLMs' ability to reason about conceptual arguments correlates with their overall capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a new benchmark for evaluating LLMs on conceptual reasoning through argument critique, showing that performance aligns with general capability measures, and provides a foundation for assessing reasoning on philosophical/AI safety questions without ground truth.

title: Compression-Based Behavioral Similarity for Open-World Sybil Discovery on Ethereum
comment: Accepted as a full paper and scheduled for presentation at the European Conference on Advances in Databases and Information Systems (ADBIS 2026)
summary: Sybil attackers are Blockchain actors that adopt the characteristics of regular users to exploit airdrops or influence governance. Current methods of Sybil actor detection include constructing graphs, which requires token transfers between examined wallets. Machine learning algorithms have been employed as well, but they treat the task as a closed-set classification problem, making them vulnerable to frequent changes in attack strategies or evasion tactics. We address the following questions: can compression-based similarity differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links? What is the effect of high-signal contracts on the discovery of Sybils, and how robust are behavioral graphs under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations? Our approach synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) traces, capturing separately transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. The high-signal contracts are filtered with our own protocol, called the Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based NCD is used to construct a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery. We validate this framework against supervised machine learning baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests. Ultimately, we contribute a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery. Its core NCD primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. We position the method as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits, rather than as a formal open-set recognition system.

AI.tldr: A compression-based behavioral analysis method for detecting Sybil wallets in blockchain without requiring financial transaction links, using symbolic grammar and Gzip-based similarity measures.
AI.motivation: Current Sybil detection methods require financial transaction graphs or use closed-set ML classification that can't adapt to evolving attack strategies. Need for methods that work without direct funding links and are robust to temporal drift and adversarial evasion.
AI.method: Synthesize symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM traces capturing transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. Filter high-signal contracts using Blind-Spot Protocol. Use Gzip-based Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) to construct behavioral graphs for Sybil discovery without supervised training.
AI.result: Validated framework outperforms supervised ML baselines, demonstrates robustness against temporal splits and synthetic camouflage stress tests. Provides training-free local discovery primitive that can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links.
AI.conclusion: Compression-based similarity can differentiate Sybil bots from organic users without direct financial links. The leakage-aware behavioral framework serves as effective training-free discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits, positioned as local discovery tool rather than formal open-set recognition system.

title: Automated Transcript Analysis for Detecting Flaws in Agentic Benchmarks
summary: Capabilities of frontier models are often assessed using agentic benchmarks. To trust these results, benchmarks must accurately measure what they claim to and be free from invalidating flaws. Previous manual audits of benchmarks such as SWE-Bench-Verified have uncovered several validity issues in transcripts. However, manual review is difficult to scale, and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface flaws that compromise benchmark validity. In this paper, we developed AI scanners to detect four types of validity issues: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. We produced grading rubrics for each to instruct human labeling, and evaluated the scanners against human labels on a held-out test set of Inspect Evals benchmarks. Our scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. Not all cases were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria and models. We highlight several open challenges to be addressed to improve scanners for stronger quality assurance claims, including broader standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance. Together, these results serve as a proof of concept for using automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality more broadly.

AI.tldr: Automated AI scanners were developed to detect validity flaws in agentic benchmarks, identifying several quality issues in popular benchmarks but revealing performance variations and standardization gaps.
AI.motivation: There's a need to trust agentic benchmark results, but manual audits are difficult to scale. Previous manual reviews uncovered validity issues, but it's unclear if automated methods can reliably detect flaws that compromise benchmark validity.
AI.method: Developed AI scanners to detect four validity issue types: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. Created grading rubrics for human labeling and evaluated scanners against human labels on a held-out test set from Inspect Evals benchmarks.
AI.result: Scanners identified verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. Scanner performance varied across benchmarks, criteria, and models, and not all cases were identified.
AI.conclusion: Results serve as proof of concept for automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality. Open challenges remain in improving scanners for stronger quality assurance, including addressing broader standardization gaps in evaluation field that degrade scanner performance.

title: Explorative Modeling: Unlocking a Third Pretraining Axis and End-to-End Generation
summary: The deep learning revolution, kicked off by AlexNet, taught us that end-to-end training beats decomposing a problem into hand-designed stages. Generative modeling, however, has remained the exception-despite generative models being remarkably capable, they are still not trained end-to-end. This is because, at its core, generative modeling is about handling distributions with many modes, and existing scalable approaches handle this the same way, by factoring the generation procedure, which prevents end-to-end generation. In this work, we introduce Explorative Modeling, a new paradigm that instead factors the training loop, exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, and training on the best, so predictions commit to modes rather than blurring them. We find Explorative Models (XMs) useful in two settings. First, increasing exploration adds a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data for existing generative models-where scaling exploration monotonically improves performance across both continuous and discrete domains (images, video, and language). Notably, gains from exploration increase with scale, climbing from 7% to 36% as data scales and from 13% to 23% as models grow, with efficiency gains more than doubling at 3x the compute. Concretely, exploration improves FLOP efficiency by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, parameter efficiency by 47%, lifts the strongest of image-generation recipes to a near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, enables scaling how end-to-end existing models are, and unlocks scaling generalization. Second, XMs enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling, matching diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps. Together, these results establish XMs as both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm.

AI.tldr: Explorative Modeling factors the training loop instead of the generation procedure, enabling end-to-end training for generative models by exploring candidate matches between generations and data and training on the best.
AI.motivation: Despite deep learning's success with end-to-end training, generative modeling has remained an exception due to its need to handle multi-modal distributions. Current approaches factor the generation procedure, preventing true end-to-end generation.
AI.method: Introduces Explorative Modeling (XMs) which factors the training loop rather than the generation procedure. It explores K candidate matches between model generations and data, then trains on the best match, forcing predictions to commit to specific modes rather than blurring them.
AI.result: XMs add exploration as a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data, with scaling benefits: performance improves 7-36% with data scale, 13-23% with model growth, 4.1x FLOP efficiency, 6.2x sample efficiency, 47% parameter efficiency. Achieves 1.43 FID on ImageNet, matches diffusion performance with 16-256x fewer inference steps on control tasks.
AI.conclusion: Explorative Models establish both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm, addressing the fundamental challenge of multi-modal distribution handling in generative AI.

title: AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge
summary: As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles, are insufficient because they enforce a "consumer" orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance frames this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic "agents" rather than the training of competent consumers of AI-generated information.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current AI literacy frameworks focus too much on technical skills and responsible use, creating passive AI consumers rather than empowered agents. It proposes a critical AI literacy framework focused on evaluation, resistance to AI assumptions, and governance participation.
AI.motivation: As generative AI becomes central to knowledge production, questions about who can access and shape this production are crucial. Existing AI literacy frameworks are insufficient because they promote a consumer orientation rather than genuine epistemic agency, potentially reinforcing structural inequalities in AI access and influence.
AI.method: The paper draws on Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and digital literacy scholarship to reconceptualize AI literacy. It proposes a three-part framework focused on contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance.
AI.result: A reconceptualized AI literacy framework that positions individuals as epistemic agents rather than competent consumers, addressing how unequal access to AI tools recapitulates epistemic injustices and requiring literacy approaches that account for structural inequities.
AI.conclusion: AI literacy must evolve beyond technical competency and responsible use to become a critical practice that empowers individuals to evaluate AI systems, resist their assumptions, and participate in governance, thereby cultivating epistemic agency rather than training passive consumers.

title: The Convergence Behavior of Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise
summary: We establish the first convergence guarantees for the plain vector-form \emph{Adam} optimizer under heavy-tailed stochastic noise. While several Adam variants are known to achieve optimal iteration complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is understood about their behavior when stochastic gradients admit only a bounded $p$-th central moment for some $p \in (1,2]$, a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning. To address this gap, we generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise.
