Building on this generalized framework, we develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam, without restrictive parameter coupling. Our results show that Adam converges to $(ρ,ε)$-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise. However, it exhibits a suboptimal iteration complexity and $p$-dependent convergence, a suboptimality that persists even in the bounded-variance case ($p=2$). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, a standard setup in related literature, the convergence rate improves to match the optimal complexity. These findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes.

AI.tldr: Adam optimizer achieves convergence under heavy-tailed noise but exhibits suboptimal iteration complexity that depends on noise tail heaviness (p-value), even in bounded-variance cases.
AI.motivation: Current Adam variants achieve optimal iteration complexity under bounded-variance noise, but little is understood about their behavior when stochastic gradients admit only bounded p-th central moments for p ∈ (1,2], a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning with heavy-tailed noise.
AI.method: Generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise, and develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam without restrictive parameter coupling.
AI.result: Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise, but shows suboptimal iteration complexity and p-dependent convergence (even when p=2). When domain radius is known and used to control online-learner output, convergence rate improves to match optimal complexity.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides new theoretical insights into Adam's robustness and limitations in heavy-tailed regimes, showing it converges but with suboptimal complexity except in specific settings where domain radius is known.

title: Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation
summary: This research evaluates the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in generating new product ideas. To do so, we compare three pools of ideas for new products targeted toward college students and priced at 50 dollars or less. The first pool of ideas was created by university students in a product design course before the availability of LLMs. The second and third pools of ideas were generated by GPT-4 from OpenAI using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, respectively. We evaluated idea quality using standard market research techniques to predict average purchase intent probability. We used text mining to assess idea similarity and human raters to evaluate idea novelty. We find that AI-generated ideas outperform human-generated ideas in terms of average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting yielding slightly higher intent than zero-shot prompting. However, AI-generated ideas are perceived as less novel and exhibit higher pairwise similarity, particularly with few-shot prompting, indicating a less diverse solution landscape. When focusing on the quality of the best ideas rather than the average ideas, we find that AI-generated ideas are seven times more likely to rank among the top 10 percent of ideas, demonstrating a significant advantage over human-generated ideas. We propose that this seven-to-one advantage is a conservative estimate because it does not account for the greater productivity of AI. Our findings suggest that despite some drawbacks, AI creativity presents a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development.

AI.tldr: AI-generated product ideas outperform human ideas in purchase intent, especially for top ideas (7x more likely to be top 10%), but are less novel and diverse than human-generated ideas.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the efficacy of large language models in generating new product ideas by comparing AI-generated ideas with human-generated ideas in terms of quality, novelty, and diversity.
AI.method: Compared three pools of product ideas targeted at college students (<$50): (1) human-generated by university students, (2) GPT-4 zero-shot prompting, (3) GPT-4 few-shot prompting. Evaluated using market research techniques for purchase intent probability, text mining for similarity, and human raters for novelty.
AI.result: AI-generated ideas outperformed human ideas in average purchase intent (few-shot > zero-shot). However, AI ideas were perceived as less novel and had higher pairwise similarity (less diversity), especially with few-shot prompting. AI ideas were 7x more likely to rank among top 10% of ideas.
AI.conclusion: Despite drawbacks in novelty and diversity, AI creativity offers substantial benefits for generating high-quality new product ideas, with a significant advantage in producing top-performing concepts.

title: FunL2O: LLM-Guided Feature Function Design for Learning to Optimize
summary: Learning-to-optimize (L2O) methods accelerate repeated optimization by training models to predict solutions, warm starts, branching decisions, or other forms of solver guidance. A critical yet largely overlooked component of these pipelines is the feature function that maps problem instances to inputs for machine learning models. Existing L2O methods typically rely on hand-crafted features, making representation design manual and largely fixed across domains. We introduce FunL2O, the first unified framework for automating feature design through LLM-driven program evolution for L2O. In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions, while a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. We evaluate FunL2O on linear and quadratic programming tasks involving solution prediction and warm-starting, as well as on mixed-integer optimization tasks using GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search. Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. These results establish LLM-driven feature evolution as a general and effective approach to automating representation design in L2O.

AI.tldr: FunL2O is a framework that uses LLM-driven program evolution to automatically design feature functions for Learning-to-Optimize methods, outperforming hand-crafted features across various optimization tasks.
AI.motivation: Current L2O methods rely on manually designed feature functions that are domain-specific, labor-intensive, and largely fixed across different optimization problems. There's a need to automate the feature design process to improve generalization and reduce manual effort.
AI.method: FunL2O employs an LLM-driven program evolution framework similar to FunSearch. It uses a loop where an LLM proposes executable feature functions, and a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model while measuring downstream optimization performance. The framework is applied to both continuous (linear/quadratic programming) and discrete (mixed-integer optimization) tasks.
AI.result: Across linear programming, quadratic programming (solution prediction and warm-starting), and mixed-integer optimization tasks (GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search), the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. Results were consistent across four different LLMs tested.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven feature evolution represents a general and effective approach to automating representation design in Learning-to-Optimize methods, establishing FunL2O as the first unified framework for this purpose.

title: ECG-InterpBench: Benchmarking the Interpretability of ECG Foundation Models with Matched-Scale Sparse Autoencoders
comment: Research paper. Includes supplementary material and publicly available source code
summary: Existing benchmarks for electrocardiogram foundation models primarily evaluate downstream predictive performance, providing limited insight into whether their internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses. We introduce ECG-InterpBench, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations. ECG-InterpBench uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments and matches their capacity across models to enable controlled comparisons. We evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five standardized encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas comprising 75 exactly matched six-model comparison blocks. The benchmark evaluates complementary dimensions of representation interpretability, including sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility. The evaluation further quantifies patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sensitivity to the sparsity parameterization. The benchmark reveals that ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. The benchmark is accompanied by executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits. ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled and reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability.

AI.tldr: ECG-InterpBench is a new benchmark that systematically evaluates interpretability of ECG foundation models using standardized sparse autoencoders to enable controlled comparisons across multiple dimensions of representation interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing ECG foundation model benchmarks mainly focus on downstream predictive performance, providing limited insight into whether their internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses.
AI.method: Uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments with matched capacity across models. Evaluates six frozen ECG foundation models across five encoder depths, five dictionary widths, and three random seeds, creating 450-cell interpretability atlas with 75 exactly matched six-model comparison blocks.
AI.result: Reveals distinct interpretability profiles among ECG foundation models. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. Provides executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits.
AI.conclusion: ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled, reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability, offering insights into model decomposition, clinical interpretation, and reproducibility.

title: DeepResearch Agent System
summary: The DeepResearch Agent System is a large language model system engineered for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks. Built upon a sparse activation architecture with 30 billion total parameters of which only 3 billion are activated per token, the system achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple agent search benchmarks while delivering 3.2 times faster inference compared to dense counterparts of equivalent scale. The system supports a 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention mechanisms that yield 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches. A dual-mode reasoning engine provides both a ReAct paradigm for basic multi-step problem solving and an IterResearch mode for high-performance iterative research with up to 20 reasoning steps, collectively delivering a 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines. Multi-tool coordination integrates retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing modules to achieve 92.1% tool-use accuracy. A reinforcement learning optimization framework based on the GRPO algorithm provides token-level policy gradients that improve training stability by 35% and accelerate convergence by 42%. An automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion achieves a 92.5% usability rate. Benchmark results include 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA. The system is fully open-sourced, including data synthesis, training, and inference code, and supports applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D support, and education.

AI.tldr: DeepResearch Agent System is an efficient 30B parameter sparse LLM for autonomous research with hierarchical attention, dual-mode reasoning, multi-tool coordination, and RL optimization, achieving SOTA on agent benchmarks while being 3.2x faster than dense models.
AI.motivation: To create an efficient large language model system for deep information retrieval and autonomous research tasks that balances performance with computational efficiency, addressing the limitations of dense models and standard long-context approaches.
AI.method: Sparse activation architecture (30B total params, 3B activated/token), hierarchical attention for 128K context, dual-mode reasoning (ReAct + IterResearch with up to 20 steps), multi-tool coordination modules, RL optimization with GRPO algorithm, and automated data synthesis pipeline.
AI.result: Achieves 3.2x faster inference than dense counterparts, 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements for long contexts, 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines, 92.1% tool-use accuracy, 35% better training stability, 42% faster convergence, and benchmark scores of 87.3% on HLE, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA.
AI.conclusion: The DeepResearch Agent System demonstrates that sparse activation architectures with hierarchical attention, dual-mode reasoning, and comprehensive tool integration can achieve state-of-the-art autonomous research capabilities with superior efficiency, and its open-source release enables broad applications in research, business, and education.

title: Context-Informed Ship Trajectory Prediction via Conditional Attention
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 29th International Conference on Information Fusion (IEEE FUSION)
summary:
Long-term ship trajectory prediction is a fundamental capability for maritime safety and autonomous navigation. While recent Transformer-based architectures have improved forecasting horizons, they predominantly rely on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system. In reality, maritime navigation is profoundly modulated by extrinsic factors like weather and constrained by static vessel characteristics. Existing multimodal approaches fundamentally model the joint distribution over states and contexts, treating environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions.
  In this work, we propose the Conditional Informer, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that formulates trajectory prediction as a conditional generation task. We employ a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates - but is not generated by - vessel dynamics. Furthermore, to address the intermittency of real-world data, we introduce a Modality Masking training strategy to prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback. Extensive experiments on AIS and ERA5 data demonstrate that our approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Crucially, Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

AI.tldr: A novel Conditional Informer architecture for ship trajectory prediction that uses conditional attention to model weather's physical influence on vessel dynamics, with modality masking to handle intermittent sensor data.
AI.motivation: Existing ship trajectory prediction models treat vessel motion as isolated from environmental factors, or treat weather and vessel data as peer features rather than encoding the physical reality that weather modulates vessel dynamics but is not generated by them. Real-world data also suffers from sensor intermittency issues.
AI.method: Proposes Conditional Informer encoder-decoder architecture with Conditional Attention mechanism where vessel state queries environmental contexts via cross-attention. Also introduces Modality Masking training strategy to handle sensor fallback and prevent catastrophic degradation during data intermittency.
AI.result: Outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning and reduces fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.
AI.conclusion: The Conditional Informer successfully models the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions rather than treating them as joint features, and Modality Masking effectively handles real-world data intermittency challenges, providing more robust and accurate long-term ship trajectory prediction.

title: What makes prompts a graph: necessary and sufficient conditions for prompt graph engineering
summary: Prompts stopped being isolated strings some time ago. In real systems, one model call feeds another, retrieval interleaves with generation, routers branch, and aggregators merge parallel results. Practice converged on a single structure to hold this together: the graph. Frameworks such as LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow expose it openly, and research systems already optimize it automatically. The vocabulary, however, lags behind. Graph names, variously, a reasoning topology inside one sampling strategy, a multi-agent conversation, or an orchestration artifact, while prompt engineering still evokes writing one good string. What is missing is a reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph. We build that definition through conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, complemented by primary grey literature. We reconstruct the genealogy of the idea, from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and the thought topologies (chain, tree, graph), to graphs compiled and optimized as artifacts. We then propose a constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering, state its four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), and operationalize them as an inclusion and exclusion test. We draw the boundary against six neighboring concepts and apply the test to six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents); it includes and excludes consistently. We close with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes. The contribution is an operational definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces 'prompt graph engineering' as a formal concept for designing AI systems where prompts are interconnected nodes in executable, improvable graphs rather than isolated strings.
AI.motivation: Current vocabulary lags behind industry practice where prompts are interconnected in complex workflows (graphs) in systems like LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow, but prompt engineering still focuses on isolated strings rather than these interconnected structures.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis through sources with persistent identifiers and primary grey literature, reconstructing the idea's genealogy from dataflow graphs through prompt chaining to optimized graphs, then proposing constitutive definition with four conditions and operational test.
AI.result: Proposes prompt graph engineering definition with four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure/prompt content, executable semantics, graph as first-class artifact), operational test, boundary against six neighboring concepts, and consistent application to six real systems.
AI.conclusion: Provides operational definition and shared vocabulary for industry practice, establishes prompt graph engineering as distinct concept, and outlines research agenda along four design tension axes.

title: Good Rankers, Bad Objectives: Bilinear Contrastive Critics under Expressive Policy Search
summary: Good action rankings do not make a contrastive critic safe to maximize. These critics increasingly act as value-like objectives for best-of-$K$ selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. Unbounded bilinear scores can let large embedding norms inflate off-support values, but cosine bounding does not remove the failure. A controlled support decomposition attributes most raw bilinear regret to norm drift. Cosine and hybrid critics nevertheless select off-support actions from most pools and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across four OGBench navigation tasks, and they fail to order fixed-query actions by value. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in a parameter-matched function-class control. Realized costs depend on the task: simulator rollouts reveal single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-$Q^*$ toy but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze, where the controller can self-correct. A training/readout decomposition traces the lost ordering to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. Candidate maximization can therefore exploit false positives caused by norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

AI.tldr: Contrastive critics fail as value-calibrated objectives for action selection due to norm drift and weak ordering, while Bellman-trained critics succeed.
AI.motivation: Contrastive critics are increasingly used as value-like objectives for action selection (best-of-K, planning, generation), but their safety and reliability for maximization needs rigorous evaluation.
AI.method: The study conducts controlled experiments with support decomposition analysis, comparing contrastive critics (bilinear, cosine, hybrid) against Bellman-trained TD-Q on four OGBench navigation tasks, with simulator rollouts to measure realized costs and training/readout decomposition analysis.
AI.result: Contrastive critics show weak calibration/inverted ordering in top score decile, fail to order actions by value, with most regret attributed to norm drift. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in parameter-matched control. Realized costs vary by task (single-step costs on PointMaze, null results on AntMaze/HumanoidMaze).
AI.conclusion: Contrastive critics are useful compatibility rankers but unsafe for action selection maximization due to norm drift, score saturation, and misranking issues; action selection requires value-calibrated scalar objectives.

title: From Minds to Models: The Intersection of Psychology and LLM Behaviours
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are often compared with the human mind because their decision-making is complex, non-linear and difficult to interpret. Psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes may therefore help examine LLM behaviour, particularly in government and healthcare. Building on prompt-based adaptations of the Implicit Association Test, this study tested whether ChatGPT produced sentiment differences across racial conditions in open-ended text. Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts. Each was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4 and GPT-4T, yielding 378 responses. Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores: positive labels retained the source score, negative labels were assigned its negative, and neutral responses were coded zero. A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044, but no effect of model, F(2, 351) = 0.07, p = .933, and no interaction, F(16, 351) = 0.23, p = .999. However, the effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, F(8, 351) = 1.53, p = .145, and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant, but was selected post hoc and is reported only as hypothesis-generating. Evidence for sentiment differences was therefore weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring also cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by a prompt. We outline design changes needed to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.
  Keywords: Implicit Bias, Psychological Research Methods, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Large Language Models, Sentiment Analysis

AI.tldr: This study uses psychological methods from implicit bias research to test whether ChatGPT shows racial sentiment differences in open-ended text responses. While initial analysis found small racial effects, these were not robust in sensitivity analyses, showing weak evidence of bias.
AI.motivation: Since large language models (LLMs) exhibit complex, non-linear decision-making similar to human cognition, the authors propose using psychological methods developed to study unobservable mental processes to investigate LLM behavior, particularly for sensitive applications like government and healthcare where bias detection is crucial.
AI.method: The study adapted psychological testing methods by crossing 14 base questions with 8 racial categories and a race-agnostic control (126 prompts total). Each prompt was submitted to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, and GPT-4T (378 responses). Sentiment scoring was based on categorical labels with positive labels keeping source scores, negative labels assigned negative scores, and neutral responses coded as zero. Analysis used two-way ANOVA followed by sensitivity analysis with rank transformation and Tukey-corrected comparisons.
AI.result: Initial ANOVA showed a small main effect of racial condition (F=2.04, p=.042, partial-eta squared=.044) but no effect of model or interaction. However, this effect disappeared in rank-transformed sensitivity analysis (F=1.53, p=.145) and no significant pairwise differences were found with Tukey corrections. Only an uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant but was selected post hoc.
AI.conclusion: Evidence for racial sentiment differences in ChatGPT was weak and analysis-dependent. The study highlights limitations of sentiment scoring (cannot distinguish evaluative bias from historical content valence) and calls for interdisciplinary development of better behavioral measures of model bias with improved study designs.

title: SE(3)-MeanFlow: Few-Step Protein Backbone Generation on Lie Groups
summary: Generative modeling of protein backbones promises the de novo design of proteins with prescribed structural and functional properties. Existing diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality backbones on SE(3)^N, but inference requires numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving a Lie group exponential map - a bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns. We introduce SE(3)-MeanFlow, a few-step generative framework that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the Lie group geometry of protein frames. Working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and in R^3, we derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, giving simulation-free training targets. We further introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch and serves as a warm-up stage, after which training switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss that is used for the remainder of pretraining and for rectification-based post-training. In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps, and its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget - at a modest cost in diversity.

AI.tldr: SE(3)-MeanFlow is a fast protein backbone generation method that extends MeanFlow to Lie group geometry, enabling few-step inference without numerical ODE integration by deriving closed-form velocity identities and using rectification-based post-training.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion and flow-matching models for protein backbone generation require numerically integrating ODEs over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving computationally expensive Lie group exponential maps. This creates a bottleneck for high-throughput protein design campaigns where fast inference is crucial.
AI.method: Extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to SE(3) Lie group geometry of protein frames. Works natively in Lie algebra so(3) and R^3, deriving closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations for simulation-free training. Uses SE(3) alpha-Flow objective to remove Jacobian-vector product from rotation branch as warm-up, then switches to small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss for pretraining and rectification-based post-training.
AI.result: In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps. The advantage widens in few-step regime where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget, though with modest cost in diversity.
AI.conclusion: SE(3)-MeanFlow provides an efficient generative framework for protein backbone design that significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining or improving quality compared to existing methods, enabling practical high-throughput protein design applications.

title: Wiring diagram extraction and gluing: a case study in classifying figure skating jumps using 3D dataset
summary: Hasse clustering is an algorithm that extracts common patterns in sequential data and represents them in graphical forms. As the number of expected clusters grows, however, the algorithm can become infeasible to run due to combinatorial complexity. In this article, we describe a theory of gluing wiring diagrams, allowing iterative applications of Hasse clustering to achieve the same result as a single application. We test our theory in the context of classifying videos of figure skating jumps.

AI.tldr: Hasse clustering algorithm becomes computationally infeasible as clusters grow; authors develop gluing theory to enable iterative applications instead of single application, tested on figure skating jump videos.
AI.motivation: Hasse clustering algorithm extracts patterns from sequential data but becomes computationally infeasible when the number of expected clusters grows due to combinatorial complexity.
AI.method: Developed a theory of gluing wiring diagrams to enable iterative applications of Hasse clustering that achieve the same results as a single application.
AI.result: The theory was tested and validated in the context of classifying videos of figure skating jumps.
AI.conclusion: The gluing theory successfully addresses the computational complexity problem of Hasse clustering by enabling iterative applications that maintain result equivalence to single applications, making the algorithm feasible for larger clustering tasks.

title: Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Channel Modeling in Low-SNR Regimes
summary: Accurate multipath parameter estimation is critical for modern wireless communication systems, particularly in challenging low-SNR environments. Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation algorithms, such as CLEAN, provide high-resolution parameter extraction but suffer from prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search. Conversely, purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and struggle to generalize across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN), a hybrid framework that embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. By replacing the exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable forward passes while delegating residual subtraction to exact mathematical models, NN-CLEAN isolates physical multipath parameters without accumulating non- physical errors. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching the traditional Grid-Search CLEAN (GS- CLEAN) baseline, while providing a massive reduction in computational complexity and substantially outperforming subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. Crucially, NN-CLEAN exhibits a near-flat scaling in execution runtime and memory consumption as batch sizes increase. This highly efficient parallelization establishes NN-CLEAN as a robust, real- time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems.

AI.tldr: NN-CLEAN is a hybrid neural network-assisted CLEAN algorithm that combines deep learning with traditional maximum likelihood estimation to achieve high-accuracy multipath parameter estimation with dramatically reduced computational complexity compared to exhaustive grid search methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation algorithms like CLEAN have prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search, while purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and struggle with generalization across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters.
AI.method: A hybrid framework called Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN) that embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. It replaces exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable neural network forward passes while delegating residual subtraction to exact mathematical models, preventing accumulation of non-physical errors.
AI.result: NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching traditional Grid-Search CLEAN baseline. It provides massive reduction in computational complexity and substantially outperforms subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. The method exhibits near-flat scaling in execution runtime and memory consumption as batch sizes increase.
AI.conclusion: NN-CLEAN establishes itself as a robust, real-time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems, offering the accuracy of traditional maximum likelihood methods with the computational efficiency of neural networks through effective parallelization and hybrid design.

title: World Action Planner: Generalizable Decision-Making with Action-Conditioned World Models
summary: Building generalizable agents for diverse applications remains a fundamental challenge. While imitation learning-based policies succeed in specific training environments, they often fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks. In this work, we propose World Action Planner, a robot planning system that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and the physical grounding of a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model. Our system enables an agent to propose initial action plans and iteratively refine them via optimization and search, reasoning over imagined world model rollouts. We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as VLAs and WAMs. Project website at worldactionplanner.github.io

AI.tldr: World Action Planner: A robot planning system combining VLMs for reasoning with world models for physical grounding, enabling iterative plan refinement through imagined rollouts for superior generalization.
AI.motivation: Building generalizable agents for diverse applications is challenging. Imitation learning-based policies succeed in specific training environments but fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks.
AI.method: Leverages Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for reasoning capabilities and multi-task pose-image conditioned world model for physical grounding. The system enables agents to propose initial action plans and iteratively refine them via optimization and search, reasoning over imagined world model rollouts.
AI.result: Achieves superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios. Significantly outperforms state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as VLAs and WAMs.
AI.conclusion: World Action Planner demonstrates an effective approach for building generalizable robotic agents by combining high-level reasoning from VLMs with physical grounding from world models, enabling robust generalization through iterative planning and refinement.

title: FADEx: Feature Attribution and Distortion-based Explanation of Dimensionality Reduction
comment: 18 pages, 17 figures, to be published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
summary: Dimensionality Reduction (DR) is a fundamental tool for high-dimensional data exploration, reducing the complexity of latent spaces of machine learning models, and assisting in the explanation of complex opaque models. However, non-linear DR techniques often function as opaque transformations themselves, making it challenging to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in the reduced space. This lack of transparency complicates the analysis and interpretation of structural patterns, hindering the ability to reason about the organization of high-dimensional data based on the projected layout. In order to address this challenge, dimensionality reduction explanation methods have shown promise in improving the understanding of the observed groups and cluster structures. Unfortunately, existing DR explanation approaches tend to suffer from limitations such as multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific dimensionality reduction methods, which hinder their use. In this work, we propose FADEx, a novel local per-instance feature attribution method that leverages local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition to provide explanations. FADEx computes the local linear models via weighted least squares, eliminating the need for out-of-sample data mapping, making it agnostic to the DR method, while simultaneously providing local feature attributions and distortion analysis. Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, we demonstrate FADEx's effectiveness and versatility in providing explanations and analytical resources for analyzing the behavior of DR methods. The results indicate FADEx yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.

AI.tldr: FADEx is a new feature attribution method for explaining dimensionality reduction (DR) techniques that uses local linear approximation and SVD to provide per-instance explanations without needing out-of-sample mapping.
AI.motivation: Non-linear dimensionality reduction methods are often opaque transformations, making it hard to understand how individual features influence data positioning in reduced spaces and complicating interpretation of structural patterns. Existing DR explanation methods have limitations like multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific DR techniques.
AI.method: FADEx uses local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). It computes local linear models via weighted least squares to eliminate the need for out-of-sample data mapping, making it agnostic to the DR method while providing both local feature attributions and distortion analysis.
AI.result: Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, FADEx demonstrates effectiveness and versatility in providing explanations and analytical resources for analyzing DR behavior. It yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.
AI.conclusion: FADEx represents a novel local per-instance feature attribution method that addresses limitations of existing DR explanation approaches by being DR method-agnostic, providing single attributions per feature, and offering both feature importance and distortion analysis capabilities for better interpretability of dimensionality reduction results.

title: CORE: In-Context Reconstruction for Unified Tabular Anomaly Detection
summary: Tabular anomaly detection (TAD), which focuses on identifying abnormal samples that deviate from the majority in tabular data, has received growing attention. Recently, there has been an emerging trend towards unified TAD, which seeks to detect anomalies across different datasets using a single generalizable model. In unified TAD, aligning heterogeneous data remains challenging. While existing methods often rely on distance-based unified feature construction, they may obscure the semantics of the original features. Moreover, existing approaches typically formulate anomaly detection as a binary classification task, which may overlook diverse anomaly patterns from various datasets and be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies. To address these challenges, we propose an in-COntext REconstruction approach for unified TAD (CORE for short). It introduces a decorrelated feature alignment module to directly align heterogeneous features into a unified representation space, which retains their semantic information. Meanwhile, CORE formulates unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem, eliminating the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies. Specifically, the in-context reconstruction module reconstructs each sample by leveraging contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, such that reconstruction errors reflect its deviation from normality, facilitating unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets.

AI.tldr: CORE proposes an in-context reconstruction approach for unified tabular anomaly detection that aligns heterogeneous features while preserving semantics and eliminates the need for labeled anomalies by reconstructing samples using contextual normal data.
AI.motivation: Current unified TAD methods face two main challenges: 1) distance-based feature alignment obscures original feature semantics, and 2) treating anomaly detection as binary classification overlooks diverse anomaly patterns and can be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies.
AI.method: CORE introduces two key modules: 1) a decorrelated feature alignment module that directly aligns heterogeneous features into a unified representation space while retaining semantic information, and 2) an in-context reconstruction module that reconstructs each sample using contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions.
AI.result: The method enables unified anomaly detection on arbitrary unseen datasets by using reconstruction errors to reflect deviations from normality, eliminating the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies.
AI.conclusion: CORE provides a more effective approach to unified tabular anomaly detection that preserves feature semantics and handles diverse anomaly patterns through in-context reconstruction rather than binary classification.

title: Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring
summary: The information flow in the graph neural networks (GNNs) is fundamentally constrained by over-squashing, where structural bottlenecks impede long range information propagation. Graph-rewiring methods, which modify graph topology, have been extensively used to alleviate this. However, existing approaches often introduce prohibitive structural and computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve the critical properties of original graphs, and increase the edge counts massively. We introduce a novel method Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring , a group-theoretic rewiring method that augments the input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group. Our method provides theoretical guarantees, a graph that exhibits spectral gap and a bounded effective resistance, creating a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

AI.tldr: SCGR is a novel graph rewiring method based on group theory that creates low-resistance bypasses for long-range communication in GNNs by augmenting graphs with Schreier-Coset graphs from special linear groups.
AI.motivation: Graph Neural Networks suffer from over-squashing where structural bottlenecks impede long-range information propagation. Existing graph-rewiring methods introduce prohibitive structural/computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve original graph properties, and massively increase edge counts.
AI.method: Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring (SCGR) - a group-theoretic method that augments input graphs with Schreier-Coset graphs derived from special linear groups. This creates low-resistance bypasses for long-range communication while providing theoretical guarantees.
AI.result: SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy. The method produces graphs with spectral gaps and bounded effective resistance.
AI.conclusion: SCGR provides an effective solution to over-squashing in GNNs through group-theoretic graph rewiring that creates low-resistance communication paths while preserving critical graph properties and avoiding excessive edge inflation.

title: Hidden APIs in Language Models: Discovering Reusable Causal Interfaces from Forked Futures
summary: Identical language-model answers can arise from hidden states that support different future computations, so current-answer probes do not establish a reusable internal interface. We introduce forked futures: future operations are sampled only after a prefix state has formed, and states are compared through the response distributions induced by those operations. This yields an empirical causal quotient over hidden states without requiring researcher-specified latent labels. Shared, Local, Mixture, and Distributed interfaces then compete under prequential causal description length subject to future-signature fidelity and matched capacity constraints. In the two detailed model evaluations, Shared has the lowest held-out description length, with gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B, while maintaining tightly clustered mean future-signature distortion; a five-backbone sweep preserves the positive direction of Sharedness Gain. The figure-aligned transplantation analysis gives Shared the strongest joint target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite profile, and API-aligned paths mediate 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for matched null paths. In the blind four-class model-organism test, 14/16 architectures are recovered, with one observed non-Shared to Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms. These results support an economical reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks, while keeping the claim explicitly conditional on the candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "forked futures" methodology to empirically compare hidden states in language models through future response distributions, identifying Shared interfaces as the most economical reusable causal interface.
AI.motivation: Current methods for probing language model hidden states don't establish reusable internal interfaces because identical answers can arise from states supporting different future computations. There's a need for an empirical method to compare hidden states without requiring researcher-specified latent labels.
AI.method: Introduces "forked futures": sample future operations only after a prefix state has formed, then compare states through response distributions induced by those operations. Four interface types (Shared, Local, Mixture, Distributed) compete under prequential causal description length with future-signature fidelity and matched capacity constraints.
AI.result: Shared interfaces achieved lowest held-out description length: gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B while maintaining tight future-signature distortion. Shared also showed strongest joint target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite profile. In blind tests, 14/16 architectures were correctly recovered with only one classification error among non-Shared organisms.
AI.conclusion: The results support an economical reusable causal interface within tested operation banks, though the claim remains explicitly conditional on candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures. The forked futures methodology provides empirical causal quotient over hidden states without requiring researcher-specified latent labels.

title: Latent States in Neural Networks: Recovering the Temporal Structure of Drifting Data from Model Weights
summary: A temporally drifting data stream may pass through discrete regimes rather than changing continuously. We ask whether such regimes are recoverable from the weights of models trained on the stream, using a hidden Markov model (HMM) fit to the chronologically ordered trajectory of those weights. We study this question in two domains known to drift over time: multimodal misinformation detection, using the Fakeddit dataset; and sentiment analysis, using the Yelp dataset. We train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows and fit an HMM to the trajectory of their aligned weights, recovering latent states that partition each timeline into coherent phases. On both datasets, classifiers generalize better to data from windows sharing the state of their training window than to windows across state boundaries. This within-state transfer advantage survives a control for temporal proximity and modestly exceeds the advantage recovered by a naive partition into contiguous states of equal size. Although the states are estimated solely from model weights, they correlate more strongly with shifts in the data's class distribution than with the weight-space geometry used to estimate them. After class divergence and lag are residualized out, the within-state advantage exceeds its permutation null on both tasks, indicating that the states recover structure relevant to transfer beyond the data distribution. Every effect replicates on both tasks but is attenuated on Yelp, whose label distribution is more temporally stable.

AI.tldr: A method using Hidden Markov Models on model weight trajectories can recover latent states in drifting data streams, improving generalization within states beyond what can be explained by temporal proximity or class distribution shifts alone.
AI.motivation: Data streams often drift over time in discrete regimes rather than continuously, and it's unclear whether these latent regimes can be recovered from the weights of models trained sequentially on the stream. The authors want to determine if these regimes are recoverable and whether they correspond to meaningful partitions for model generalization.
AI.method: Train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows of drifting data, then fit a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to the chronological trajectory of aligned model weights. This recovers latent states that partition the timeline. Test generalization by evaluating classifiers on data from windows sharing the same state versus across state boundaries, controlling for temporal proximity.
AI.result: Classifiers generalize better within the same recovered state than across state boundaries, even after controlling for temporal proximity. This within-state transfer advantage modestly exceeds naive contiguous partitioning and survives permutation testing after residualizing out class distribution divergence and lag effects. States correlate more with data class distribution shifts than weight-space geometry.
AI.conclusion: HMMs applied to model weight trajectories can recover meaningful latent states in drifting data streams that improve generalization. These states capture structure relevant to transfer beyond just data distribution shifts, though effects are attenuated when label distributions are more stable over time.

title: SCOPE: Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization
comment: 43 pages; Kiet, Duc, and Bang contributed equally
summary: Black-box combinatorial optimization requires systematically identifying high-quality solutions under a limited evaluation budget, yet the unknown objective function provides little guidance for deciding where the search should explore next. We introduce SCOPE, a general framework for Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization. Rather than directly optimizing the inaccessible objective, SCOPE learns a set of synthetic objectives conditioned on the accumulated search history, where each objective is designed to expose a distinct and potentially useful preference over candidate solutions. These objectives are then used to evolve search policies that generate diverse candidates, whose true quality is subsequently assessed through black-box evaluations. The outer loop adaptively updates and selects synthetic objectives according to how effectively their induced policies discover promising regions. In contrast, the inner loop returns a portfolio of top-performing policies to reduce the risk of relying on a single surrogate preference. This formulation reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling the search process to exploit observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.

AI.tldr: SCOPE introduces a framework for black-box combinatorial optimization that learns synthetic objectives to guide policy evolution, improving search performance under limited evaluation budgets.
AI.motivation: Black-box combinatorial optimization suffers from limited guidance in search exploration due to unknown objective functions, making it challenging to identify high-quality solutions under evaluation budget constraints.
AI.method: SCOPE learns synthetic objectives conditioned on search history, each exposing distinct preferences over candidates. These objectives evolve search policies generating diverse solutions. An outer loop adaptively updates objectives based on policy effectiveness, while an inner loop returns a portfolio of top policies to reduce risk.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems show SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.
AI.conclusion: SCOPE successfully reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling exploitation of observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity in discrete solution spaces.

title: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Collider Physics with Multi-Domain Adaptation
summary: We present a lightweight approach to foundation modeling (\textbf{NEXUS}) that leverages pre-trained learning from collider physics data towards out-of-domain tasks in other scientific datasets, using a fully connected autoencoder model with approximately 3 million parameters. The model pre-trains with no supervision over a large-scale collision dataset from the Large Hadron Collider modeled by charged particle track features. Downstream tasks for collider analyses, such as kinematic regression and event classification, are developed on pre-trained model weights and achieve improved accuracy with only small labeled datasets when compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch. The benefits of pre-training are additionally investigated through latent space interpretation and application to other domains, including gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity. Furthermore, the relative computational simplicity of NEXUS is demonstrated compared to transformer approaches at comparable scale, opening the door to power-efficient inference and real-time or edge applications of foundation models in scientific experiments.

AI.tldr: NEXUS is a lightweight foundation model that uses a fully connected autoencoder (3M parameters) pre-trained on LHC particle collision data without supervision, achieving improved accuracy on downstream collider physics tasks and showing transfer learning capabilities to other scientific domains.
AI.motivation: To create a computationally efficient foundation model for scientific data that can leverage unsupervised pre-training on collider physics data and transfer to various out-of-domain scientific tasks while being lightweight enough for real-time or edge applications.
AI.method: Uses a fully connected autoencoder with ~3 million parameters pre-trained without supervision on large-scale collision datasets from the Large Hadron Collider (charged particle track features). Model weights are then fine-tuned for downstream tasks like kinematic regression and event classification.
AI.result: The pre-trained model achieves improved accuracy on collider analysis tasks with small labeled datasets compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch. It demonstrates transfer learning capabilities to other scientific domains (gravitational waves, flood forecasting, neural activity). The approach is computationally simpler than transformer models at comparable scale.
AI.conclusion: NEXUS presents an effective lightweight foundation modeling approach that enables power-efficient inference and real-time applications in scientific experiments while demonstrating successful transfer learning from collider physics to diverse scientific domains.

title: ReDiPPO: Reference-Guided Value Calibration and Discrepancy-Aware Token Reweighting for Mathematical Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for enhancing the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Among existing policy optimization methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains particularly appealing because its learned critic can, in principle, provide token-level credit assignment. However, in mathematical reasoning tasks characterized by long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, reliable token-level credit assignment remains challenging. The standard critic often fails to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states, resulting in noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. In this paper, we propose ReDiPPO, a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework for mathematical reasoning. ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as training-time privileged signals to provide more accurate value estimation. Meanwhile, it retains a standard critic and quantifies the token-level reference-standard discrepancy between the standard value estimate and the reference-guided value estimate. This discrepancy serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight the corresponding token-level advantages during PPO optimization. Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines, including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO, in final reasoning performance. Our code is available on https://github.com/cii030/ReDiPPO.

AI.tldr: ReDiPPO: Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework that improves token-level credit assignment in mathematical reasoning by using reference answers to guide value estimation and weighting advantages based on estimation difficulty.
AI.motivation: While PPO is appealing for mathematical reasoning due to potential token-level credit assignment, standard critics fail to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states in tasks with long horizons and sparse rewards, leading to noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates.
AI.method: Proposes ReDiPPO with two key components: (1) a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as privileged signals for more accurate value estimation, and (2) quantification of token-level discrepancy between standard and reference-guided value estimates, which serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight token-level advantages during PPO optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong baselines including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO in final reasoning performance.
AI.conclusion: ReDiPPO effectively addresses the challenge of token-level credit assignment in mathematical reasoning by leveraging reference answers to guide value estimation and adaptively weighting advantages based on estimation difficulty, leading to superior policy optimization and reasoning performance.

title: Sparsity Induced Identifiability in Matrix Tri-Factorisation
summary: Matrix factorisation is a fundamental tool for exploiting low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional data, with applications such as data compression, denoising, structure discovery, interpretable representation learning, and dimensionality reduction. Compared to conventional two-factor models, matrix tri-factorisation provides greater modelling flexibility, while sparsity constraints often improve both interpretability and recovery performance. Although the role of sparsity has been extensively studied for two-factor matrix factorisation, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain largely unexplored. To address this gap, we establish, to the best of our knowledge, the first rigorous theoretical study for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation. Our analysis is enabled by a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, while preserving the structural information necessary to the recovery of the original factor matrices from the observations. Building upon this decomposition, we derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results that characterise how coefficient sparsity influences the sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validate the proposed theory and demonstrate close agreement between the theoretical results and empirical observations.

AI.tldr: First rigorous theoretical study of sparsity-induced identifiability in real-valued matrix tri-factorization, establishing recovery guarantees and showing how coefficient sparsity affects recovery conditions and structure preservation.
AI.motivation: Matrix tri-factorization provides greater modeling flexibility than two-factor models, and sparsity constraints improve interpretability and recovery performance. However, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorization with sparsity constraints remain largely unexplored, creating a significant research gap.
AI.method: Developed a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original tri-factorization problem into two coupled auxiliary factorization problems while preserving structural information needed for factor matrix recovery. Used this decomposition to derive theoretical guarantees for sparsity-induced identifiability.
AI.result: Established recovery guarantees and structural consistency results characterizing how coefficient sparsity influences sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behavior, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validated the theory.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first rigorous theoretical foundation for sparsity-induced identifiability in real-valued matrix tri-factorization, with both theoretical guarantees and empirical validation showing close agreement between theory and observations.

title: HealthCAT: An Interpretable Encoder-only Transformer Framework for Health Indicator Prediction and Temporal Interpretation of Wearable Sensor Data
summary: Wearable sensors continuously capture fine-grained multivariate time-series data, providing opportunities to model behavioural patterns associated with health outcomes. However, existing deep learning methods prioritise predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research. In this study, we present HealthCAT, a flexible framework that integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations. These interpretations can be mapped back onto behavioural cycles that are relevant to the domain (e.g., time-of-day), supporting individual-level analysis of wearable sensor data. We evaluated HealthCAT using two real-world wearable sensor datasets (306 participants in total). HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17\% in F1-score and 12\% in accuracy on both datasets ($p<0.05$). In masking experiments, the time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions ($p<0.05$), indicating that the identified time steps are predictively informative. By coupling predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, HealthCAT moves wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics towards temporal patterns that support health monitoring, behavioural pattern analysis, and intervention design in health research. The significance of this work is that it enables accurate prediction of health indicators from wearable sensor data while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur, rather than relying solely on aggregated summary measures.

AI.tldr: HealthCAT is a flexible framework that uses an Encoder-only Transformer with Attentive Class Activation Token to provide interpretable, time-step-level analysis of wearable sensor data while maintaining high predictive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning methods for wearable sensor data prioritize predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research where understanding behavioral patterns is crucial.
AI.method: HealthCAT integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations that can be mapped onto behavioral cycles (e.g., time-of-day).
AI.result: HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17% in F1-score and 12% in accuracy on two real-world datasets (306 participants). In masking experiments, the identified time steps carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all conditions.
AI.conclusion: HealthCAT enables accurate prediction of health indicators from wearable sensor data while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur, moving beyond aggregated metrics toward temporal patterns that support health monitoring, behavioral analysis, and intervention design.

title: Expanding Data-Agnostic Pivotal Instances Selection Models with Proximity Trees and Ensemble Learning
summary: As decision-making processes grow more complex, machine learning tools have become essential for tackling business and societal challenges. However, many existing methods rely on decision-making procedures that are difficult to interpret. Since humans naturally make decisions by comparing new cases with a few representative examples, we aim to design an approach that selects such pivots to construct an interpretable predictive model. Inspired by decision trees, we propose a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model based on the similarity between pivots and input instances. Our method functions both as a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model. Extending beyond single pivots, we incorporate pairs of pivots that are used by proximity and oblique trees, as well as ensembles, which enhance the versatility and effectiveness of our proposal. Additionally, our approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation. Experiments across diverse datasets, including tabular data, text, images, and time series, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming alternative instance selection strategies and achieving competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hierarchical, interpretable pivot selection method that selects representative examples (pivots) for decision-making, extending to pivot pairs and ensembles, working across diverse data modalities while maintaining minimal pivots.
AI.motivation: As ML tools become essential for complex decision-making, existing methods lack interpretability. Since humans naturally compare new cases with representative examples, the authors aim to design an interpretable approach that selects such pivots to make ML models more understandable and aligned with human decision processes.
AI.method: Proposes a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model inspired by decision trees, based on similarity between pivots and input instances. Extends beyond single pivots to include pairs of pivots (used by proximity and oblique trees) and ensembles. The approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation across tabular data, text, images, and time series.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse datasets show the method outperforms alternative instance selection strategies and achieves competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots. The approach functions both as a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical pivot selection method provides an effective, interpretable solution for decision-making across various data types, aligning ML models with human cognitive processes through representative example comparison while maintaining competitive performance with minimal model complexity.

title: HALO: Heterogeneous Admission through Localized Obligations for Safe Agentic Execution
summary: Recent agentic AI systems may return a heterogeneous response containing notices, requests, handoffs, and actions. Conditions can change before external use, so components from the same response need not remain supported together. Rejecting the whole response discards useful components, whereas checking components independently can leave a dependent without its prerequisite. We present Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations (HALO), a runtime protocol that preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites also remain supported, rechecks each exact action before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates. HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components, including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes, while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

AI.tldr: HALO (Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations) is a runtime protocol that intelligently preserves supported components in heterogeneous AI system responses by ensuring prerequisite dependencies remain intact, allowing safe partial adoption of responses when conditions change.
AI.motivation: Modern agentic AI systems produce heterogeneous responses containing various components (notices, requests, handoffs, actions). When conditions change before execution, entire responses may become invalid, but rejecting everything discards useful components while independent component checking can leave dependencies unsatisfied.
AI.method: HALO is a runtime protocol that: 1) Preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites also remain supported, 2) Rechecks each exact action before dispatch, 3) Allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates, ensuring localized obligations are met.
AI.result: HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components (including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes), while whole-response policies retained 0/248. In PX4/Gazebo simulations, HALO blocked all stale routes, observed no matching stale setpoints, and completed all fresh recoveries.
AI.conclusion: HALO provides an effective runtime admission control protocol for heterogeneous AI responses, enabling safe partial adoption of valid components while ensuring prerequisite dependencies, outperforming whole-response policies and preventing stale actions in dynamic environments.

title: Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation
summary: Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models denoise a sequence over many steps, but to keep each step cheap, they factorize the transition across positions and decide every token independently. This makes few-step generation challenging for text when the target couples two positions, such as a subject and a verb that must agree. An independent update commits to them separately, and many function evaluations are spent repairing the mismatch. Existing few-step methods buy back the lost correlation by distilling or rectifying a slow teacher, and so inherit the teacher's quality ceiling. We ask instead whether a model can express correlated steps natively, and answer with Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent. Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. We show that a single step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model, since one latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory. We also show that the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is a special case of our LKF model at M=1. The experiments for unconditional text generation on the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks show that our LKF model learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over the likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The gain grows with M, and at M=8, it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/lkf.git

AI.tldr: LKF (Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps) introduces a new flow-matching kernel with correlated components via shared latent variables, enabling few-step text generation that preserves dependencies between positions (like subject-verb agreement) without teacher distillation.
AI.motivation: Existing discrete diffusion and flow-matching models factorize transitions across positions, making independent token updates that struggle with positional correlations (like subject-verb agreement) in few-step generation. Current few-step methods inherit teacher model limitations through distillation or rectification.
AI.method: LKF uses a flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a shared latent variable. Each component is cheap to compute conditioned on the latent, and the mixture is summed in closed form for small M. A single latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the denoising trajectory, maintaining the same time complexity as factorized models.
AI.result: On One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks, LKF improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over likelihood baselines without losing diversity. Performance improves with larger M, and at M=8, surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers.
AI.conclusion: LKF demonstrates that models can express correlated denoising steps natively without distillation, enabling efficient few-step text generation that preserves positional dependencies through latent-variable mixture models.

title: Evaluating and Pricing Advertisements in AI-Generated Responses
summary: As search increasingly shifts toward LLM-driven answer engines, advertising is becoming embedded within the generated response itself and should therefore be evaluated for both user utility and commercial value. The key challenge is click-through intent: behavioural logs are unavailable, human annotation resists calibration, and frontier LLM judges conflate intent with linguistic fluency. These gaps compound, as principled pricing presupposes a continuous intent signal, while generating such a signal presupposes supervision that is currently unavailable. We construct the missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, and distil it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent, together with the three companion dimensions of ad quality, as smooth, differentiable estimates. Validated through sign-certain behavioural perturbations, the evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% versus 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalises without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgements across five annotators, with agreement rising in the evaluator's confidence. Upon its estimates we build the pricing layer directly, deriving the unique payment rule under which truthful bidding is optimal, demonstrating it on a best-of-k allocation, and extending the mechanism to non-monotone allocations. The same differentiable signal stands ready as a training objective for ad generation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a parameter-efficient evaluator for LLM-generated ad responses that predicts click-through intent and ad quality, then uses these differentiable estimates to build optimal pricing mechanisms.
