AI.motivation: As search shifts to LLM-driven answer engines, advertising is becoming embedded in generated responses. The key challenge is evaluating click-through intent, which faces three gaps: 1) no behavioral logs available, 2) human annotation resists calibration, and 3) frontier LLM judges conflate intent with linguistic fluency. These gaps compound because principled pricing needs continuous intent signals, but generating such signals requires supervision that doesn't exist.
AI.method: Constructs missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework. Distills this supervision into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent along with three companion dimensions of ad quality as smooth, differentiable estimates. The evaluator is validated through sign-certain behavioral perturbations. The differentiable estimates are then used to build a pricing layer that derives the unique payment rule for optimal truthful bidding, demonstrated on best-of-k allocation and extended to non-monotone allocations.
AI.result: The evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% vs 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalizes without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgments across five annotators (with agreement rising in evaluator confidence). The pricing mechanism built on these estimates enables optimal truthful bidding and can be extended to non-monotone allocations.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully bridges the supervision gap for evaluating LLM-generated ads by developing a psychologically grounded evaluator that provides differentiable intent signals. This enables both principled pricing mechanisms and serves as a training objective for ad generation, addressing the dual needs of user utility and commercial value in LLM-driven answer engines.

title: When Does Explicit View Routing Work? A Controlled Study of Multi-View Graph-Text Alignment
summary: Graph-text retrieval typically maps a graph and its description to a single embedding, even when a query concerns only one semantic aspect, such as a class label or molecular property. Multiple heads can separate these aspects, but a change in the query head may alter retrieval even when the wrong text is sent to that head. Such behavior demonstrates architectural channelization, not necessarily semantic routing. We examine the conditions under which this distinction can be resolved. Our controlled version of MV-GTA uses deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. Correct routing and per-sample derangements form a causal test of whether retrieval depends on content. On BBBP and BACE, correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305 to 0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head exceeds the best wrong head by 0.303 to 0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across the two datasets. In a matched three-seed comparison, one joint model obtains mean topology, label, and property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877; three separately trained Single specialists obtain 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation also improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140 and 0.147 over a matched-exposure canonical control. Consistency and hard-template extensions, however, reduce canonical retrieval in some settings. The evidence is therefore limited to explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and observed multi-interface consolidation. It does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether multi-head graph-text retrieval architectures actually perform semantic routing (sending queries to appropriate heads based on content) or just architectural channelization. Using controlled experiments on chemical datasets, they find evidence for explicit label and property routing but not free-form routing.
AI.motivation: Current graph-text retrieval systems map entire graph-description pairs to single embeddings, even when queries concern specific semantic aspects. While multiple heads could separate these aspects, it's unclear whether they actually perform semantic routing or just architectural channelization (where changing query heads alters retrieval even with wrong text).
AI.method: Created a controlled version of MV-GTA with deterministic text segments, isolated text encoders, view-specific graph heads, and external relevance labels (RDKit descriptors). Used causal testing with correct routing vs. per-sample derangements to determine if retrieval depends on content. Tested on BBBP and BACE datasets with property paraphrase augmentation.
AI.result: Correct routing improved label and property nDCG by 0.305-0.685 over deranged training. Expected graph heads exceeded wrong heads by 0.303-0.453. Topology didn't specialize consistently. Joint models performed better than separate specialists in some metrics (0.720/1.000/0.877 vs 0.633/0.976/0.859). Property paraphrase improved unseen-template nDCG by 0.140-0.147.
AI.conclusion: The paper finds evidence for explicit, externally-grounded label and property routing and multi-interface consolidation, but no evidence for free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction. The distinction between semantic routing and architectural channelization is partially resolved under controlled conditions.

title: Rehearse: Stepping Back from the Confidence Cliff in Self-Improving Autoresearch
summary: Autoresearch improves machine-learning code by proposing changes, running full training jobs, and keeping changes that improve the metric. The efficiency of this loop depends not only on generating ideas, but also on the agent's ability to decide, before spending a training run, whether a proposed modification is likely to work. We study how the reliability of this pre-execution judgment changes over the course of an autoresearch trajectory. In public AutoSOTA logs (Li et al., 2026; Tsinghua FIB Lab, 2026), the fraction of helpful modifications falls from 70% in the first two iterations to 43% by iteration 6+. On 296 same-baseline modification pairs from 39 paper-derived AutoSOTA tasks, each containing one modification that improved the metric and one that did not, with measured outcomes hidden, an LLM judge given candidate rationales but no prior-attempt history reaches 79.5% accuracy on the pairs where strict consensus returns a verdict. On the full 366-pair benchmark, however, this ability weakens substantially late in the loop. As successful changes accumulate, selective accuracy - accuracy conditioned on a strict-consensus verdict - falls from 82.8% to 56.9%, while the judge remains willing to decide. We call this operational pattern the confidence cliff. Rehearse implements the loop change as a lightweight skill for autoresearch loops: propose several ideas, compare them before execution, run the most promising, and judge with a focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes. This focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops, Rehearse improves the endpoint under the same training-run budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting.

AI.tldr: Rehearse improves autoresearch efficiency by comparing ideas before execution and using focused memory of past attempts, overcoming the "confidence cliff" where LLM judgment accuracy declines as successful changes accumulate.
AI.motivation: Autoresearch efficiency depends on pre-execution judgment of proposed modifications, but LLM judges show declining accuracy over time as successful changes accumulate - a "confidence cliff" problem.
AI.method: Proposed Rehearse: propose multiple ideas, compare them before execution, run the most promising, and judge with focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes.
AI.result: Rehearse raised late selective accuracy from 56.9% to 83.5%. Across 4,000 training runs over three loops, it improved endpoint performance under same budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting.
AI.conclusion: The confidence cliff is a real phenomenon in autoresearch, and Rehearse's focused outcome memory effectively mitigates it, improving research efficiency through better pre-execution judgment.

title: Subtract or Replay? Exact Deletion from Language-Model Memory
summary: Exact deletion from persistent language-model memory depends on how that memory represents a record. Addressable influence can be removed by algebraic decrement; influence transformed by later writes inside shared recurrent state requires rebuilding from before the write. We test this distinction in two pretrained models against explicit record-omitted references. First, we replace Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory. After low-rank recovery at 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree at the next-token output to median KL $5.4\times10^{-15}$ over 31 support-token deletions, with $+2.0\%$ perplexity relative to a matched fine-tune. A masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks. At 4B and 12B, certificate ordering persists but utility cost rises to $11.2\%$ and $44.3\%$. Second, in a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes admit a fixed decrement and diagonal decay a corrected one, whereas the delta rule makes $12$--$49\%$ of a record's contribution suffix-dependent. Checkpointed rewind-and-replay deletes real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, matching never-ingested logits and all recurrent states bit for bit within a deterministic MLX implementation; replaying a correction provides exact amendment. Exact deletion is therefore a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes.

AI.tldr: Exact deletion from persistent language-model memory is possible when using appropriate memory representations - addressable influence can be removed by algebraic decrement, while transformed influence requires rebuilding from before the write.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates how to achieve exact deletion from persistent language-model memory, which depends on how that memory represents records. There's a need to understand the distinction between addressable influence (which can be algebraically decremented) and influence transformed by later writes inside shared recurrent state (which requires rebuilding).
AI.method: Two approaches tested: 1) Replace Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory, with low-rank recovery at 1B, 4B, and 12B scales; 2) In a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, test different memory representations (additive writes, diagonal decay, delta rule) and use checkpointed rewind-and-replay for deletion.
AI.result: At 1B scale, decrement and retained-key refit achieve median KL of 5.4×10^-15 with only +2.0% perplexity increase; deletion is indistinguishable from never-ingested baseline. At larger scales (4B, 12B), ordering persists but utility cost rises. For Kimi Linear hybrid, checkpointed rewind-and-replay successfully deletes real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, matching never-ingested logits exactly.
AI.conclusion: Exact deletion is a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes. The approach works for different model architectures and scales, though with varying utility costs.

title: Guiding Large Language Models with Genetic Programming-Evolved Heuristic Knowledge for Dynamic Multi-Mode Project Scheduling
summary: In dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, activities have alternative execution modes and uncertain durations, while precedence relations and limited resources constrain their execution. Heuristic priority rules support fast online decisions, but their design requires substantial domain expertise. Genetic programming (GP) hyper-heuristics can automatically evolve such rules. Large language models (LLMs), meanwhile, provide a flexible interface for interpreting scheduling information and explaining decisions. However, zero-shot LLM decisions may lack domain knowledge, consume many tokens, and vary across repeated queries. GP-evolved rules therefore provide a potential source of scheduling knowledge for guiding LLM decisions. Unlike existing LLM--GP hybrids that use LLMs to support heuristic evolution, we transfer knowledge in the reverse direction, using knowledge extracted from high-quality GP rules to guide an online LLM decision maker. We extract knowledge from high-quality GP rules and inject it through Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, and Rule Follow. These mechanisms are evaluated in terms of scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and the feature focus expressed in generated rationales. GP-derived guidance generally improves the unguided LLM, but its representation matters. Simplifying the decision context or supplying explicit decision logic is more effective than highlighting important features. Feature Selection offers the best token efficiency, whereas Rule Follow achieves strong performance at greater token cost. Guidance also improves decision stability and changes the features expressed in generated rationales.

AI.tldr: Genetic programming-evolved scheduling rules guide large language models for improved dynamic multi-mode project scheduling decisions through knowledge transfer mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Heuristic priority rules for dynamic multi-mode project scheduling require domain expertise to design, and while LLMs offer flexible interfaces for scheduling decisions, their zero-shot decisions lack domain knowledge, are token-intensive, and unstable. GP-evolved rules provide potential scheduling knowledge to address these LLM limitations.
AI.method: Proposes reverse knowledge transfer from GP to LLMs using four mechanisms: Feature Selection (simplifying decision context), Feature Hint (highlighting important features), Rule Reference (supplying explicit decision logic), and Rule Follow. Evaluates these mechanisms on scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and rationale feature focus.
AI.result: GP-derived guidance generally improves unguided LLMs, but effectiveness depends on representation. Feature Selection provides best token efficiency, while Rule Follow achieves strong performance at greater token cost. Guidance improves decision stability and changes the features expressed in generated rationales.
AI.conclusion: GP-evolved rules can effectively guide LLMs for scheduling decisions, with representation choice significantly impacting performance. Reverse knowledge transfer (from GP to LLM) complements existing LLM-GP hybrids, offering practical improvements in scheduling quality, efficiency, and stability.

title: Memory Efficient Tabular Foundation Models
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures Accepted at FMSD @ ICML 2026
summary: Tabular Foundation Models, such as TabPFN, have received a large amount of recent attention due to their performance on in-context tabular machine learning tasks, which often exceeds classical baselines. However, practical deployment considerations of these models has received less attention. In this paper we investigate the memory requirements for these models. We demonstrate that employing model compression approaches can enable memory reductions of up to 7.6 with similar levels of performance, reducing deployment requirements by nearly 87%. Our work provides insight to practitioners seeking efficient deployment of these models in practical settings.

AI.tldr: TabPFN and similar tabular foundation models can be compressed to reduce memory requirements by 7.6× (87% reduction) with minimal performance loss, enabling practical deployment.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models like TabPFN have shown superior performance for in-context tabular ML tasks but their practical deployment considerations, particularly memory requirements, have received little attention.
AI.method: The paper investigates memory requirements of tabular foundation models and employs model compression approaches to reduce memory footprint while maintaining performance.
AI.result: Model compression enables memory reductions of up to 7.6 times (87% reduction) with similar performance levels compared to uncompressed models.
AI.conclusion: Compression techniques make tabular foundation models more practical for deployment, providing insights for practitioners seeking efficient model deployment in real-world settings.

title: SpatialCLI: Learning to Reason With Spatial Tools, Then Without Them
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in embodied agents to interpret visual inputs, reason about spatial relationships, and make task-level decisions based on that reasoning. However, a fundamental capability mismatch remains: general VLMs can reason about the overall task but often miss the visual details that determine success, while specialist vision models can capture those details but cannot translate them into task-level decisions. In this work, we propose SpatialCLI, a framework that teaches VLMs to reason with spatial tools and progressively internalize the specialist perceptual capabilities they provide. SpatialCLI proceeds in three stages: (1) Call exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment the VLM's perception; (2) Learn uses Cold-Start SFT and agentic RL to improve tool use; and (3) Internalize verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to internalize specialist perceptual capabilities. We further introduce SpatialCLI-Bench, a 516-example benchmark for compositional perception across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose. On MindCube, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%), while retaining 73.8% without tools after internalization.

AI.tldr: SpatialCLI teaches vision-language models to use spatial tools and internalize specialist perceptual capabilities, achieving significant performance improvements on embodied reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: There's a fundamental capability mismatch: general VLMs can reason about overall tasks but miss visual details, while specialist vision models capture details but can't make task-level decisions. Current VLMs lack the ability to properly utilize spatial perception tools.
AI.method: SpatialCLI uses a three-stage framework: 1) Call - exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment perception, 2) Learn - uses Cold-Start SFT and agentic RL to improve tool use, 3) Internalize - verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to internalize specialist perceptual capabilities.
AI.result: On MindCube benchmark, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools (surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools at 72.1%), and retains 73.8% without tools after internalization. Also introduces SpatialCLI-Bench with 516 examples for compositional perception tasks.
AI.conclusion: SpatialCLI effectively bridges the gap between general reasoning and specialist perception by teaching VLMs to use spatial tools and internalize their capabilities, significantly improving performance on embodied reasoning tasks while maintaining capability even without tools.

title: Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings
summary: New venture start-ups need to ``survive'' through multiple stages of reaching milestone targets. We investigate the strategies for start-ups in a milestone-oriented setting. We examine a model of an entrepreneurial start-up firm, where its state is captured by a diffusion process. The entrepreneur can choose between multiple activities (or controls), which incur different cost and determine the drift and the variance of the process. Depending on whether the process reaches a fixed upper boundary or a lower one, the start-up firm succeeds or fails. Continuous-time stochastic models with multiple ($\ge 3$) controls are typically very challenging to deal with. In this work, we are able to completely solve for the optimal policy and provide an explicit characterization of its structure. In particular, the optimal policy only uses controls from a set characterized by a so-called efficient frontier curve that orders the controls by two intuitive measures: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). A unique feature of our model is that depending on the model parameters, the efficient frontier curves can be of different types, resulting in qualitatively different structures of the optimal policy. As far as we know, this is the first study that analyzes a stochastic control model which admits efficient frontier curves of different types. Our work provides start-up firms with intuitive measures to evaluate their activities and offers valuable insights on how the optimal strategies in a milestone-oriented setting change qualitatively contingent upon the specific scenario. We believe the results provide a foundational block in the study of entrepreneurial decision-making.

AI.tldr: Entrepreneurial startups should evaluate activities using riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio) measures to determine optimal milestone achievement strategies.
AI.motivation: Startups need to survive through multiple milestone stages, but continuous-time stochastic models with multiple controls (≥3) are typically very challenging to solve. There's a need to understand optimal strategies for milestone-oriented entrepreneurial decision-making.
AI.method: Develop a stochastic control model where a startup's state follows a diffusion process. The entrepreneur can choose between multiple activities (controls) with different costs, drifts, and variances. The process reaches success/failure based on hitting fixed upper/lower boundaries.
AI.result: Completely solved for optimal policy with explicit characterization. The optimal policy uses controls from an efficient frontier curve ordering activities by riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). Efficient frontier curves can be of different types based on parameters, leading to qualitatively different optimal policies.
AI.conclusion: This is the first study analyzing a stochastic control model with efficient frontier curves of different types. Provides startups with intuitive measures to evaluate activities and shows how optimal strategies change qualitatively based on scenarios. Forms a foundational block for entrepreneurial decision-making research.

title: Albilich: Steerable Proof-State Orchestration for LLM-Based Mathematical Research with CAS Integration
summary:
Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, yet long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. We present Albilich, an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch in mathematics that combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management.
  We evaluate Albilich on the RealMath benchmark (Zhang et al. 2025) and on open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook (Khukhro and Mazurov 2026). It solved 10/10 problems on RealMath with CAS and 9/10 with no CAS. On the Kourovka problems, Albilich produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem20.2. Anablation on Problem 17.91 demonstrates 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. An ablation on Problem 21.142 demonstrates higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proof routes in the absence of the advisor agent. These results support Albilich as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

AI.tldr: Albilich is an open-source agentic harness for mathematical research that combines LLM reasoning, computer algebra systems, literature retrieval, and context management, showing strong performance on mathematical benchmarks and open problems.
AI.motivation: While large language models can contribute to mathematical research, long-horizon proof attempts are difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. There's a need for better systems to manage AI-assisted mathematical research.
AI.method: Albilich combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management in an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch in mathematics.
AI.result: On RealMath benchmark: solved 10/10 problems with CAS and 9/10 without CAS. On Kourovka Notebook open problems: produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem 20.2. Ablations showed 32.0% token reduction with CAS and higher verifier-rejection rates without advisor agent.
AI.conclusion: Albilich serves as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research, demonstrating effectiveness in solving mathematical problems and open research questions.

title: A Montage-Agnostic Encoder for Calibration-Light Cross-User Gesture Recognition from Surface Electromyography
summary: Pattern-recognition control promises a myoelectric prosthesis that responds to many intended gestures rather than one or two, but the promise has stayed in the laboratory. A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A montage-agnostic encoder is introduced that reads each electrode with shared weights and locates it by its physical coordinate rather than its index, so one architecture ingests any channel count without montage-specific parameters. Trained across users, it exceeds a per-user Hudgins and linear-discriminant classifier by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 for every held-out subject and by 0.108 on DB2, and falls below it on the ten-subject DB5. Each of the encoder's three key components individually accounts for more than half of its 3-shot macro F1 in an otherwise budget-matched ablation study. A controlled subject-count sweep shows the margin is close to flat from nine training subjects to thirty-nine, so the training pool binds only as a stability floor below which cross-user training fails to converge; what tracks the direction of the comparison across the three databases is instead the strength of the per-user baseline, which signal fidelity sets. Comparing against an LDA baseline depends on budget spent training models and on how good that baseline is, and self-supervised pretraining had no benefits once a supervised model was adequately trained.

AI.tldr: A novel montage-agnostic encoder for myoelectric pattern recognition enables cross-user generalization without per-user calibration, outperforming traditional methods in most scenarios but performance depends on baseline strength and training budget.
AI.motivation: Current myoelectric pattern recognition systems for prosthetics require extensive per-user calibration and don't generalize well across users, limiting practical adoption beyond the laboratory. There's a need for systems that can work across different users without extensive individual calibration.
AI.method: Developed a montage-agnostic encoder that processes each electrode with shared weights and uses physical coordinates rather than channel indices, allowing one architecture to handle any channel count without montage-specific parameters. Trained across multiple users and evaluated using ablation studies and controlled subject-count sweeps.
AI.result: The encoder outperformed traditional Hudgins and LDA classifiers by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 and 0.108 on DB2 for all held-out subjects, but fell below on DB5. Each of the three key components contributed significantly to performance. Cross-user training showed stable performance from 9 to 39 training subjects, with performance bound mainly by signal quality rather than training pool size. Self-supervised pretraining provided no additional benefit once supervised training was adequate.
AI.conclusion: The proposed montage-agnostic encoder enables effective cross-user myoelectric pattern recognition without per-user calibration, addressing a major barrier to practical adoption. Performance depends more on baseline signal quality than training pool size, and supervised training alone is sufficient once adequately implemented.

title: MECA: A Mechanism-Centered Agent for Constructing Well-Specified and Valuable Mathematical Conjectures
comment: 78 pages, 5 figures. Includes appendices and the full collection of 100 generated conjectures
summary: Automatically constructing well-specified and valuable mathematical conjectures remains a central challenge in AI-assisted mathematical discovery. Many existing open problems and conjectures are often too broad, underspecified, or difficult to connect to plausible proof or refutation strategies. We view a mathematical mechanism as a structure or reasoning principle that connects the assumptions of a candidate problem to its target conclusion, such as an inequality, invariant, decomposition, or reduction to an intermediate claim. We present MECA (MEchanism-centered Conjecture Agent), a multi-agent framework that constructs conjectures by jointly developing candidate statements and their supporting mechanisms. Explorer agents propose mechanisms, test how they apply, and revise the candidate conjecture accordingly, while critic agents assess their mathematical validity and research value. Their feedback guides changes to the assumptions, scope, and conclusion. Through this process, MECA transforms broad research directions into precise conjectures with substantive mathematical support while retaining a clearly identified unresolved core. We evaluate MECA in two complementary settings. First, we compare it with a generate-and-revise baseline on reconstructing preselected target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind source materials. Second, we construct 100 semi-open problems from literature-derived seeds and existing open problems and evaluate them through independent proof and refutation attempts by automated provers. Our results indicate that mechanism-centered refinement produces well-specified and research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current automated provers.

AI.tldr: MECA is a multi-agent framework that creates mathematical conjectures by jointly developing statements and supporting mechanisms through explorer and critic agents, producing well-specified research-worthy problems challenging for automated provers.
AI.motivation: Existing mathematical conjectures and open problems are often too broad, underspecified, or difficult to connect to plausible proof/refutation strategies, making AI-assisted mathematical discovery challenging.
AI.method: Multi-agent framework with explorer agents that propose mechanisms, test applications, and revise conjectures, and critic agents that assess mathematical validity and research value, guiding changes to assumptions, scope, and conclusions.
AI.result: MECA outperforms generate-and-revise baselines in reconstructing target-paper conclusions, and successfully constructs 100 semi-open problems from literature that remain challenging for automated provers.
AI.conclusion: Mechanism-centered refinement produces well-specified, research-worthy conjectures that retain clearly identified unresolved cores while being challenging for current automated theorem provers.

title: Recognition and Label-Free Adaptation Across Recording Sessions in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding
summary: Recognition accuracy obtained during a recording session does not persist when a user puts on the electrodes again after the electrodes had previously been removed. The electrodes may have moved slightly, the skin may be drier or wetter, or the elbow may be positioned differently; these factors all contribute to day-to-day variability and therefore represent a major obstacle to implementing successful pattern-recognition based myoelectric control systems in daily practice. However, simply recalibrating a user's hand for 20 min at every doff/don event is a clearly unrealistic expectation. A montage-agnostic encoder built for cross-user, cross-montage transfer is trained here using data collected during a particular recording session, and then applied to data collected later in a different recording session without adjusting anything, on the ten intact subjects of NinaPro DB6. The performance of this approach is compared to that of a per-user LDA classification pipeline, and to that of two published approaches that only rely on source data collected from the same recording session. Carried unchanged across recording sessions, the encoder retains 0.688 macro-F1 against 0.540 for the per-user pipeline, and, on the per-window metric the published baselines use, sits above both published source-only results, a band of two points that locates the encoder rather than ranking it. Of five label-free test-time adaptations, only feature-statistic alignment improves every subject; batch-normalisation re-estimation, a standard method in the domain-adaptation literature, collapses this architecture entirely. Aligning the encoder's feature statistics to the new session recovers about what a single labelled calibration repetition would.

AI.tldr: A montage-agnostic encoder trained on one EMG recording session maintains significant performance when applied to new sessions without recalibration, outperforming user-specific classifiers and published methods.
AI.motivation: Myoelectric control systems suffer from day-to-day variability due to electrode movement, skin condition changes, and arm positioning differences, making pattern recognition unreliable across sessions. Frequent recalibration (20+ minutes) is impractical for daily use.
AI.method: Developed a montage-agnostic encoder trained for cross-user, cross-montage transfer using data from one recording session. Applied it unchanged to data from different sessions on the same subjects (NinaPro DB6 dataset). Compared against per-user LDA classification and two published source-only approaches, plus tested five label-free test-time adaptation methods.
AI.result: The encoder retained 0.688 macro-F1 across sessions vs 0.540 for per-user pipeline. Outperformed both published baselines on per-window metrics. Among adaptation methods, only feature-statistic alignment consistently improved all subjects, recovering performance equivalent to one calibration repetition, while batch-normalization re-estimation collapsed the architecture.
AI.conclusion: Montage-agnostic encoders can significantly reduce calibration burden for myoelectric control systems by maintaining performance across sessions. Feature-statistic alignment emerges as the only consistently effective adaptation method, offering practical calibration efficiency improvements.

title: New Synchronous Computation Dynamics for Hopfield Networks
summary: The dynamics of the original Hopfield network is asynchronous (sequential) (updates the state of only one neuron per time step). In this paper, we propose a new tool and a new dynamics to reduce the processing time by updating one or more neurons simultaneously per instant while ensuring process convergence and aiming for the maximum energy decrease at each step, thus guaranteeing the shortest total processing time. From the point of view of synchronous dynamics, calculating the next network state at which energy decreases the most from the current state while ensuring convergence is itself a combinatorial optimization problem. We develop and use a new tool to solve it. We call this new tool Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) and, based upon it, we develop a new synchronous dynamics which we call SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter). In this paper, we review the original asynchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks and present a new tool and a new synchronous dynamics with its theoretical justification and four computational experiments to assess the speed up in processing time empirically.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new synchronous dynamics called SD-DDF for Hopfield networks that updates multiple neurons simultaneously to reduce processing time while ensuring convergence and maximum energy decrease per step.
AI.motivation: The original Hopfield network uses asynchronous (sequential) updates where only one neuron updates per time step, which leads to longer processing times. The authors aim to accelerate processing by updating one or more neurons simultaneously while maintaining convergence properties.
AI.method: The authors develop a new tool called Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) to solve the combinatorial optimization problem of determining the optimal set of neurons to update simultaneously for maximum energy decrease. Based on DDF, they propose SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter) as a new synchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks.
AI.result: The paper presents theoretical justification for the new synchronous dynamics and validates it through four computational experiments that empirically assess the speed-up in processing time achieved by SD-DDF compared to the original asynchronous dynamics.
AI.conclusion: SD-DDF offers a theoretically justified synchronous alternative to traditional Hopfield network dynamics that can significantly reduce processing time while maintaining convergence and energy minimization properties.

title: Baikal: Structured Search for Deep Research over Data Lakes
summary: Deep research over data lakes requires an LLM agent to investigate evidence across thousands of heterogeneous tables and passages to synthesize a report. Existing methods perform iterative retrieval and generation, letting accumulated context determine what to investigate next, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget. To address this, we cast deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem and present Baikal - a framework that clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, then searches over them adaptively to balance exploration and exploitation. Within each selected region, Baikal generates and investigates region-grounded subquestions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates and guide search under policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian $ε$-greedy and UCB. We evaluate Baikal on 15 queries each over HybridQA and TAT-QA data lakes containing 10,993 and 2,757 tables, respectively, together with 227K Wikipedia passages and 13K financial report passages. We assess research quality with a new rubric covering groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility, and use GPT-5-mini to score Baikal and strong baselines, including DeepSearcher and an OpenCode research agent with retrieval and clustering variants. Across both data lakes, Baikal performs strongly under several region-selection policies; its best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Our analyses attribute these gains to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, which improves groundedness and diversity and yields more useful findings under the same subquestion budget. These results demonstrate the value of structured semantic exploration for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes.

AI.tldr: Baikal is a framework for deep research over data lakes that organizes heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions and uses adaptive search policies to balance exploration and exploitation, improving report quality by 28-36% over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for deep research over data lakes use iterative retrieval and generation that can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under fixed budgets, leading to incomplete or biased reports.
AI.method: Baikal clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, searches over them adaptively, generates region-grounded subquestions, uses finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates, and applies policies like random, LLM-guided, Bayesian ε-greedy, and UCB for region selection.
AI.result: Baikal improves report scores by 28% on HybridQA (10,993 tables + 227K passages) and 36% on TAT-QA (2,757 tables + 13K passages) over strongest baselines, with gains attributed to better groundedness, diversity, and utility through organized semantic exploration.
AI.conclusion: Structured semantic exploration through clustering evidence and adaptive search policies significantly improves systematic research quality over heterogeneous data lakes by enhancing evidence coverage and report utility.

title: MUGEN: A Unified Framework for Efficient Motion Understanding and Generation
summary: Grounding human motion in language, and language in motion, is a central step toward physical AI systems that can understand, generate, and communicate human behavior. Unified motion--language systems first coupled the two directions through a shared discrete motion codebook, but quantization limits generation quality. The strongest generators buy quality back at growing cost: stacked residual codebooks enlarge the representation; masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, and denoising chains of tens to hundreds of steps stretch inference; even the continuous-latent designs among them reach their latent only through an iterative diffusion head; and none of this decoding machinery serves understanding. We therefore propose MUGEN, a unified motion--language framework that pays neither cost: no codebook, one draw. A single adaptive-length autoencoder compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots, the system's only motion representation: the language model generates them for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states let each slot read from the transformer depth it needs, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, so a single draw carries the text-conditional, cross-slot variation a description permits. At a decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass, MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D while raising retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.

AI.tldr: MUGEN is a unified motion-language framework that generates continuous motion latents directly from text using a single language model draw, avoiding quantization and complex multi-stage decoding while achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Current unified motion-language systems suffer from quantization limits that reduce generation quality. To compensate, they use expensive techniques like stacked residual codebooks, masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, and diffusion processes - none of which help with motion understanding. There's a need for a simpler, more efficient approach.
AI.method: MUGEN uses a single adaptive-length autoencoder to compress any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots. A language model generates these slots for text-to-motion and reads them for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states allow each slot to access appropriate transformer depth, and a calibrated head predicts joint distribution over all latents with one draw.
AI.result: MUGEN achieves state-of-the-art results: leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D, raises retrieval precision above real-motion reference under standard evaluator, achieves best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses discrete-token state-of-the-art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.
AI.conclusion: MUGEN demonstrates that a unified motion-language framework can achieve superior performance with minimal decoding cost (K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass), eliminating the need for complex quantization or multi-stage decoding approaches.

title: VeriSkill: A Self-Evolution Framework for Program Verification Skills
summary: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations, all of which depend on reusable skills. A natural remedy is skill self-evolution: distilling skills from trajectories and refining them through feedback. However, existing evolution methods struggle with program verification tasks because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback. In this paper, we propose VeriSkill, a self-evolution framework built for program verification. It attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills, admitting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics. Experiments show that VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

AI.tldr: VeriSkill is a self-evolution framework for LLM-based program verification that attributes verification failures to specific skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines skills while preserving program semantics.
AI.motivation: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations that depend on reusable skills. Existing skill evolution methods struggle with program verification tasks because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback.
AI.method: VeriSkill attributes verification failures to specific skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills. It only admits revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics, using a self-evolution framework built specifically for program verification tasks.
AI.result: Experiments show that VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.
AI.conclusion: The proposed VeriSkill framework effectively addresses the challenges of skill evolution in program verification by providing a targeted approach to identifying skill deficiencies, learning from verification failures, and refining skills while maintaining program correctness.

title: Prox: Training-Free FFN Activation Sparsity via Approximate Intermediate-Channel Salience in LLMs
summary: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) dominate memory traffic and computation in large language model (LLM) inference, making them a primary target for activation sparsification. However, existing training-free methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. We observe that the SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective channel-selection signal, but obtaining it requires costly dense computation. To address this, we present \emph{Prox}, a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs. Prox hinges on the key insight: sparse execution requires only the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be constructed from the magnitude ranking of its entries rather than their exact values. Specifically, Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to a $1.99\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup at 70\% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

AI.tldr: Prox is a training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs that achieves high sparsity with minimal quality degradation by constructing channel masks from magnitude rankings rather than exact values, enabling substantial speedups in LLM inference.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) dominate memory traffic and computation in LLM inference, making them prime targets for activation sparsification. Existing training-free methods suffer significant quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. The intermediate state in SwiGLU FFNs provides an effective selection signal but requires costly dense computation to obtain.
AI.method: Prox uses a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs. Stage 1 leverages input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared channel mask based on magnitude rankings of intermediate state entries. Stage 2 computes only the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections in the SwiGLU FFN.
AI.result: Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to 1.99× end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity, and demonstrates compatibility with quantization and sparse attention techniques.
AI.conclusion: Prox successfully addresses the limitations of existing training-free sparsification methods by using magnitude rankings to construct channel masks, enabling high sparsity with minimal quality degradation and significant speedups in LLM inference while maintaining compatibility with other optimization techniques.

title: SpecCal: Ambiguity-Aware Candidate Calibration for Infrared Spectrum-Based Molecular Structure Reconstruction
summary: Inferring molecular structures from infrared (IR) spectra is a fundamental yet challenging problem. A key difficulty is that an IR spectrum provides limited structural information: different molecules may share similar functional groups and local vibrational patterns, leading to highly similar spectral responses. Thus, even when an observed spectrum has a unique underlying structure, reconstructing it from the spectrum remains ambiguous. Existing IR-to-molecule models usually generate a ranked set of candidate molecules, but this set is largely determined by the model's learned generation preference and may not fully capture the structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints. To address this limitation, we propose SpecCal, a training-free candidate calibration framework for IR-to-molecule prediction. SpecCal operates on the candidate outputs of existing base models and improves the prediction set by re-ranking current candidates while introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. The framework is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, requiring no parameter updates for integration with diverse base models. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Further analyses demonstrate that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity provides a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra. The code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SpecCal-B18A.

AI.tldr: SpecCal is a training-free calibration framework that improves molecular structure reconstruction from IR spectra by re-ranking existing model candidates and adding spectrally-consistent alternatives.
AI.motivation: IR spectra provide limited structural information due to similar functional groups and vibrational patterns, causing reconstruction ambiguity. Existing models generate candidate molecules based on learned preferences rather than optimal spectral constraints.
AI.method: SpecCal is a plug-and-play, model-agnostic framework that operates on candidate outputs of base IR-to-molecule models. It improves prediction sets by re-ranking existing candidates and introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency, without requiring parameter updates.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. It provides practical improvements for molecular reconstruction under spectral ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: SpecCal demonstrates that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity effectively improves molecular reconstruction from IR spectra, offering a flexible, training-free solution that can work with diverse existing models.

title: Compliance2LoRA: On-Demand Safety Alignment on Arbitrary Policy Subsets via Hypernetwork-Generated LoRA Adapters
summary: Post-training alignment in large reasoning models (LRMs) has significantly improved their adaptability to diverse safety compliance settings. However, as LRMs personalization for downstream users takes center stage, the demand for varying levels of policy compliance grows as different user-specific LRMs must adhere to distinct subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM for each policy subset introduces severe combinatorial overhead. While in context learning methods overcome this combinatorial overhead, they introduce additional computational challenges associated with long context generation. To address this challenge, we propose \ours, a unified adaptive hypernetwork-based framework for multi-policy compliance. In our framework, safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, which learns to produce policy compliant LoRA weights for downstream LRM. When added to the LRM these weights enable the generation of responses compliant with the specified policy subsets. In this work, we demonstrate that training such a hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sized and different evaluation datasets. This highlights the effectiveness and practicality of adaptive hypernetwork based alignment in LRMs.

AI.tldr: Hypernetwork-based framework for on-demand policy compliance in large reasoning models without retraining or long context overhead.
AI.motivation: As LRMs are personalized for different users with varying safety policy requirements, training separate models for each policy subset creates combinatorial overhead, while in-context learning methods introduce computational challenges with long context generation.
AI.method: Proposes a unified adaptive hypernetwork framework where safety policies serve as inputs to a LoRA adapter generator that produces policy-compliant LoRA weights, which when added to the LRM enable compliant responses without modifying the base model.
AI.result: The framework enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance, working across reasoning models of different sizes and evaluation datasets.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive hypernetwork-based alignment is an effective and practical approach for multi-policy compliance in large reasoning models.

title: Annotating Topical Legal Insights from Case Proceedings
summary: In this paper, we mainly concentrate on finding concepts or topics from the legal case proceedings, since adopting a structured representation for legal documents, as opposed to a mere bag-of-words flat text representation, can significantly enhance processing capabilities. To achieve this objective, we put forward a set of diverse concepts for legal case proceedings. With this motivation, we propose LeDA, a system for Legal Data Annotation. The system offers the generic functionality of annotating and adjudicating entities or concepts within documents via a web-based interface. A novel feature of our system is that it allows to dynamic create new tags for annotation, which is a particularly useful provision for situations where there exists no pre-defined ontology for the entities (concepts) that need to be annotated - these being rather discovered by annotators as they continue examining more documents. The system that we demonstrate is currently in use to annotate a set of concepts from legal documents to construct semantic representations of documents as bags of concepts that can then be used for several downstream tasks, such as prior case retrieval, judgment prediction, and so on. Along with the system features in general, we also describe how LeDA was used by 3 assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

AI.tldr: LeDA is a web-based legal data annotation system that enables dynamic creation of annotation tags for legal concepts, allowing annotators to discover and tag concepts without predefined ontologies during document examination.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to move beyond simple bag-of-words representations for legal documents by creating structured semantic representations based on legal concepts/topics. This structured representation can significantly enhance processing capabilities for downstream legal applications like prior case retrieval and judgment prediction.
AI.method: The paper proposes LeDA, a web-based annotation system that allows: 1) annotating and adjudicating entities/concepts in legal documents, 2) dynamic creation of new annotation tags as annotators discover concepts during document examination (useful when no pre-defined ontology exists), and 3) collaborative annotation workflow with multiple assessors.
AI.result: The system is currently being used to annotate concepts from legal documents to construct semantic representations as "bags of concepts." It has been successfully deployed with 3 assessors annotating legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings, enabling the creation of structured representations for downstream legal tasks.
AI.conclusion: LeDA provides a flexible, dynamic annotation framework for legal documents that enables the discovery and annotation of legal concepts without requiring pre-defined ontologies. This approach facilitates the construction of semantic document representations that can power various legal AI applications.

title: Back from the Future: Key-Value Cache Management by Counter-Causal Surprise
summary: Key-value (KV) cache management through compression and eviction strategies has emerged as an important research direction in recent years. Computational demands of large language models (LLMs) and their multi-modal variants during output generation can be partially alleviated by caching previous key and value calculations needed by subsequent scaled dot-product attention operations. However, this leads to another problem: the size of the resulting KV cache grows linearly with context length and quickly consumes all available GPU memory when either the prompt or the generated output are long. KV cache management periodically prunes entries from the cache thereby reducing its memory footprint while attempting to retain sufficient information for accurate generation. A by-product is faster inference speed. We propose a simple yet effective KV eviction scheme motivated by the insight that past tokens which can be well-predicted from more recent tokens are redundant and their associated keys and values can be removed from the cache. To score entries for eviction we run the model on the tokens in their original order, reusing the key and value representations already stored in the KV cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so that each position attends only to its future context. This is in-distribution, tied directly to the actual cache contents, and requires no additional training. To further reduce cost, we additionally propose a fast single-layer approximation that restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer, achieving a significant speedup per refresh cycle at marginal accuracy cost. We evaluate our strategy on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets showing competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art methods. Reference code is available at https://github.com/metacognitionai/counter_causal.

AI.tldr: A counter-causal attention-based KV cache eviction method that identifies and removes redundant tokens which can be predicted from more recent tokens, improving memory efficiency and inference speed without requiring training.
AI.motivation: The KV cache in LLMs grows linearly with context length, consuming excessive GPU memory for long prompts/outputs. Current KV cache management strategies need to balance memory reduction with generation accuracy while maintaining fast inference speeds.
AI.method: Proposes using counter-causal attention to score cache entries for eviction: tokens that can be well-predicted from future context are deemed redundant. The method runs the model in original order with a counter-causal attention mask (each position attends only to future tokens) to compute redundancy scores using existing KV cache. Also introduces a fast approximation using only the last transformer layer for speed.
AI.result: The method shows competitive or improved performance over state-of-the-art approaches on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets, with the fast approximation achieving significant speedup per refresh cycle at marginal accuracy cost.
AI.conclusion: The proposed counter-causal attention-based KV eviction scheme is an effective, training-free solution for KV cache management that reduces memory footprint while maintaining generation accuracy and improving inference speed, with practical applicability demonstrated through open-source implementation.

title: MemeBench: What LVLMs Miss When Interpreting Culture-Dependent Memes
summary: Large vision-language models have improved at describing visual content, but accurate descriptions do not ensure interpretation when meaning depends on knowledge beyond the pixels. Memes expose this gap because they rely on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Most meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where an explanation breaks down. We introduce MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations, centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent online subcultures. Its VIKR schema decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. Across 26 LVLMs, every model covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it, and even the strongest retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. To test whether this diagnosis can guide improvement, we introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase. Across four controlled models, KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% and, compared with generic retrieval, repairs more answers and breaks fewer. Yet both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison. MemeBench reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap.

AI.tldr: MemeBench is a diagnostic benchmark for testing vision-language models' ability to interpret memes, using VIKR schema to decompose explanations into Visual, Identity, Knowledge, and Reasoning components. It reveals models perform better on visible content than required knowledge, with a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap, and shows that entity-guided retrieval (KAR) can help fill these gaps.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language models are good at describing visual content but struggle with interpreting memes that require cultural knowledge, background information, and community conventions beyond what's visible in the pixels. Most meme benchmarks only provide labels or scores without explaining where interpretations break down.
AI.method: Created MemeBench with 1,253 Chinese and English memes focused on anime, comics, games, and online subcultures. Used human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations (Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, Reasoning mechanisms). Tested 26 LVLMs and introduced KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase, to test if diagnosis can guide improvement.
AI.result: All models cover visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed for interpretation, with strongest models retaining 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. KAR improves VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% across four controlled models compared to generic retrieval. Both retrieval methods improve Identity and Knowledge coverage but reduce Visual coverage in every comparison.
AI.conclusion: MemeBench provides a diagnostic tool that reveals whether meme interpretations succeed, identifies what's missing, and shows whether targeted evidence can fill identified gaps. The benchmark demonstrates that current LVLMs need better integration of cultural knowledge for accurate meme interpretation, and entity-guided retrieval can help address these deficiencies.

title: Kalman Meets Curriculum: Efficient Dynamic Prompt Selection for Adaptive RL Finetuning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet its effectiveness critically depends on selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty for the current policy. This is challenging because prompt difficulty evolves throughout training. Existing online methods therefore face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but typically assume stationary difficulty, making them ill-suited to RL's non-stationary training dynamics. To address these issues, we propose a Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection method (KGPS), which reformulates prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem rather than static difficulty prediction. KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model, with process noise coupled to the magnitude of policy updates so that uncertainty increases when the policy changes more substantially. A Kalman filter then maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones. The resulting procedure is adaptive to policy drift and requires no additional rollouts beyond standard policy training. Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks, as well as multiple RL algorithms, show that KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, establishing state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods. For example, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while even improving the average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: KGPS is a prompt selection method for RL-finetuned LLMs that uses Kalman filtering to dynamically track prompt difficulty, requiring fewer rollouts while improving performance over existing methods.
AI.motivation: RL finetuning enhances LLM reasoning, but selecting appropriately difficult prompts is challenging because prompt difficulty evolves during training. Existing methods either require expensive evaluations or assume stationary difficulty, which is ill-suited for RL's non-stationary dynamics.
AI.method: Proposes Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection (KGPS), which reformulates prompt selection as dynamic state estimation. Models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model with process noise coupled to policy updates. Uses Kalman filter to maintain calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty and selects prompts by maximizing posterior-expected training utility.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks show KGPS consistently improves final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, uses 83% fewer rollouts while improving average performance by 0.12 points across six math reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: KGPS establishes state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods by providing an adaptive, efficient approach that handles RL's non-stationary training dynamics without requiring additional rollouts beyond standard policy training.

title: STEREODISCO: Discovering Stereotypicality in LLMs
summary: LLMs encode, convey, and perpetuate stereotypes. Prior computational research focuses on a small set of semantic axes investigated in social psychology, and operates on word embeddings produced by language models, leaving open which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how LLMs internally represent such axes. We introduce STEREODISCO, a framework that adapts the semantic differential method (Osgood et al., 1957) to the systematic study of stereotypes in LLM internal representations. STEREODISCO constructs approx. 2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections. As a case study, we apply STEREODISCO to social group stereotypes with LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT. We find that the two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, suggesting that LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from that documented in social psychology. We also discover stereotypical axes not investigated in prior work -- including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which human annotators independently confirm.

AI.tldr: STEREODISCO: A framework that systematically identifies stereotypical semantic axes in LLMs using WordNet antonyms and probing techniques, revealing LLM stereotypes diverge from human psychology.
AI.motivation: Prior computational research on LLM stereotypes focuses on a limited set of semantic axes from social psychology and operates on word embeddings, leaving gaps in understanding which other semantic axes carry stereotypes and how LLMs internally represent them.
AI.method: STEREODISCO adapts the semantic differential method to study LLM internal representations. It constructs ~2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as geometric axes in LLM activation spaces via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes using statistical tests over concept projections.
AI.result: LLaMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and Mistral-7B-INSTRUCT agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, showing LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from social psychology. Discovered novel stereotypical axes (humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, cowardly vs. brave) confirmed by human annotators.
AI.conclusion: LLMs encode stereotypes that differ from human psychological documentation, and STEREODISCO provides a systematic framework for uncovering previously unstudied stereotypical semantic axes in LLM representations.

title: Real-Time Hard Peak Age-of-Information Safety with No-Regret Learning
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE Real-Time Systems Symposium (RTSS)
summary: Safety-critical IoT systems such as industrial closed-loop control, V2X coordination, and remote teleoperation require every sensor's peak Age of Information (peak AoI, also abbreviated PAoI) to stay below a hard per-slot deadline, not merely an average bound. Existing approaches meet this requirement only under restrictive assumptions: stochastic channels for Whittle-index AoI, simulator rollouts for deep reinforcement learning, or sublinear cumulative violation for long-term constrained online convex optimization. Under adversarial coefficients, OCO-PAoI-Hard guarantees zero per-slot violation of the modeled AoI state under one-step viability and O(sqrt(T)) regret against any static safe comparator; packet-level safety requires stronger service assumptions. Our key observation is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline collapses exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, turning hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility through one Euclidean projection per slot, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. We establish closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio. On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard attains zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines miss between 1.65 percent and 64.0 percent of slots, and the empirical normalized regret stays below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

AI.tldr: A new online convex optimization framework (OCO-PAoI-Hard) guarantees zero per-slot violation of peak Age of Information deadlines for safety-critical IoT systems under adversarial conditions, outperforming existing approaches that only work under restrictive assumptions.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical IoT systems (industrial control, V2X coordination, remote teleoperation) require hard per-slot deadlines for peak Age of Information, not just average bounds. Existing approaches only work under restrictive assumptions: stochastic channels, simulator rollouts, or sublinear cumulative violation constraints, making them inadequate for adversarial environments.
AI.method: Key insight: fractional peak-AoI deadline constraints collapse to affine half-space constraints on resource allocation vectors. The method uses strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop with one Euclidean projection per slot to enforce feasibility. It reduces classical virtual queue to an a-posteriori certificate while preserving no-regret behavior through gradient steps.
AI.result: Theoretical results: zero per-slot violation of modeled AoI state under one-step viability, O(√T) regret against any static safe comparator, closed-form static/dynamic regret bounds, Ω(√T) minimax lower bound, margin-safe variant against execution noise, deadline-induced competitive ratio. Empirical results: zero violations across all seeds on four-sensor adversarial trap channel, outperforming baselines (1.65%-64.0% missed slots), empirical regret stays below theoretical envelope.
AI.conclusion: OCO-PAoI-Hard provides the first framework for hard real-time scheduling of peak AoI deadlines under adversarial conditions, transforming the problem into time-varying constrained online convex optimization with provable zero per-slot safety guarantees and optimal regret scaling.

title: Sign Language Question Answering: A New Task, Benchmark, and Baseline for Sign Language Understanding
summary: Recent advances in sign language (SL) understanding (SLU) have led to remarkable progress in tasks such as continuous SL recognition and SL translation. However, these tasks are designed with predefined objectives, requiring models to learn a fixed mapping from sign videos to glosses or spoken-language sentences. As a result, they provide only a limited assessment of whether a model truly understands the semantic content of SL videos. To address this limitation, \textbf{we first propose a new task, Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA)}, which evaluates SL understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. Unlike previous SLU tasks, SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses multiple reasoning capabilities beyond recognition and translation. To facilitate this task, \textbf{we further construct two SignQA benchmarks} based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating question-answer pairs from existing gloss and sentence annotations using carefully designed templates. The resulting datasets cover five complementary question categories, including position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. \textbf{Finally, we propose a simple yet effective baseline model} equipped with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy, enabling effective knowledge transfer from existing SLU tasks while enhancing question-aware temporal feature modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future research on SLQA. Datasets are available at:{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hulala/SignQA-2026}.

AI.tldr: Proposes Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA) as a new task to comprehensively evaluate sign language understanding beyond traditional recognition/translation tasks, introduces two benchmarks, and presents an effective baseline model.
AI.motivation: Existing sign language understanding tasks (recognition/translation) are limited as they only test fixed mappings from videos to glosses/sentences, providing insufficient assessment of true semantic understanding of sign language content.
AI.method: 1) Introduces SLQA task for answering arbitrary natural language questions about sign videos; 2) Creates two SignQA benchmarks using template-based automatic generation of question-answer pairs from PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily; 3) Develops baseline with Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and in-domain knowledge transfer strategy.
AI.result: The baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across five question categories (position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, translation understanding), establishing strong benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: SLQA provides more flexible and comprehensive evaluation of sign language understanding capabilities, and the proposed approach effectively transfers knowledge from existing SLU tasks while enhancing question-aware feature modeling.

title: First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization Over Distributed Networks for Robust Coreset Selection
summary: With the rapid advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT), massive amounts of data are generated across distributed edge networks. Training models on full data incurs significant computational overhead and storage bottlenecks, rendering coreset selection a critical paradigm. Furthermore, given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the escalating demand for model robustness in real-world deployments, developing an effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital, yet remains largely unexplored.
