To this end, this work first characterizes the hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, and formulates the distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. Furthermore, to effectively solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner, the \underline{F}ederated \underline{F}irst-order \underline{C}onstrained \underline{T}rilevel \underline{O}ptimization (F$^2$CTO) is proposed, which synergistically integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation and a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, F$^2$CTO is the first method developed for distributed robust coreset selection, as well as the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization problems with level-wise constraints. Additionally, we prove that the proposed method achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-3/2})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed F$^2$CTO.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes F²CTO, the first federated optimization framework for distributed robust coreset selection in IoT edge networks, formulated as a trilevel optimization problem with provable convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: With IoT's rapid growth, massive distributed data makes full-data training computationally expensive. Local data privacy concerns and the need for robust models in real-world deployments create a gap: no existing distributed optimization framework effectively addresses robust coreset selection.
AI.method: The paper first formulates distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. It then proposes F²CTO (Federated First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization), which integrates hierarchical composite value-function reformulation with a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm.
AI.result: F²CTO achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε^{-3/2}) for finding an ε-stationary point. Empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the method's effectiveness and efficiency. This is the first distributed approach for both robust coreset selection and trilevel optimization with level-wise constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed F²CTO framework successfully addresses the critical challenge of distributed robust coreset selection in IoT edge networks, providing an efficient federated optimization solution with theoretical convergence guarantees and practical performance benefits.

title: MemTxn: A Transaction Boundary for Source-Supported Updates and Complete-State Recovery in Agent Memory
summary: Persistent memory lets long-running large language model agents reuse information across sessions and tasks. Yet errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval, but they do not provide a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery. We therefore propose MemTxn, a governance layer outside the answer model. MemTxn verifies whether an update is supported by its source. It also selects the visible version when facts conflict and restores the application-visible state after a fault. The system uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes, a Temporal Resolver to select versions, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state. On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations. It outperforms Dense by 17.06--24.07 points in five representative settings.

AI.tldr: MemTxn is a transaction system for LLM agent persistent memory that ensures reliable updates, conflict resolution, and fault recovery, outperforming existing approaches in accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: Persistent memory enables LLM agents to reuse information across sessions, but errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems focus on storage/retrieval but lack transaction boundaries for reliable updates and recovery.
AI.method: MemTxn is a governance layer outside the answer model with three key components: Ordered PatchTest to validate writes against sources, Temporal Resolver to select versions when facts conflict, and durable snapshot journal to recover state after faults.
AI.result: MemTxn accepted all 60 supported originals and rejected all 179 hard negatives in item-disjoint audit; restored complete active map under persistent multi-key faults; achieved highest average F1 across all configurations on MemoryAgentBench, outperforming Dense by 17.06-24.07 points.
AI.conclusion: MemTxn effectively addresses the reliability gap in LLM agent persistent memory by providing transaction boundaries, validation, conflict resolution, and fault recovery mechanisms, demonstrating superior performance over existing systems.

title: Certifying when decision-time information justifies adaptive experimentation
summary: Adaptive laboratories choose measurements during experiments, yet most methods begin after adaptation is permitted. We introduce Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories (\OPAL{}), a framework that decides whether adaptation should be enabled at all. \OPAL{} uses a precommitted contract to require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk and positive executed value after cost. We establish an impossibility boundary: source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derive a target-calibrated recovery. Applied to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion; its 5.18\% false-activation upper bound remained below a 7.5\% limit. Among six methods, only \OPAL{} combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing authorization as a distinct layer for safe adaptive science.

AI.tldr: OPAL is a framework that decides whether to enable adaptive measurements in experiments by using precommitted contracts requiring non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk, and positive executed value after cost.
AI.motivation: Current adaptive laboratory methods begin after adaptation is permitted, but there's a need to decide whether adaptation should be enabled at all. Adaptive science requires ensuring safe and valuable adaptation rather than assuming it's always beneficial.
AI.method: OPAL uses a precommitted contract requiring three criteria: (1) non-trivial adaptation, (2) controlled target risk, and (3) positive executed value after cost. It establishes impossibility boundaries and derives target-calibrated recovery methods for authorization decisions.
AI.result: Applied to an 11,265-compound Cell Painting dataset, OPAL's frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities, and achieved strictly positive executed value under worst-case completion with 5.18% false-activation upper bound (below 7.5% limit). Among six methods, only OPAL combined non-zero activation with this level of risk control.
AI.conclusion: OPAL establishes authorization as a distinct layer for safe adaptive science, distinguishing policy misalignment from non-certifiability. It enables controlled adaptation decisions rather than blanket permission, which is crucial for pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies.

title: Crossing the Margin Cliff: Toward Relearn-Robust LLM Unlearning via Margin Calibration
summary: Large language model unlearning is consistently fragile under relearn attacks. On TOFU, fine-tuning on twenty forget examples substantially recovers held-out forget-set ROUGE for every method we evaluate, and we trace this fragility to optimization geometry. The per-token answer margin of fourteen post-hoc methods spanning gradient, preference, and distillation families converges into a narrow band above the retain reference in 41 of 42 method--size cells, a regularity we call the margin cliff. We prove that this cliff follows whenever the retain coupling holds the diagnostic log-odds of forget content above a floor, a condition that token-saturating losses induce at stationarity and that we verify directly on 34 of 42 cells. Margin Calibration (\textsc{MC}) is a plug-in polish adding a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus, restoring forget-side pressure where the native loss saturates. Under a stated gradient-dominance condition, whose on-trajectory gradient signature we measure by instrumenting the polish, its stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an attack-budget upper bound on the relearn margin lift. Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells (panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L $0.41$ to $0.18$) and lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. A deployment variant matches these gains without a retain-trained reference.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Margin Calibration (MC), a method that makes language model unlearning more robust against relearn attacks by addressing optimization geometry issues, specifically the "margin cliff" phenomenon where previous methods fail.
AI.motivation: Current large language model unlearning methods are fragile and can be easily reversed through relearn attacks (fine-tuning on forget examples), particularly on benchmark datasets like TOFU where fine-tuning on just 20 forget examples substantially recovers performance on the forget set.
AI.method: The authors identify a "margin cliff" phenomenon where per-token answer margins converge into a narrow band above retain references. They propose Margin Calibration (MC) - a plug-in polish that adds a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus, which restores forget-side pressure where native losses saturate.
AI.result: MC wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells across multiple models (Llama-3, Llama-2-7B, Phi-3.5) and datasets, reducing post-attack ROUGE-L from 0.41 to 0.18 on average and lowering raw membership AUC on 13/14 cases, with reduced retain-side utility as the main trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Margin Calibration effectively addresses the fragility of language model unlearning by tackling optimization geometry issues, providing a theoretically-grounded solution that offers attack-budget upper bounds on relearn margin lift while maintaining practical effectiveness across diverse models and datasets.

title: Evaluation Protocols and Cross-Subject Generalization in EEG Emotion Recognition
comment: 41 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables including supplementary information. Submitted to Applied Intelligence
summary: Reported accuracy in electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not only the classifier. We separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, then use one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV as an illustrative case. In a protocol-matched subject-dependent check, the SEED result was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference value; the 3.40-point SEED-IV difference remained unresolved. Across 30 matched SEED subject-session trajectories, checkpoint selection based on repeated test-set evaluation increased mean window accuracy from 0.7855 at epoch 80 to 0.8892. Under five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, validation-selected checkpoints achieved training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 on SEED and 0.9920 on SEED-IV. Accuracy for entirely held-out participants was 0.5348 (95% conditional subject-level bias-corrected and accelerated [BCa] interval [0.4667, 0.5985]) on SEED. The SEED-IV estimate was 0.3954 ([0.3343, 0.4648]) and is reported only as secondary sensitivity evidence because its protocol-matched compatibility check remained unresolved. The observed train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting, but they do not isolate subject identity from implementation, preprocessing, representation, or distributional factors. Supporting analyses further showed that participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, while a development-selected tail-risk ensemble did not establish a positive gain in a separate final evaluation. Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results should therefore be reported as answers to different questions.

AI.tldr: EEG emotion recognition accuracy depends heavily on evaluation procedures, not just classifiers, with significant gaps between subject-dependent and held-out subject performance highlighting the need for clear reporting distinctions.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that reported accuracy in EEG emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not just the classifier, and to establish proper evaluation protocols for different research questions.
AI.method: Used archived DGCNN on SEED and SEED-IV datasets, separating target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rules. Performed protocol-matched subject-dependent checks, checkpoint selection via repeated test-set evaluation, five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, and held-out participant testing with statistical confidence intervals.
AI.result: Subject-dependent validation-selected checkpoints achieved near-perfect accuracies (0.9990 on SEED, 0.9920 on SEED-IV), but held-out subject performance dropped significantly (0.5348 on SEED, 0.3954 on SEED-IV). Checkpoint selection boosted mean window accuracy from 0.7855 to 0.8892. Participant rankings varied with representation and time scale, and tail-risk ensembles didn't show positive gain in final evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The substantial train-to-held-out-subject gaps suggest issues beyond simple optimization underfitting. Different evaluation procedures (subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, cross-session) answer different research questions and should be clearly reported separately to provide a complete picture of model performance.

title: Virtual Process Dossier: A Process-Aware Data Catalogue
summary: We propose the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that also captures workflow provenance. We developed VPD for multi-stage manufacturing use-cases where downstream AI-based optimization tasks require to distinct between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. VPD provides these datasets in a FAIR manner and makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit. Our contributions are: (1) the VPD ontology that serves as the catalogue's semantic core; (2) the VPD provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment; and (3) the VPD user interface that provides human-centered interaction with the VPD Knowledge Graph. The ontology and code are available at https://github.com/kubeluk/VirtualProcessDossier .

AI.tldr: A Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue called Virtual Process Dossier (VPD) that captures workflow provenance for manufacturing, making datasets FAIR and supporting AI optimization tasks.
AI.motivation: In multi-stage manufacturing, downstream AI-based optimization tasks need to distinguish between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. There's a need for a solution that provides datasets in a FAIR manner and makes workflow provenance explicit.
AI.method: Developed the VPD ontology as semantic core, created a provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into production environments, and built a user interface for human-centered interaction with the Knowledge Graph.
AI.result: Created a working VPD system that provides datasets in a FAIR manner and makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit for manufacturing use-cases.
AI.conclusion: VPD successfully addresses the need for distinguishing datasets in manufacturing workflows, provides FAIR data access, and makes workflow provenance transparent through its Knowledge Graph-based approach with ontology, integration framework, and user interface.

title: Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution
summary: Looped Transformers create a useful train- and test-time compute axis by reusing the same Transformer block over recurrent depth, increasing effective depth at a fixed parameter count. However, that shared block must then govern an entire trajectory of varying hidden states over trained and extrapolated depths. Furthermore, in additive-injection looped Transformers, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced at every recurrent step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state. In this paper, we propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), which is designed to reconcile input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. Specifically, SCSE retains input dependence through its learned anchor and initial deviation, allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through its zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is thereby a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias is the next deviation produced from the anchor itself and vanishes in SCSE, while nonzero deviations remain active and support state-dependent recurrent computation. Our theory shows that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero. Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablation studies identify the learned anchor and the anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as the primary contributors to the gain, and a trained-model case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

AI.tldr: Looped Transformers reuse the same block over recurrent depth for efficiency, but struggle with varying hidden states and input conditioning. The authors propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE) which reconciles input conditioning with reference-preserving recurrence through learned anchors and zero-deviation masks, ensuring exact anchor invariance.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers create a useful compute axis by reusing Transformer blocks over recurrent depth, increasing effective depth at fixed parameters. However, the shared block must handle varying hidden states across trained and extrapolated depths. Additive-injection looped Transformers have an input-conditioned signal reintroduced at each step, making it hard to preserve input-conditioned references while applying shared transitions.
AI.method: Propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE) which: 1) Retains input dependence through learned anchors and initial deviations, 2) Allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, 3) Guarantees exact anchor invariance through zero-deviation masks, making the anchor a one-step fixed point by construction, 4) Eliminates the zero-deviation forcing bias (setting it to zero) to resolve design choices in favor of exact anchor invariance.
AI.result: SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion. Ablation studies show the learned anchor and anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence are primary contributors to gains. Trained-model case studies demonstrate effective recurrent motion.
AI.conclusion: SCSE successfully reconciles input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence in looped Transformers. By guaranteeing exact anchor invariance through zero-deviation masks and learned anchors, it provides a principled solution that improves recurrent quality across multiple language modeling benchmarks while offering theoretical clarity about design choices.

title: Simplifying Neural Networks During Training
summary: Understanding and exploiting the training dynamics of overparameterized deep neural networks remains a central challenge in modern machine learning. Recent evidence on Neural Collapse (NC) shows that class representations and classifiers exhibit highly structured geometry, while the Tunnel Effect suggests that only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction. We combine these two perspectives and propose an NC-inspired training framework for simplifying deep networks during training. Our method monitors representation dynamics through the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable and efficient proxy for the variability collapse behavior, to identify both the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage at which simplification becomes viable. We then replace the trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model. Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of the full model. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at: https://github.com/LorenzoSciandra/NNS.

AI.tldr: A training framework that simplifies deep neural networks by monitoring representation dynamics to identify optimal simplification points and replace trailing layers with lightweight classification heads, achieving significant parameter reductions with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Despite recent insights into neural network training dynamics (Neural Collapse and Tunnel Effect), practical methods to simplify overparameterized deep networks during training while maintaining performance remain underdeveloped.
AI.method: Monitors representation dynamics using Inverse Fisher Criterion as a proxy for variability collapse to identify: 1) split point between feature extraction and classification layers, and 2) optimal training stage for simplification. Then replaces trailing layers with lightweight classification head and continues training reduced model.
AI.result: Substantial parameter reductions achieved while maintaining accuracy comparable to full models across image-classification benchmarks using MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures.
AI.conclusion: By combining insights from Neural Collapse and Tunnel Effect, this framework provides an effective approach to simplify deep networks during training, enabling parameter-efficient models without sacrificing performance.

title: Understanding Submodular Information Measure Based Objectives for Representation Learning: A Variance and Separation Perspective
summary:
Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for representation learning and multimodal learning. In particular, the SCORE framework~\cite{majee2024score} demonstrated that SIMs can serve as effective objectives for supervised contrastive learning. Despite their empirical success, however, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood.
  In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. We show that Total Information (TI) objectives characterize intra-class structure: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation that emphasizes rare and confusable classes. We further show that Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture complementary notions of inter-class structure: Graph Cut MI is closely related to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation through Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap.
  We validate these theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap. Across all settings, the empirical behavior closely matches the proposed theory. Our results provide the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures and offer principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a theoretical framework connecting Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) to classical representation learning concepts, showing how different SIM objectives characterize intra-class and inter-class geometric/statistical properties, validated through synthetic experiments.
AI.motivation: Despite the empirical success of Submodular Information Measures in representation and multimodal learning, their geometric and statistical properties remain poorly understood, creating a gap between practical success and theoretical understanding.
AI.method: Developed a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical representation learning concepts, analyzed Total Information and Mutual Information objectives for intra-class and inter-class structure characterization, and validated through controlled synthetic experiments varying variance, covariance, class imbalance, separation, and multimodal overlap.
AI.result: Showed that: 1) TI objectives characterize intra-class structure (Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance/covariance volume, Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation); 2) MI objectives capture inter-class structure (Graph Cut MI relates to centroid separation, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation via Mahalanobis distance, Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode overlap). Empirical behavior across all synthetic settings closely matches theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures, offering principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning based on specific geometric/statistical needs.

title: Back to All-Entity Ranking: Sampler-Dependent Evaluation in Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs
summary:
Next-destination prediction in continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) commonly ranks an observed interaction against sampled negative destinations. The resulting score is conditional on both the negative distribution and the number of candidates chosen by the researcher. We show that a non-uniform negative distribution changes the Bayes-optimal ranking, while even a finite candidate set drawn uniformly can destabilize model rankings and measured module effects.
  Time-varying source-destination history membership and model operations that use this information directly transmit the sampler's influence to the evaluation score. We examine this mechanism using a factorial evaluation of repeated and new positives against seen and unseen negatives, a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, and controlled representation interventions. Across six models on LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three of the four datasets. The measured effect of the same module also changes in magnitude and direction with the candidate-set size and training objective.
  These results establish that model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the stated candidate configuration. All-entity ranking evaluates every destination in a fixed catalog, eliminating negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original CTDG scorer. We therefore recommend all-entity ranking as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

AI.tldr: Next-destination prediction in dynamic graphs should use all-entity ranking instead of sampled-negative evaluation, as sampling choices affect model rankings and ablation conclusions.
AI.motivation: Current next-destination prediction methods use sampled negative destinations for ranking, which makes evaluation conditional on the negative distribution and candidate set size. This introduces instability in model comparisons and measured module effects.
AI.method: The authors conduct factorial evaluation of repeated vs new positives against seen vs unseen negatives, use a minimal scorer based on pair-history membership, and perform controlled representation interventions across six models on four datasets (LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, Wikipedia).
AI.result: Results show that model rankings change between uniform-20 sampled evaluation and full catalog evaluation on three of four datasets. Module effects change in magnitude and direction based on candidate-set size and training objective.
AI.conclusion: Model superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the evaluation configuration. All-entity ranking eliminates negative-selection bias and sampling variation while keeping the original scorer, making it preferable for architecture comparisons when destinations are enumerable.

title: FedOGL: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Open-World Multimodal Graph Learning
summary: Federated graph learning enables collaborative training over decentralized graph data without sharing raw graph information. As such risks evolve, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams, retain historical categories, and reject samples outside the known class space. In this setting, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting samples outside the current known class space. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs is not merely a classifier-level failure: old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedOGL}, a semantic-structural memory preservation framework. On the client side, FedOGL preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, FedOGL maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by \textbf{42.67\%}, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: FedOGL is a federated graph learning framework that addresses catastrophic forgetting in multimodal graph streams by preserving historical knowledge through semantic-structural memory preservation while learning emerging classes from private client data.
AI.motivation: In federated graph learning, clients need to learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting unknown samples. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs occurs not just at classifier level but through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation.
AI.method: FedOGL uses a semantic-structural memory preservation framework with two main components: 1) Client-side: preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. 2) Server-side: maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by 42.67% compared to best-performing baselines, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: FedOGL effectively addresses catastrophic forgetting in federated multimodal graph learning by preserving both semantic and structural knowledge through its dual client-server memory preservation mechanism, enabling robust continual learning while respecting data privacy constraints.

title: Orca: Neural Operators for Causal Reasoning in Continuous Time
summary: Structural causal models are the standard language for reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, but they describe static variables, typically measured once, and usually forbid cyclic dependencies. Many systems we care about, such as patients, climates, and economies, instead evolve continuously in time, are observed at irregular time points, and contain feedback loops. We argue that neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in this setting, and propose Orca, a framework in which each node of the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. We extend existing neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms: a mechanism computes the function value of a node from its parent nodes by taking several parent functions as input, respects the arrow of time, and treats latent exogenous noise as a function that can be inferred and reused for counterfactuals. We formalize the model class and demonstrate counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples. Code is available at https://github.com/gerritgr/orca

AI.tldr: ORCA is a framework that extends causal reasoning from static structural causal models to continuous-time systems using neural operators, enabling counterfactual reasoning for evolving systems with feedback loops.
AI.motivation: Structural causal models are limited to static variables measured once and typically forbid cyclic dependencies, but many real-world systems (patients, climates, economies) evolve continuously in time, are observed at irregular time points, and contain feedback loops.
AI.method: Proposes ORCA framework where each node of the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces using neural operators, extending architectures to respect the arrow of time and treat latent exogenous noise as inferable functions.
AI.result: Demonstrated counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples, showing the framework can handle evolving systems with feedback loops.
AI.conclusion: Neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in continuous-time systems, bridging the gap between traditional static causal models and real-world evolving systems with feedback dynamics.

title: Tight Sample Complexity for Low-Rank Adaptation: Matching Bounds and Rank Selection
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard mechanism for fine-tuning large pretrained models, yet its statistical properties remain only partially understood. Existing generalization results provide upper bounds of the form O~(sqrt(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n), but a matching lower bound is missing, and the question of how to choose the LoRA rank r has no formal answer. Both gaps are closed here. A local Rademacher argument establishes an upper bound of O~(rd/n) on the excess risk of the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, whenever the target adaptation has rank at most r. A matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) is then proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d x d}; the bound applies to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class. Combining the two yields a rank-selection dichotomy. For the constrained empirical risk minimizer, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For adaptive estimators of the nuclear-norm-then-truncate type, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Theta~(r* d / n) regardless of r. Taken together, the three results characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning within the well-specified locally quadratic regime, and identify the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself. Predictions of the theory are verified on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on real LoRA fine-tuning across three (model, task) configurations covering DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC. All configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

AI.tldr: This paper provides a complete statistical characterization of LoRA fine-tuning, establishing matching upper and lower bounds on excess risk, identifying optimal rank selection rules, and showing that the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty is specific to unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than the LoRA class itself.
AI.motivation: Despite LoRA becoming the standard for fine-tuning large pretrained models, its statistical properties are only partially understood. Existing generalization results lack matching lower bounds, and there's no formal guidance on how to choose the LoRA rank r. The paper aims to close both gaps and characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning.
AI.method: Uses local Rademacher arguments to establish upper bounds on excess risk, develops a Fano-type packing of rank-r subspaces to prove matching minimax lower bounds, analyzes rank-selection dichotomy for different estimators (constrained ERM vs adaptive estimators with nuclear-norm regularization followed by truncation), and validates predictions through synthetic trace-regression benchmarks and real LoRA fine-tuning experiments on DistilBERT and RoBERTa across multiple tasks.
AI.result: Establishes upper bound O~(rd/n) and matching lower bound Ω(rd/n) on excess risk; shows optimal rank equals intrinsic rank r* for constrained ERM (over-ranking hurts); demonstrates that for adaptive estimators, over-ranking is harmless with rate saturating at Θ~(r*d/n) regardless of r; validates theory with U-shaped validation loss patterns in real experiments, with statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks in two configurations.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete statistical characterization of LoRA fine-tuning, showing the statistical complexity is Θ~(rd/n) in the well-specified locally quadratic regime. It identifies the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself, providing formal guidance on rank selection for practical applications.

title: Search as Computation Allocation
summary: Many algorithms spend an internal resource before returning a decision and are evaluated only by the quality of that terminal output. We formalize such procedures as terminal computation-allocation problems: costly computations produce observations, update beliefs about a latent environment, and matter only through terminal decision loss. Bellman equations characterize optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. We then relate value of computation (VOC) to information. Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, whereas under simple regret VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity; moreover, information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly, although it gives a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions illustrate the same model under different computation topologies. Finally, under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases. The theory identifies a shared decision problem without asserting that one acquisition rule is universally optimal.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes terminal computation-allocation problems where costly computations produce observations and update beliefs, but only the terminal decision matters. It connects value of computation to information theory, showing relationships and limitations of information gain metrics.
AI.motivation: Many algorithms use internal computational resources before making final decisions, but are only evaluated by the quality of their terminal outputs. There's a need to formalize how computational effort should be optimally allocated in such terminal decision-making scenarios, connecting computational value to information theory principles.
AI.method: The paper formalizes terminal computation-allocation problems using Bellman equations to characterize optimal allocation under various constraints (fixed budgets, priced computation, exact certification). It analyzes relationships between value of computation (VOC) and information metrics, particularly showing connections between mutual information and myopic VOC under log loss, and relating VOC to knowledge-gradient under simple regret. The framework is applied to different computation topologies including bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions.
AI.result: The analysis shows that mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, while under simple regret VOC becomes a knowledge-gradient quantity. Importantly, information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly despite providing a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Under explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error models, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search emerging as limiting cases.
AI.conclusion: The theory provides a unified framework for understanding computational resource allocation in terminal decision problems without asserting universal optimality of any specific acquisition rule. It reveals fundamental connections between information theory and computational decision-making while highlighting limitations of naive information gain metrics.

title: Event-Structured Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differentiable Critical Clearing Boundaries
summary: Transient-stability assessment determines whether a power system can recover after a disturbance and is therefore essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages. A key metric is the critical clearing time (CCT), which specifies the maximum time available to clear a fault before synchronism is lost. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. We propose an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns its representation with the pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin defines a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction through a distilled readout. We further prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate, in which exact event chaining eliminates separate state-interface defect terms. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show that ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: An event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) for power system transient stability assessment that accurately estimates critical clearing times by aligning with swing dynamics and enforcing exact state chaining across fault events.
AI.motivation: Transient-stability assessment is essential for power system reliability but challenging due to complicated fault-clearing dynamics requiring repeated simulations. Traditional methods struggle with reliable critical clearing time (CCT) estimation across various fault severities and clearing times.
AI.method: Proposes an event-structured PINN that aligns with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics with exact state chaining across event interfaces. Uses a smooth trajectory-induced stability margin for differentiable CCT boundary approximation, enabling accurate boundary extraction and local sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over neural-surrogate baselines on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Shows effectiveness in full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The ES-PINN framework provides an effective and computationally efficient approach for reliable transient stability assessment and CCT estimation by leveraging event-structured physics-informed learning with exact state chaining across fault events.

title: An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding
summary:
Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

AI.tldr: A new benchmark MSEval evaluates multi-agent coding on real-world software projects with authentic environments, measuring performance across multiple dimensions including functional success, latency, and token cost.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent coding benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical costs (time and money), conflate reasoning with communication, and only reward superficial completion rather than measuring real-world effectiveness.
AI.method: They create MSEval with 10 authentic full-stack projects across 10 domains, using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics. The execution engine LegoGent tests 10 collaboration topologies with agents coordinating via periodic sync intervals and deploying through native CI/CD pipelines. The grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost.
AI.result: Across 100 runs, MSEval shows organizational topology is as important as model capability in shaping speed-cost-quality trade-offs. For identical tasks and models, varying topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with highest quality, while heavy managerial oversight degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software, revealing that team structure significantly impacts multi-agent coding performance in practical settings.

title: NMINE: Normalized Mutual Information Neural Estimation
summary:
Mutual information is a general measure of statistical dependence that captures both linear and nonlinear relationships between random variables. For continuous and multidimensional variables For continuous multidimensional variables, mutual information must be estimated from samples. Because mutual information is unbounded, its values are not directly comparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation by converting mutual information into a normalized dependency score. Recent work has demonstrated the practical value of normalized mutual information in applications such as molecular dynamics {arXiv:2405.04980} and interpretable machine learning {arXiv:2409.16768}, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability {arXiv:2410.07642}.
  In this paper, we propose a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables. The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator {arXiv:1801.04062} with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators {arXiv:1905.12957}. Mutual information is estimated using the Donsker--Varadhan representation, while marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution, from which entropy is recovered. The resulting estimator provides a neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation {arXiv:2405.04980}.
  Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline. These results indicate that neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

AI.tldr: A neural network-based estimator for normalized mutual information that improves accuracy over traditional k-nearest-neighbor methods for continuous multidimensional variables.
AI.motivation: Mutual information is a valuable statistical measure but is unbounded and not comparable across different datasets or dimensions. Normalized mutual information addresses this, but existing estimators have limitations in dimensionality sensitivity and numerical stability.
AI.method: Combines MINE-based neural mutual information estimation with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators. Uses Donsker-Varadhan representation for mutual information and learns divergence between marginal distributions and uniform reference distributions to recover entropy.
AI.result: Experiments on Gaussian data from 1 to 8 dimensions show improved accuracy over KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline.
AI.conclusion: Neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings, offering better accuracy than traditional k-nearest-neighbor approaches.

title: Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is central to improving long-CoT reasoning in large language models. Critic-free methods such as GRPO convert response-level rewards into advantages and uniformly broadcast them across tokens, overlooking their unequal contributions to the final outcome. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead provides dense distributional supervision by minimizing the forward KL divergence between an unprivileged policy and a privileged self-teacher, implicitly assuming that the resulting likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. We test this premise by fixing each sampled trajectory and re-scoring it under two opposing outcome conditions, one asserting correctness and the other incorrectness. Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in the induced optimization signals. Large shifts also concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, whereas tokens carrying problem-specific reasoning content are less sensitive. These findings show that privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, while their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Based on these observations, we propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple extension of GRPO that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates. Targeted ablations further corroborate our diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that privileged self-teacher shifts in OPSD don't provide reliable answer-aligned directions, instead reflecting counterfactual sensitivity. They propose CSCR, a GRPO extension that reallocates credit away from highly sensitive tokens, improving performance on long-CoT math reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing methods like GRPO and OPSD have limitations: GRPO uniformly broadcasts rewards across tokens ignoring unequal contributions, while OPSD assumes privileged self-teacher shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information, which may not be true.
AI.method: The authors test OPSD's premise by fixing sampled trajectories and re-scoring under opposing outcome conditions. They analyze token sensitivity patterns and propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), which reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages while preserving the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction.
AI.result: Findings show: 1) Most affected tokens shift in same direction under both correct/incorrect conditions, 2) Large shifts concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, 3) Problem-specific reasoning tokens are less sensitive, 4) Privileged shifts don't provide reliable answer-aligned directions. On long-CoT math reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline. Ablations confirm privilege-induced directions are unreliable and moderate downweighting is most effective.
AI.conclusion: Privileged self-teacher shifts in on-policy self-distillation fail to provide reliable answer-aligned learning directions. Instead, shifts primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity, not token-level learning value. The proposed CSCR method addresses this by reallocating credit away from highly sensitive tokens, leading to improved performance in long-chain-of-thought reasoning tasks.

title: VESTIGE: A Knowledge-Guided Masking Strategy for Corruption-Aware Fine-Tuning of Genomic Transformers, Validated on Ancient DNA Reconstruction
summary: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning applies a uniform masking probability across every token position, assuming reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic. When the degradation process is characterised and concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption fails: at peak damage sites the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. We introduce VESTIGE, a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. We apply it to ancient DNA (aDNA) reconstruction, where cytosine deamination produces a position-dependent C-to-T / G-to-A gradient quantified per-position by mapDamage2. Rescaling so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% - identical to standard MLM - isolates spatial redistribution as the sole variable, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed across both DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes). Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE leads standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions (three genes) even under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, the 1.76% remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts. The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile - FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore - substitutes directly for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

AI.tldr: VESTIGE is a parameter-free MLM masking method that aligns masking distribution with position-specific corruption profiles, outperforming standard uniform masking for degraded sequence reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Standard MLM uses uniform masking across positions, which fails when degradation is position-dependent (e.g., aDNA cytosine deamination), causing models to underperform random predictors at peak damage sites.
AI.method: VESTIGE replaces standard MLM collator by scaling masking distribution to match empirically measured per-position corruption profiles (like mapDamage2 for aDNA), keeping mean masking rate identical to isolate spatial redistribution as the only variable.
AI.result: VESTIGE consistently outperforms standard MLM across all terminal-zone widths (+4.18 to +10.35 pp improvement), reduces validation cross-entropy by 13%, produces high-quality ESMFold reconstructions (TM-score > 0.95), and passes biosecurity checks with 98.2% clearance.
AI.conclusion: VESTIGE enables knowledge-guided training for degraded/noisy sequences by incorporating measurable corruption profiles, making it domain-agnostic for applications from ancient DNA to nanopore sequencing.

title: Dynamic Spectral Filtering for Temporal Graph Learning: Learning Evolving Propagation Operators
summary: Temporal graph learning is commonly organized around the evolution of node states or the encoding of interaction histories. We study an underexplored, operator-centric question: should the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time? We introduce Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), which represents propagation at snapshot t by a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. DSF explicitly treats these compact multi-order coefficients as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes updates, while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes. On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs attain AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K to 133K trainable parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds of training per epoch. Against the closely related DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3 to 8.6 times fewer parameters, 25 to 33 times less GPU memory, and 5 to 19 times less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3 to 38.6 times less GPU memory. These results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement.

AI.tldr: Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF) introduces evolving graph propagation mechanisms with time-dependent Chebyshev polynomial coefficients treated as recurrent states, achieving high efficiency and competitive performance on temporal link prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Most temporal graph learning focuses on node state evolution or interaction history encoding, leaving the question of whether graph propagation mechanisms should themselves evolve over time largely unexplored. The authors aim to address this operator-centric gap and create computationally efficient temporal graph models.
AI.method: DSF represents propagation at each snapshot using Chebyshev polynomial filters with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. These coefficients are treated as compact recurrent temporal states, updated through a recurrent branch with multiplicative global and order-specific gates to regulate their magnitude. The temporal state remains independent of node count, ensuring efficiency.
AI.result: On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, DSF achieves AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860 respectively, using only 93K-133K parameters, 68-182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6-2.1 seconds per training epoch. Compared to DEFT baseline, DSF uses 8.3-8.6× fewer parameters, 25-33× less GPU memory, and 5-19× less time per epoch while maintaining competitive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Direct spectral-response evolution serves as a useful temporal inductive bias for graph learning, particularly when computational efficiency is a primary requirement. DSF demonstrates that evolving propagation mechanisms themselves can be effective and efficient for temporal graph tasks.

title: Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules
summary: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

AI.tldr: Dynamic batch size scheduling guided by learning rate schedule improves large language model training efficiency compared to static batch sizes.
AI.motivation: Current deep learning practices typically use static batch sizes throughout training, ignoring the interaction between learning rate and batch size on training dynamics, which limits optimization efficiency.
AI.method: Analyze deep learning dynamics through convex optimization lens to derive joint characterization of loss in terms of both learning rate and batch size schedules. Develop closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any given learning rate schedule.
AI.result: Derived joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines. The dynamic batch size schedule significantly improves large language model training efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic batch size scheduling, when properly coordinated with learning rate schedules, is crucial for efficient large language model training and outperforms traditional static batch size approaches.

title: MMHBench: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark for Mental Health Understanding in Long-Form Videos
summary: Mental health understanding in long-form videos requires nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states. Existing benchmarks largely reduce this task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. To address this limitation, we introduce MMHBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding, comprising 268 long-form videos and 2,184 carefully curated questions. MMHBench organizes the evaluation into two complementary settings: (1) third-person assessment, consisting of 605 questions that focus on the interpretation of observable behaviors and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking, comprising 1,579 questions that require perspective-conditioned reasoning to identify the interpretation of the mental state supported by the available multimodal evidence. We propose a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives. The generated questions are refined through multi-role feedback and iterative optimization, followed by expert-guided verification to ensure quality and validity. Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), spanning both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

AI.tldr: MMHBench is a new multimodal benchmark for mental health understanding in long-form videos, featuring 268 videos with 2,184 curated questions across third-person assessment and first-person perspective-taking tasks, created using a Multi-Agent Question Generation framework and revealing significant challenges for current MLLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing mental health benchmarks reduce the complex task of mental health understanding to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or just rely on superficial correlations. The field lacks comprehensive benchmarks that capture nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states in long-form videos.
AI.method: 1) Introduced MMHBench with 268 long-form videos and 2,184 carefully curated questions organized into two settings: third-person assessment (605 questions) and first-person perspective-taking (1,579 questions). 2) Developed a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives. 3) Implemented multi-role feedback and iterative optimization for question refinement. 4) Conducted expert-guided verification to ensure question quality and validity. 5) Evaluated 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) including both open-source and closed-source models.
AI.result: The extensive evaluation demonstrated that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging for current state-of-the-art MLLMs. The benchmark revealed significant gaps in models' ability to perform nuanced reasoning about psychological phenomena, even among leading closed-source models.
AI.conclusion: MMHBench addresses a critical gap in mental health AI evaluation by providing a comprehensive benchmark that requires true understanding of psychological phenomena rather than superficial pattern recognition. The benchmark's design with multi-perspective questions and rigorous validation process establishes a new standard for evaluating mental health understanding in long-form videos, highlighting the limitations of current models and pointing toward future research directions.

title: Improving the Robustness/Accuracy Tradeoff Against Adversarial Attacks Using Information Bottleneck Distillation Through Dual Teachers
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in classical machine learning problems. However, they are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Countermeasures proposed in the literature, notably Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) introduced by Kuang et al., degrade the classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving the robustness to adversarial inputs. In this work, we extend the IBD framework by introducing an extra teacher model (clean teacher) trained with only clean inputs, into the distillation process from a robust teacher model trained by adversarial training. The features of both clean and robust teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that the proposed method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to the original IBD, while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. Furthermore, our methods are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the recent dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly in terms of the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. We also analyze the impact of different training settings that have different influences on the attention module.

AI.tldr: A dual-teacher information bottleneck distillation method that improves clean accuracy while maintaining adversarial robustness by incorporating both clean and robust teachers with cross-layer attention.
AI.motivation: Current adversarial defense methods like Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) degrade classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving robustness. There's a need for methods that maintain both clean accuracy and adversarial robustness.
AI.method: Extends IBD framework by adding a clean teacher model trained only on clean inputs alongside the robust teacher. Features from both teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix that learns attention patterns between different network layers.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to original IBD while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. It's competitive with state-of-the-art approaches like B-MTARD, particularly in harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The dual-teacher approach with cross-layer attention effectively balances clean accuracy and adversarial robustness, addressing a key limitation of existing adversarial defense methods. The attention mechanism analysis provides insights into how different training settings affect feature transfer.

title: A Cross-Architecture Audit of Direction-Based Inference-Time Defences in Vision-Language Models
summary: Inference time defences against vision language model jailbreaks often subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream at a chosen decoder layer. We compare five defence candidates across 15 model and layer cells from four architectural families under a magnitude controlled protocol that matches the intervention size for each prompt and pairs every direction with a random control of the same norm. The candidates are the mean image conditioning shift, a CMRM style refusal direction, a ShiftDC style attack specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss remains at the measurement noise floor in every family. The prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, while the attack specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction specific in 13 of 15 cells, but strongly architecture specific and nontransferable across the only dimension compatible pair, LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. We also connect text only and multimodal refusal geometry. The CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells, with mean 0.35, range 0.17 to 0.65, 15 to 25 times the random vector null, and a sign test p value of about 3e-5. These results show that the two recipes recover partially overlapping geometry and that direction based defences should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family.

AI.tldr: Study compares five inference-time defenses against vision-language model jailbreaks using magnitude-controlled interventions, finding no single method dominates both safety and utility across different architectures.
AI.motivation: Current inference-time defenses against VLM jailbreaks use various directional interventions, but it's unclear which approaches work best across different model architectures while maintaining utility.
AI.method: Compares five defense candidates across 15 model-layer combinations from four architectural families using a magnitude-controlled protocol with matched intervention sizes. Methods include: mean image conditioning shift, CMRM refusal direction, ShiftDC attack-specific residual, prompt instruction to ignore image, and random control.
AI.result: No single defense dominates both refusal recovery and utility preservation. Image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and maintains utility. Prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL. Attack-specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. Image conditioning direction is architecture-specific and nontransferable between LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. CMRM direction shows significant alignment with image conditioning shift across all models.
AI.conclusion: Different defense methods work best on different architectures; direction-based defenses should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family as refusal geometry shows partial overlap across methods but strong architectural specificity.

title: ROCS: Request-Oriented Compute Sharing for Efficient Large-Scale Recommendation
summary:
Modern recommendation models gain prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints cap how far systems can scale.
  In this work, we propose Request-Oriented Compute Sharing (ROCS), a modeling and inference paradigm that exploits a unique property of recommendation inference: each user request is evaluated against many candidates, while request-side features are shared across candidates. ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request rather than once per candidate, significantly improving inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality. To realize this paradigm, we develop Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, and Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures. To support efficient GPU deployment, we co-design In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) that significantly accelerates ROCS model execution.
  Experiments on public benchmarks show that ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, ROCS achieves up to a 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

AI.tldr: ROCS (Request-Oriented Compute Sharing) is a recommendation system paradigm that improves inference efficiency by sharing request-side computations across candidate evaluations, achieving up to 3x QPS improvement without quality loss.
AI.motivation: Modern recommendation models face production cost constraints that limit scaling despite potential quality gains. The unique property of recommendation inference - each user request is evaluated against many candidates while request-side features are shared - presents an opportunity for optimization.
AI.method: ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible and isolates candidate-dependent representations. The authors develop: 1) Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, 2) Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures, and 3) In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) for efficient GPU deployment.
AI.result: Experiments show ROCS improves quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. Production-scale results include: up to 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation, and 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with 50% QPS gain on short-form video ranking models.
AI.conclusion: ROCS has been successfully deployed across large-scale recommendation systems (ads, organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages) with varying inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

title: IFHierBench: Hierarchical Instruction Following for Large Language Models
summary: Instruction-following ability is critical for deploying large language models in real-world applications, where downstream components depend on the output satisfying specific constraints. Modern deployments increasingly handle the full task in a single LLM call, with one prompt specifying a layered output whose overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy concrete constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat the constraint set as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, so they cannot scope a check to a particular section of the output. We introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies satisfaction at every scope. Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy and that accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. Reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability.

AI.tldr: IFHierBench is a new hierarchical instruction-following benchmark that reveals current LLMs struggle with nested constraints, with even top models barely exceeding 50% accuracy on prompts with multi-level structural requirements.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM deployments increasingly require handling full tasks in single calls with layered output structures where overall artifacts, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy specific constraints.
