Existing benchmarks treat constraints as flat lists applied uniformly to responses, lacking the ability to scope checks to particular output sections, which doesn't reflect real-world usage where hierarchical constraints are common.
AI.method: The authors introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark with 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints. Each prompt is paired with a deterministic checker that verifies constraint satisfaction at every scope (overall artifact, sections, and nested fields). They evaluate seven leading proprietary and open-weight models on this benchmark.
AI.result: Even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy, and accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. This indicates that reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, with performance worsening significantly as the hierarchical complexity increases.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs have significant limitations in hierarchical instruction-following with nested constraints. This motivates the need for future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability in real-world applications where layered output structures are common.

title: DAS-PMVC: A Framework for Partial Multi-View Clustering via Dual Alignment and Structure Enhancement
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: In recent years, multi-view clustering has attracted widespread research interest. However, due to limitations in data collection devices, data across different views often suffer from misalignment, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). To mitigate the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, this paper proposes a framework for partial multi-view clustering via dual alignment and structure enhancement (DAS-PMVC), which leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance. Specifically, DAS-PMVC includes three parts: \textbf{anchor graph structure alignment}, where sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space are derived from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; \textbf{structure-enhanced feature learning}, where the model learns view structure information through pretraining and combines multi-view graph convolutional networks to further extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure to improve the discriminative power of representations; and \textbf{a dual alignment strategy}, where initial alignment is performed through the anchor graph in the pretraining phase, and contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm are introduced in the training phase to further optimize the alignment of latent features. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority.

AI.tldr: DAS-PMVC is a new partial multi-view clustering framework that addresses view misalignment through dual alignment and structure enhancement, outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Multi-view clustering faces challenges due to data collection limitations causing misalignment across views (partial view alignment problem). Existing methods struggle with view asymmetry and irrelevant samples that degrade clustering performance.
AI.method: Proposes DAS-PMVC framework with three key components: (1) anchor graph structure alignment for initial view alignment using consistent latent space, (2) structure-enhanced feature learning combining pretraining and multi-view graph convolutional networks for better feature extraction, and (3) dual alignment strategy using contrastive learning and Hungarian algorithm for further optimization.
AI.result: Experimental results on various datasets show DAS-PMVC outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, demonstrating effectiveness and superiority.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DAS-PMVC framework effectively addresses partial view alignment problems in multi-view clustering through dual alignment and structure enhancement, providing a robust solution that improves clustering performance over existing approaches.

title: One Anchor for All: Unified Multilingual and Multimodal Safety Alignment for LVLMs
summary: As large vision-language models (LVLMs) are deployed globally, the combination of multilingual instructions and visual information makes malicious attacks more covert and sophisticated than ever before. However, existing methods isolate language and modality defenses, which, coupled with the scarcity of safety data and high fine-tuning costs, makes it difficult for models to defend against compound attacks. To address this severe challenge, we propose a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework driven by modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). First, we identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples, quantifying functional saliency through activation strength and downstream impact. Then, by intersecting these unimodal neurons within each language, we extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) responsive to both visual and textual risks, bridging the safety representation gap between modalities. Furthermore, using English as a semantic anchor, we intersect MS-Neurons across languages to identify modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons), serving as key defenses against compound attacks. Finally, we update only this minimal subset of shared neurons (~0.03% of parameters), transferring English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

AI.tldr: A neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework that identifies shared safety neurons across modalities and languages to defend against multilingual multimodal compound attacks with minimal parameter updates.
AI.motivation: As large vision-language models are deployed globally, malicious attacks combining multilingual instructions and visual information become more covert and sophisticated. Existing methods isolate language and modality defenses, have scarce safety data, and high fine-tuning costs, making them ineffective against compound attacks.
AI.method: Proposes MLS-Neurons framework: 1) Identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful/benign samples, measuring activation strength and downstream impact. 2) Extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) by intersecting unimodal neurons across visual and textual risks. 3) Identify modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons) by intersecting MS-Neurons across languages using English as semantic anchor. 4) Update only minimal subset of shared neurons (~0.03% parameters).
AI.result: The method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility of the models.
AI.conclusion: The neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework effectively addresses compound multilingual multimodal attacks by identifying and updating shared safety neurons, enabling efficient safety alignment with minimal parameter updates while maintaining model utility.

title: Train Small, Deploy Large: Zero-Shot GNN Transfer Through Geometric Renormalization
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes and typically require scalable training techniques for even larger graphs. This raises a central question: when can a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining? We introduce a zero-shot transfer protocol in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), and the resulting weights are transferred directly to the original network. Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. We further find that learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. These findings suggest that structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

AI.tldr: GNNs trained on geometrically coarse-grained graphs can be zero-shot transferred to full-resolution graphs with preserved performance, suggesting structural similarity matters more than network size for transferability.
AI.motivation: GNNs face scalability challenges at million-node scales requiring complex training techniques. The paper investigates whether models trained on scaled-down graph replicas can be deployed on full-resolution graphs without retraining, addressing the infrastructure sensitivity of large-scale GNN applications.
AI.method: Introduces zero-shot transfer protocol where GNNs are trained on graphs coarse-grained via geometric renormalization (GR). The trained weights are then directly transferred to the original full-resolution graphs without additional training.
AI.result: Training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves most of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training costs. Learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales across synthetic and real-world networks.
AI.conclusion: Structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures that can efficiently operate across different graph resolutions.

title: Meta-Task: Turning Terminal Task Synthesis into a Terminal Task for Scalable Agent Training
summary: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, yet acquiring such data remains a significant challenge. Existing synthesis methods face two key limitations: (1) weak reliability caused by the disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability due to dependence on existing repositories. We propose Meta-Task, a framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself: an agent operates within a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, so that synthesized components are checked for internal consistency and executability within the generation loop itself. Building upon this, we decouple the target task requirements along multiple dimensions, introduce a multi-phase mechanism that dynamically designs novel task specifications before producing the actual tasks, and incorporate optional external material support to enhance diversity and realism. We additionally apply LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure the quality of the final training data. Experiments on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

AI.tldr: Meta-Task is a framework that transforms terminal task synthesis into a terminal task itself, using an agent in a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks while ensuring executability and quality.
AI.motivation: Existing terminal task synthesis methods suffer from weak reliability due to disconnect between task generation and real execution, and limited diversity/scalability due to dependence on existing repositories. There's a need for diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories for training terminal agents at scale.
AI.method: Proposes Meta-Task framework that: 1) Treats terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself, 2) Uses an agent in real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, 3) Decouples target task requirements along multiple dimensions, 4) Implements multi-phase mechanism to dynamically design novel task specifications before producing actual tasks, 5) Incorporates optional external material support, and 6) Applies LLM-as-Judge filtering for quality assurance.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively on Terminal-Bench 2.0, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.
AI.conclusion: Meta-Task provides an effective framework for scalable, diverse, and verifiable terminal task synthesis that addresses key limitations of existing methods, enabling better training data generation with less data requirement while maintaining high quality and reliability.

title: Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold
summary: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

AI.tldr: A framework that treats RL-trained policies as local solution probes, then constructs complementary teacher ensembles through expansion (RGRPO) and compresses them via distillation (TU-OPD) to create stronger students than any individual teacher.
AI.motivation: RL-trained policies often amplify only a subset of valid solution modes, making them incomplete teachers. They should be viewed as local probes of multi-basin reasoning manifolds rather than globally reliable supervisors.
AI.method: Expand-then-compress framework: 1) Expansion stage uses Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) to train complementary teachers from common initialization, redirecting later rounds toward uncovered examples. 2) Compression stage uses reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) where students learn from their own response prefixes, with weighted losses based on teacher quality. 3) Consensus-Residual Decomposition preserves specialist token preferences during teacher aggregation.
AI.result: Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms strongest individual teacher across mathematical reasoning (+2.0%), code generation (+8.3%), and instruction following (+6.9%) domains while retaining single-model inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Stronger students are obtained not by selecting single better teachers, but by deliberately constructing and compressing complementary teacher unions, establishing this as a simple but powerful principle for policy distillation.

title: The Geometric Nature and a Free Proxy for Flow-Matching Uncertainty
summary: Flow matching (FM) has become a popular action head paradigm for modern embodied models. However, as a conditional generative model, it does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks even when it misinterprets the scene or encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Therefore, determining when an FM-generated action can be trusted is essential for safe deployment, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods on real-time control suffer from several issues: extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability. In this work, we provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing that uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Building on this observation, we introduce denoising acceleration ($\mathrm{accel}$), a highly-generalizable and cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that $\mathrm{accel}$ is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty and further test its utility in online failure detection. Results show that $\mathrm{accel}$ identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or even outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budget. Code and demos available at: https://github.com/rrrrrrzy/fm-geometry.

AI.tldr: Acceleration of the denoising trajectory provides a free, efficient uncertainty proxy for flow matching models, enabling online failure detection without extra training or computation.
AI.motivation: Flow matching models used in embodied AI lack explicit uncertainty estimation, making it hard to know when generated actions are trustworthy, especially for OOD inputs. Existing uncertainty estimation methods are too costly or impractical for real-time control.
AI.method: Introduces denoising acceleration as a cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass. Based on geometric interpretation showing FM uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction velocity field.
AI.result: Acceleration proves to be a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty and effectively identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or outperforming more expensive baseline methods across various settings.
AI.conclusion: Denoising acceleration provides an efficient, generalizable way to estimate uncertainty in flow matching models for real-time embodied AI deployment, enabling safer operation without additional computational cost.

title: RIPPLE: Generating Multi-Channel Phase, Not Recovering It
summary: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity, while phase is delegated to a recovery module---Griffin--Lim, a vocoder, or a latent decoder---applied independently to each channel. For multi-channel waveforms this delegation is costly: the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in the phase relationships between channels, precisely what channel-independent recovery cannot produce. The cost is also invisible, since the magnitude-based metrics common to both fields barely move when inter-channel phase coherence collapses---so a pipeline can discard the physical information in its output while still scoring well. We argue that phase should be generated, not recovered, and present RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning), which reinterprets Griffin--Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator: initialized from the source phase, this prior carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines it toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation---two physically unrelated domains---RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on the coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. The seismic case is decisive: across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the $57.3^\circ$ random expectation, whereas learned phase reduces it to $33.8^\circ$.

AI.tldr: RIPPLE generates phase relationships between multi-channel signals instead of recovering them independently per channel, preserving physical spatial information that traditional magnitude-based methods lose.
AI.motivation: Current generative models focus on synthesizing magnitude spectra while delegating phase recovery to independent channel modules like Griffin-Lim or vocoders. This approach fails for multi-channel data (spatial audio, seismograms) where physical content resides in phase relationships between channels. Channel-independent phase recovery discards this crucial spatial information, but the loss goes unnoticed because standard magnitude-based metrics don't measure inter-channel phase coherence.
AI.method: RIPPLE reinterprets Griffin-Lim as a phase prior rather than final estimator. It initializes from source phase to preserve inter-channel structure, then uses a rectified flow to refine toward target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. The method generates phase rather than recovering it independently per channel.
AI.result: Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation, RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on coherence metrics. In seismic applications, per-channel recovery left S-wave polarization error near 57.3° (random expectation), while learned phase reduced it to 33.8° across architecturally distinct generators.
AI.conclusion: Phase should be generated, not recovered independently for each channel. RIPPLE demonstrates that explicitly modeling inter-channel phase relationships preserves physical spatial information crucial for multi-channel audio and seismography applications, overcoming a fundamental limitation of traditional magnitude-focused approaches.

title: Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL
comment: full version of a paper accepted at ISWC26
summary: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates automated learning of SHACL shapes for graph validation using positive and negative example nodes, focusing on a core SHACL fragment equivalent to Description Logic ELI with various recursive semantics.
AI.motivation: SHACL shapes are crucial for data graph validation, and automatic shape learning is essential for knowledge graph applications. The need exists to learn shape expressions from example nodes that correctly classify positive and negative examples.
AI.method: The paper uses the fitting approach: given sets P (positive nodes) and N (negative nodes) from an input graph, compute a shape expression C that validates at every node in P and none in N. The focus is on a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to Description Logic ELI, considering three semantics for recursive shape catalogues: well-founded, stable, and supported.
AI.result: The authors address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation problems. They establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.
AI.conclusion: The research provides foundational complexity results for SHACL shape learning, characterizing the computational difficulty of fitting problems in different semantic frameworks and identifying tractable special cases.

title: LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

AI.tldr: LSPO introduces a scaffolding mechanism that recovers lost gradients on "cliff" prompts where standard RLVR fails, improving mathematical reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: RLVR for mathematical reasoning has a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts where all sampled rollouts fail, the group-normalized advantage is zero, so GRPO produces no gradient. This prevents learning precisely on the most challenging prompts at the frontier of model capability.
AI.method: LSPO (LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization) detects cliff prompts during sampling, fits a small LoRA adapter via supervised learning on ground-truth solutions, re-rolls cliffs with base-plus-adapter model, splices successful completions back into RL batch with importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base model alone. The adapter receives only supervised gradient and is discarded.
AI.result: On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, LSPO outperforms DAPO baseline across 16 (benchmark, pass@k) metrics. Gains include +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1. Average improvement across all cells is +3.8 points.
AI.conclusion: LSPO effectively recovers gradients lost in standard RLVR on cliff prompts, enabling better learning on challenging mathematical reasoning problems and achieving consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks.

title: From Scoring to Acting: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
summary: Recent work on LLM agents is shifting from external capability elicitation to capability internalization, enabling agents to retain useful skills without retrieval at inference time. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising direction, but many existing methods typically supervise students by scoring actions along student-generated trajectories. Such supervision has two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. We therefore advocate outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories. Based on this view, we propose Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD). OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show that OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

AI.tldr: OVCSD is a novel self-distillation method that uses outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories to effectively internalize skills in LLM agents, outperforming existing methods while using minimal privileged interactions during training.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) methods have limitations: 1) teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and 2) action-level scores underutilize information from both teacher and student rollouts and their behavioral relationships. This motivates a need for better supervision that verifies teacher actions against actual outcomes and leverages comparative learning across trajectories.
AI.method: OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, retains only outcome-verified successful continuations, and applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence point to distill the post-divergence teacher suffix behavior.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7% and 5.4% absolute success-rate improvements over strongest baselines on respective benchmarks, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-verified teacher supervision combined with comparative learning over trajectories provides an effective approach for internalizing skills in LLM agents, enabling better skill retention without retrieval at inference time while being computationally efficient.

title: Revisiting Predictive Process Monitoring in the Age of Foundation Models: A Comparative Study of Sequence, Tabular, and LLM Approaches
summary: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) leverages event logs to forecast the future of running process instances, for instance, predicting the next activity, the remaining time until case completion, or the time to the next event. While PPM research in recent years has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, foundation-model approaches---particularly large language models (LLMs)---are increasingly explored for PPM. At the same time, tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM. Thus, it remains unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape. This paper compares the three modeling paradigms both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The results show that sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction, whereas tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs usually lagging behind despite higher cost.

AI.tldr: This paper compares three predictive process monitoring paradigms: classical sequence models (LSTMs), large language models (LLMs), and tabular foundation models, finding that sequence models perform best for next activity prediction while tabular foundation models are competitive for temporal tasks.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the evolving landscape of predictive process monitoring where deep sequence models have dominated, but foundation models (LLMs and tabular models) are increasingly being explored without systematic comparison. There's uncertainty about whether classical sequence models remain competitive against newer approaches.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a controlled benchmark comparing three modeling paradigms: classical sequence models (LSTMs), large language models (LLMs), and tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities. The comparison was performed across multiple datasets and prediction tasks in PPM.
AI.result: Sequence models consistently performed best for next activity prediction tasks. Tabular foundation models were competitive on temporal prediction tasks (remaining time, time to next event). LLMs generally lagged behind other approaches despite having higher computational costs.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that classical sequence models remain strong performers in predictive process monitoring, particularly for activity prediction, while newer foundation models show promise in specific areas but come with different trade-offs in performance and cost.

title: MARS-RA: Rank Aggregation for Credit Assignment via Multimodal Comparisons in Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation
summary: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly in embodied AI settings characterized by limited and delayed feedback as well as dynamically changing numbers of active agents. We propose MARS-RA, a framework that reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents generated by large multimodal models. This shift from absolute to relative estimation ensures robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation, converting comparison results into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping. We provide theoretical justification for the convergence and robustness of the proposed framework, and show that Shapley values can be used as an interpretive reference. Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types indicate that MARS-RA can guide agents toward effective cooperation.

AI.tldr: MARS-RA reformulates credit assignment in multi-agent RL as a rank aggregation problem using LLM-generated pairwise comparisons, converting relative estimations to contribution scores for reward shaping with provable convergence.
AI.motivation: Credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent RL is challenging in embodied AI settings due to limited/delayed feedback, noise, and dynamically changing numbers of active agents. Existing absolute estimation methods struggle with these conditions.
AI.method: Proposes MARS-RA framework that transforms credit assignment into rank aggregation: 1) Uses large multimodal models to generate contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents, 2) Converts relative comparisons to contribution scores, 3) Applies potential-based reward shaping, and 4) Provides theoretical justification including convergence analysis.
AI.result: Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types show that MARS-RA can effectively guide agents toward cooperative behavior. The framework demonstrates robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation through relative estimation.
AI.conclusion: MARS-RA offers a theoretically justified solution to credit assignment in noisy, dynamic multi-agent environments by leveraging LLMs for relative comparisons and rank aggregation, enabling effective cooperation with provable convergence properties.

title: Learning-Augmented and Randomized Algorithms for Line Aggregation with Delays
summary: This paper studies learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. We consider advice given as online suggested service lengths, and evaluate the algorithms in terms of robustness and consistency. For each $λ\in (0,1]$, we first propose a deterministic learning-augmented \textsc{Balance} algorithm that is $(4/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(4+λ)$-consistent. We also propose a randomized algorithm for the problem in the classical adversarial model, which is $(e+1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic $5$-competitive \textsc{Balance} benchmark~\cite{bienkowski2013chain}. Notably, this competitive ratio is even lower than the lower bound of $4$ for deterministic online algorithms. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of $e$ on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms, improving the previous lower bound of $e/(e-1)$. Besides, we combine the two ideas and obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm that is $(e/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(e+λ)$-consistent. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to complement our theoretical analysis and evaluate the empirical performance of our algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper presents learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation algorithms on a line metric with delays, achieving improved competitive ratios through suggested service lengths and randomization.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses online aggregation problems with delays on a line metric, motivated by improving upon existing deterministic algorithms like Balance which has a 5-competitive ratio. There's a need to incorporate learning-augmented approaches (using suggested service lengths as advice) and randomization to achieve better competitive ratios that surpass deterministic lower bounds.
AI.method: The authors propose multiple algorithms: 1) A deterministic learning-augmented Balance algorithm parameterized by λ ∈ (0,1], 2) A randomized algorithm for classical adversarial settings, 3) A randomized learning-augmented algorithm combining both approaches. The analysis uses competitive ratio framework, evaluating robustness and consistency for learning-augmented algorithms, and numerical experiments to validate theoretical results.
AI.result: Key results: 1) Deterministic learning-augmented algorithm achieves (4/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (4+λ)-consistency. 2) Randomized algorithm achieves (e+1)-competitiveness, beating deterministic 5-competitive Balance and surpassing the deterministic lower bound of 4. 3) Lower bound of e for randomized algorithms, improving previous e/(e-1) bound. 4) Randomized learning-augmented algorithm achieves (e/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency. Experimental results complement theoretical analysis.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that both learning-augmented approaches (using suggested service lengths) and randomization significantly improve competitive ratios for online aggregation with delays on line metrics. The randomized algorithm achieves e+1 competitiveness, breaking deterministic lower bounds, while the learning-augmented algorithms provide flexible trade-offs between consistency and robustness. The combined randomized learning-augmented approach offers the best of both worlds.

title: Share the Judge, Learn the Deferral: Where Specialization Helps LLM Evaluation
summary: Agentic systems have widened the gap between producing candidate outputs and reviewing them. This paper asks a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be built into an evaluator's weights, or into the rule that decides when its judgment can be trusted? We study 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples. Supplying the correct rubric improves locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points over a response-only control; replacing it with an unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. Dividing the same training corpus among eight criterion-family LoRA judges, however, loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage at a 5% risk target from 24.44% to 5.43%. Matching the bank's stored capacity with one rank-64 adapter does not reproduce this loss. Nor is the result explained by learning rate or optimizer steps. Initializing the family adapters from a shared, trained judge recovers test accuracy to 76.85%, 19.94 points above scratch training at the same learning rate (95% interval 18.88-21.02). The result changes when specialization governs deferral rather than judgment. On RewardBench 2, learned correctness heads route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade without changing any reward score. Across 20 locked repartitions, the cascade attains 89.40% accuracy, compared with 84.75% for 8B alone, at 0.415 normalized parameter compute. Every run passes an exact one-sided 95% risk audit; margin-based rules remain near 84.8% accuracy while using at least 0.94 compute. These results suggest a qualified design rule: share the learning of judgment until there is enough data to justify a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether domain specialization in agentic systems should be embedded in evaluator weights or in trust-based deferral rules, finding that shared judgment learning with domain-specific adaptation in audited boundaries yields better performance and efficiency.
AI.motivation: As agentic systems create gaps between generating outputs and reviewing them, there's a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be built into evaluator weights or into rules that decide when to trust judgments?
AI.method: The study analyzes 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples, experimenting with: 1) supplying correct vs. unrelated rubrics, 2) dividing training data among criterion-family LoRA judges, 3) using shared trained judges as initialization, 4) implementing learned correctness heads for routing through model cascades, and 5) conducting risk audits across 20 locked repartitions.
AI.result: Correct rubrics improve accuracy by 2.11 points; unrelated ones hurt by 2.66. Dividing data among specialized judges loses 10.05 points and reduces audited coverage. Initializing from shared judges recovers accuracy by 19.94 points. Cascades with learned routing achieve 89.40% accuracy vs 84.75% for single models, using only 0.415 normalized parameter compute while passing risk audits.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest a qualified design rule: share judgment learning until sufficient data justifies splitting, and place domain-specific adaptation in audited release boundaries rather than in evaluator weights.

title: Contrastive Concept Importance: Explaining Pairwise Class Decisions Through Automatically Extracted Concept Representations
summary:
Concept-based explanations are a prevalent way to explain the decisions of complex black-box methods through semantically meaningful, human-interpretable concepts. To attribute the contribution of such concepts to a model's decisions, feature attribution methods are used to quantify how strongly each concept contributes to a model output. These attributions are typically computed for a single output class and therefore answer a non-contrastive "why P?" question. In many situations, however, such as cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question to ask is "why P rather than Q?".
  We introduce contrastive concept importance (CCI), which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast, or foil, class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The resulting scores are signed, indicating whether a concept supports the target over the foil or the foil over the target, and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This makes it possible to distinguish globally important concepts from concepts that specifically influence a class-pair distinction, including whether their effect is shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.
  We evaluate the method on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion and deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy. The results show that contrastive concept importance reveals class-pair-specific model behavior that is not captured by ordinary concept importance alone, and that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces contrastive concept importance (CCI), a new method that explains AI decisions by comparing why a model predicts one class over another, rather than just explaining single predictions.
AI.motivation: Current concept-based explanations only answer "why P?" questions, but in cases like misclassifications, class confusion, or close predictions, the more natural question is "why P rather than Q?" Existing methods don't capture these contrastive explanations between classes.
AI.method: CCI attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast (foil) class to visual concepts extracted automatically. It produces signed scores indicating whether each concept supports the target over the foil or vice versa, and decomposes contributions into target-logit and foil-logit effects.
AI.result: Evaluation on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases shows CCI reveals class-pair-specific model behavior not captured by ordinary concept importance. It identifies whether concepts affect fine-grained distinctions vs broad category evidence, and can distinguish globally important concepts from class-pair-specific ones.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive concept importance provides more nuanced explanations for AI decisions, particularly in ambiguous cases, by explaining relative preferences between classes rather than absolute predictions, offering better insight into model behavior during class-confusion scenarios.

title: SKIMIX: Multi-Agent Harness-Time Scaling with Skill Mixture for Dynamic Harness Engineering
summary: AI agents increasingly rely on large skill libraries, but selecting, combining, and maintaining skills remains difficult. We propose SKIMIX, a multi-agent framework in which agents with different skill portfolios collaborate through iterative refinement. SKIMIX combines embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution. Across six reasoning benchmarks, multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but offers limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and most improvements arise during the first refinement round. These results show that task characteristics determine whether skill-level ensembles help and provide practical guidance for scalable agent design.

AI.tldr: SKIMIX is a multi-agent framework that enables agents with different skill portfolios to collaborate through iterative refinement, significantly improving open-ended mathematical reasoning but showing limited benefits for multiple-choice tasks.
AI.motivation: AI agents increasingly rely on large skill libraries, but selecting, combining, and maintaining skills remains difficult. There's a need for better approaches to leverage diverse skill sets across agents.
AI.method: SKIMIX is a multi-agent framework where agents with different skill portfolios collaborate through iterative refinement. It combines embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution techniques.
AI.result: Across six reasoning benchmarks, multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but offers limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and most improvements arise during the first refinement round.
AI.conclusion: Task characteristics determine whether skill-level ensembles help, and these results provide practical guidance for scalable agent design. Multi-agent collaboration shows promise for open-ended reasoning tasks but may not benefit all task types equally.

title: Class-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Counterfactual Explanation Generation
summary: Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) enhance the interpretability of black-box models by generating alternative instances with adjusted feature values that achieve a contrastive outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach for CFE generation, enabling efficient exploration of counterfactual instances while ensuring control over key metrics like validity, sparsity, and proximity. Previous studies have formulated RL states exclusively using features derived from the predictors in the supervised dataset. This study explores the impact of including an instance's predicted class, alongside features derived from the predictors, in the RL state representation for generating CFEs. The hypothesis is that class-awareness enhances exploration efficiency and improves policy optimality. We compare the proposed class-aware RL method with the class-blind RL method, which is similar but excludes the instance's class information from the state representation. The comparison was conducted using seven datasets from diverse domains, varying in size. The results show that during training, class-aware RL offers benefits in terms of convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction. Moreover, it generates significantly more valid CFEs compared to class-blind RL. Finally, the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL's action-selection, as shown by the SHAP and LIME values, underscoring the significance of class-awareness in RL for CFE generation. The impact is heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets.

AI.tldr: A class-aware reinforcement learning approach for counterfactual explanations that includes predicted class information in the RL state representation improves exploration efficiency and generates more valid counterfactuals compared to class-blind methods.
AI.motivation: Previous RL methods for counterfactual explanation generation use only feature information from predictors in their state representation. The authors hypothesize that including an instance's predicted class alongside feature information can enhance exploration efficiency and improve policy optimality for counterfactual generation.
AI.method: The study proposes a class-aware RL method that includes the instance's predicted class alongside features derived from predictors in the RL state representation. This is compared with a class-blind RL method that excludes class information. Experiments were conducted across seven diverse datasets of varying sizes to evaluate the impact of class-awareness.
AI.result: Class-aware RL showed benefits in convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction during training. It generated significantly more valid counterfactual explanations compared to class-blind RL. Class-based features consistently ranked among the most influential predictors in action selection according to SHAP and LIME analyses.
AI.conclusion: Including predicted class information in RL state representation for counterfactual explanation generation leads to heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets, demonstrating the importance of class-awareness in RL approaches.

title: MMLDSum-LLM: Multimodal Long-Document Summarization with Visual-Alignment and Keyword-Aware
summary: Multimodal long documents are core carriers of professional knowledge, where critical evidence is sparsely distributed across paragraphs and modalities. This easily causes key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in summarization by multimodal LLMs. These issues stem from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment. To address this, we introduce MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. We further propose MMLDSum-LLM, a reproducible two-stage training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by GRPO with a multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control). Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol - including LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE - demonstrate that our approach significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.

AI.tldr: A framework for multimodal long-document summarization that addresses attention drift and cross-modal hallucination issues through a two-stage training approach with specialized loss functions and multi-objective reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Multimodal long documents contain sparsely distributed critical evidence across paragraphs and modalities, which often leads to key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in current multimodal LLM summarization approaches, caused by attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and inter-modal alignment gaps.
AI.method: Introduced MMLDSum-Bench (a high-quality benchmark covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions) and MMLDSum-LLM (a two-stage training framework: 1) supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by 2) GRPO with multi-objective reward combining keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control).
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models show the approach significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency, evaluated through LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MMLDSum-LLM framework effectively addresses the challenges of multimodal long-document summarization by combining specialized loss functions and multi-objective reinforcement learning, resulting in substantially better key information coverage and cross-modal consistency compared to existing approaches.

title: S-CEReBrO: Breaking the Memory Barrier in Continuous EEG Monitoring
comment: This is the pre-rebuttal version of a paper accepted at MICCAI 2026. The camera-ready version will be posted following the embargo
summary: Foundation models offer a promising paradigm for Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis, leveraging generalizable representations from vast unlabeled datasets. Yet, Transformer-based architectures face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to the signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. To address this, we introduce S-CEReBrO (Streaming CEReBrO), an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture designed for continuous monitoring. Our novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory as only the active window requires resident attention maps. Empirical scaling analysis confirms that windowed alternating attention can process signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. Compared to low-rank linear attention on long contexts, windowed alternating attention requires 55% of the memory while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours of recordings from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks, with up to 60% fewer parameters. This work represents a significant step toward the realization of efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring. An accompanying code repository is available.

AI.tldr: Streaming CEReBrO (S-CEReBrO) enables continuous EEG monitoring by using windowed alternating attention to overcome Transformer memory bottlenecks, achieving state-of-the-art performance with fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based architectures for EEG analysis face memory overflow during continuous monitoring due to global attention mechanisms coupling attention memory state to signal duration.
AI.method: Introduced S-CEReBrO with novel Windowed Alternating Attention that factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, ensuring constant KV cache memory as only the active window needs resident attention maps.
AI.result: Windowed alternating attention can process signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention, with 55% less memory and 2.1X higher inference throughput. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves SOTA on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: S-CEReBrO represents a significant step toward efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring by overcoming Transformer memory bottlenecks through windowed alternating attention.

title: MUL-T: Decoding Spatial Cellular Architecture in Multiplexed Tissue Images
summary: Understanding tissue organisation in multiplexed imaging requires modelling both cellular phenotypes and their spatial context. Existing approaches typically rely on handcrafted features, such as marker intensity statistics or cell-type proportions, which often fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels. We introduce MUL-T, a lightweight transformer framework that reframes tissue architecture as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. By learning contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision, the model captures higher-order cellular interactions while remaining computationally efficient. We evaluate MUL-T on several clinically relevant downstream tasks, including core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction. Across tasks, MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines and achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model, despite substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.

AI.tldr: MUL-T is a lightweight transformer framework that treats tissue organization in multiplexed imaging as a masked contextual prediction task, learning cellular interactions efficiently without task-specific supervision and outperforming feature-based methods on clinical prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for understanding tissue organization in multiplexed imaging rely on handcrafted features like marker intensity statistics or cell-type proportions, which fail to scale or generalize across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels.
AI.method: MUL-T reframes tissue architecture as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens, learning contextualized [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision to capture higher-order cellular interactions while remaining computationally efficient.
AI.result: MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines across clinically relevant downstream tasks (tumor pattern classification, patient grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, cross-dataset treatment response) and achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model with substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.
AI.conclusion: MUL-T provides an effective, efficient approach for modeling tissue organization in multiplexed imaging that scales better across heterogeneous cohorts than handcrafted feature-based methods, enabling improved clinical predictions with reduced computational requirements.

title: Exact Action Values Are Not Enough: Rollout-Verified Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of a Reasoning Model for Multi-Zone VAV Control
summary: Multi-zone variable-air-volume control must balance thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and electricity use across several continuous actuators. Model predictive control and reinforcement learning are widely studied, but deployment typically requires building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. We first test whether a frontier reasoning model (an LLM trained to use additional inference-time computation) can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training. With that capability established, we then test whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model. Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator. Relative to a Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature and CO$_2$ compliance. Without building-specific training, GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced the ventilation margin. For RFT, deterministic rollouts restore a saved state, apply one candidate, and follow TD3 to score each action. Auditing a learned critic against these rollouts exposed a failure hidden by its near-perfect across-time correlation ($r=0.9998$): within-state ranking was unreliable; the critic selected the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement in sampled-action return; the open-weight controller used more electricity than the baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better. Exact rollout scores rank sampled actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

AI.tldr: LLM-based VAV control without building-specific training outperforms traditional methods, but reinforcement fine-tuning struggles due to unreliable critic ranking despite high correlation.
AI.motivation: Existing MPC and RL approaches for VAV control require building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. The paper explores whether frontier reasoning models (LLMs) can achieve competitive control from text without building-specific training, and whether reinforcement fine-tuning can transfer control knowledge to locally deployable models.
AI.method: 1) Test GPT-5 for VAV control using only text descriptions without building-specific training; 2) Test TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning to transfer knowledge to open-weight models; 3) Evaluate five controllers over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator; 4) Use deterministic rollouts to audit learned critics and evaluate action selection.
AI.result: TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature/CO2 compliance. GPT-5 without building-specific training achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced ventilation margin. RFT failed: critic showed near-perfect correlation (r=0.9998) but poor within-state ranking (selected best candidate in only 5/10 states). 200 RFT steps produced no improvement, and the open-weight controller performed worse than baseline. GPT-5 predicted transitions much better than RFT models.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can achieve competitive VAV control without building-specific training, outperforming traditional methods. However, reinforcement fine-tuning struggles due to unreliable critic ranking despite high correlation scores. The authors recommend transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based reinforcement fine-tuning for better performance.

title: DataClawEval: A Benchmark for Data Engineering Agents in Real Industrial Harness
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly being deployed to automate complex workflows, promising to revolutionize data management and processing. However, existing benchmarks predominantly focus on simplified Text-to-SQL translation or data analysis, leaving the critical and complex domain of end-to-end data engineering largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce DataClawEval, the first comprehensive benchmark designed specifically to evaluate the end-to-end task completion capabilities of autonomous agents in real-world data engineering scenarios. Built upon production-grade code authored by professional enterprise data engineers, it comprises 100 rigorous, end-to-end tasks spanning five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Rather than non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge scoring, each task is executed within a case-specific, isolated sandbox and graded by deterministic, rule-based scripts. Evaluating 16 frontier agents exposes critical limitations: The strongest model attains only 74.9 overall, and no single model dominates, as each excels on a different engine, revealing strict domain specialization rather than omnipotent proficiency. Thus, autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge. We release our dataset, containerized environments, and deterministic evaluation scripts at https://github.com/Dicemy/DataClawEval/tree/master

AI.tldr: DataClawEval is the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating autonomous agents' end-to-end task completion in real-world data engineering, revealing significant limitations in current LLM-based systems.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on simplified tasks like Text-to-SQL or basic data analysis, leaving the complex domain of end-to-end data engineering largely unexplored despite increasing deployment of LLMs for automating data workflows.
AI.method: Created DataClawEval benchmark with 100 rigorous end-to-end tasks based on production-grade code from professional data engineers, covering five execution engines (PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, FlinkSQL). Uses deterministic, rule-based evaluation in case-specific isolated sandboxes instead of LLM-as-a-judge scoring.
AI.result: Evaluation of 16 frontier agents shows critical limitations: strongest model achieves only 74.9% overall, no single model dominates across all engines, revealing strict domain specialization rather than omnipotent proficiency.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge. The benchmark exposes significant gaps in current LLM-based agents' capabilities for real-world data engineering tasks.

title: ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow
summary: In the physical world we inhabit, space and time are fundamentally continuous. However, existing machine learning paradigms for world modeling are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, thereby exhibiting significant inefficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical world. We introduce Physical-Time Flow (\textbf{PT-Flow}), a novel approach that learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in a well-structured representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct \textbf{ODEWorld}, a continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. By extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field, ODEWorld effectively addresses the long-standing representation collapse issue in latent world model literature. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction. Moreover, its continuous nature allows for arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward prediction, which is impossible for most discrete-time models. Lastly, ODEWorld can provide rich planning-oriented information to facilitate downstream policy learning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. \href{https://dstate.github.io/odeworld_website/}{Project Website}.

AI.tldr: PT-Flow introduces a continuous-time latent velocity field using ODEs for world modeling, enabling arbitrary temporal resolution and backward prediction in video generation and robotic control.
AI.motivation: Existing machine learning world models are confined to discrete-time prediction, which is inefficient for capturing physical world dynamics that are fundamentally continuous in space and time.
AI.method: Developed Physical-Time Flow (PT-Flow) that learns continuous latent velocity fields parameterized by ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in structured representation space. Built ODEWorld model that extracts time-variant features and enforces ODE properties on both dynamical representation space and latent velocity field.
AI.result: ODEWorld addresses representation collapse in latent world models, enables high-quality image reconstruction after long-horizon prediction, supports arbitrary temporal resolution and backward prediction, and provides planning-oriented information for policy learning.
AI.conclusion: ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control by modeling continuous-time physical world dynamics.

title: SKILL-KD: Contrastive Skill Distillation for LLM Agents
summary: Skill-based prompting has become a practical mechanism for improving large language model (LLM) agents, yet existing skill acquisition methods often treat skills as experience summaries, memory entries, or direct summaries of successful demonstrations. This creates a mismatch for weaker student agents: when a student fails because it lacks task knowledge or operational strategy, its failed trajectory may not contain enough evidence to infer the missing behavior, while the teacher trajectory may be too implicit to be internalized as reusable guidance. We propose SKILL-KD, a contrastive skill distillation framework that treats skills as an explicit distillation medium between agents of different capabilities. Given a student failure and the teacher trajectory on the same task, SKILL-KD distills their actionable discrepancy into a textual skill patch, evaluates the patch by re-running the student, and iteratively refines the patch when the student still fails. To prevent repeated local updates from causing skill drift, SKILL-KD further maintains trace-linked edit histories and performs Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, deciding whether each patch should add a new rule, delete or modify an existing rule, or be skipped. Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.

AI.tldr: SKILL-KD is a contrastive skill distillation framework that distills actionable discrepancy between teacher and student agents into textual skill patches, with iterative refinement and drift-aware consolidation.
AI.motivation: Existing skill acquisition methods treat skills as experience summaries or memory entries, creating a mismatch for weaker student agents. When students fail due to lacking task knowledge or strategy, their failed trajectories may not contain enough evidence to infer missing behaviors, while teacher trajectories may be too implicit to be internalized as reusable guidance.
AI.method: SKILL-KD treats skills as an explicit distillation medium between agents. Given a student failure and teacher trajectory on the same task, it distills their actionable discrepancy into textual skill patches, evaluates patches by re-running the student, and iteratively refines them. To prevent skill drift from repeated updates, it maintains trace-linked edit histories and performs Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, deciding whether each patch should add, delete, modify rules, or be skipped.
AI.result: Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.
AI.conclusion: SKILL-KD provides an effective framework for skill distillation that addresses the limitations of existing approaches by using explicit skill patches, iterative refinement, and drift-aware consolidation to transfer capabilities from stronger to weaker agents.

title: Harnessing the Potential of Optimizing Data Mixtures via Bayesian Domain Reweighting
summary: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally influenced by the distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data. While manual heuristics were prevalent in early models, they increasingly fail to capture the intricate synergies between domains as data complexity grows. To overcome the issue, a dominant approach seeks to fit a proxy function mapping between domain weights and their corresponding validation losses, and then find the optimal domain weights to minimize validation losses. These methods rely on strong structural assumptions, such as rank invariance or scaling laws, which are often violated, resulting in non-negligible estimation bias. A promising approach is to directly optimize the weighting scheme from data. However, it suffers from unstable optimization trajectory and prohibitive computational overhead, limiting its potential to search better domain weights configurations. This paper presents a Bayesian domain weighting method to infer the weights from a Dirichlet distribution via introducing Gamma prior information learned from observations. Experimental results demonstrate that proposed method could achieve stable and efficient domain weights learning, and identifies optimal mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods, revitalizing optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale applications.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian domain weighting method using Dirichlet distribution with Gamma priors enables stable and efficient learning of optimal domain mixture weights for LLM pre-training, outperforming both manual heuristics and search-based function-fitting approaches.
AI.motivation: Current methods for optimizing domain weights in LLM pre-training data have limitations: manual heuristics fail with increasing data complexity, while function-fitting methods rely on problematic structural assumptions (rank invariance/scaling laws) that lead to estimation bias. Direct optimization approaches suffer from unstable optimization and high computational costs.
AI.method: Proposes a Bayesian domain weighting method that infers domain weights from a Dirichlet distribution by incorporating Gamma prior information learned from observations. This provides a probabilistic framework for stable weight optimization without relying on restrictive structural assumptions.
AI.result: The method achieves stable and efficient domain weights learning, identifies optimal domain mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods, and demonstrates computational efficiency suitable for large-scale applications.
AI.conclusion: The Bayesian approach successfully revitalizes optimization-based domain weighting for LLM pre-training, overcoming key limitations of existing methods and enabling effective multi-domain data composition optimization at scale.

title: IndustryForge-27B: A Domain-Enhanced Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial CAD
summary: Automating industrial CAD design and manufacturing places distinctive demands on multimodal foundation models: the model must see engineering drawings and 3D geometry screenshots, write correct parametric-modelling scripts and Windows COM API code, and cover the full range from single parts to assemblies. General-purpose multimodal models fall short on these tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow to support the diverse calls that upper-layer agents issue. We build IndustryForge-27B on top of Qwen3.5-VL-27B by curating and integrating six industrial-CAD sub-corpora totalling $\sim$52k multimodal samples---CAD Visual QA (CAD-VQA), parametric CAD code (text2cadquery), assembly-level CAD code (text2cadquery-assembly), and three COM sub-corpora for Inventor / SolidWorks (com_2d / com_3d / com_assembly)---and training with a unified multi-task SFT recipe. Across four CAD-domain benchmarks IndustryForge-27B lifts the base model by $+33.65$~pp on average and outperforms the strong closed-source model GPT-5.4 on all four; across eleven general-capability benchmarks it retains, and slightly improves upon, the base model ($+1.56$~pp mean, no catastrophic forgetting). IndustryForge-27B will serve as the common substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, providing a unified starting point for a full-stack industrial agent that spans from CAD design to industrial-software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

AI.tldr: IndustryForge-27B is a specialized multimodal foundation model for industrial CAD that outperforms general-purpose models and GPT-5.4 by integrating six CAD sub-corpora and achieving strong performance while maintaining general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Industrial CAD design and manufacturing require models that can process engineering drawings, 3D geometry, write parametric scripts and Windows COM API code, and handle everything from parts to assemblies. General-purpose multimodal models fail at these specialized tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow for the diverse needs of upper-layer agents.
AI.method: Built on Qwen3.5-VL-27B, the authors curated and integrated six industrial-CAD sub-corpora totaling ~52k multimodal samples: CAD Visual QA, parametric CAD code, assembly-level CAD code, and three COM sub-corpora for Inventor/SolidWorks. They trained with a unified multi-task supervised fine-tuning recipe.
AI.result: IndustryForge-27B improved the base model by +33.65 percentage points on average across four CAD-domain benchmarks and outperformed GPT-5.4 on all four. Across eleven general-capability benchmarks, it retained and slightly improved upon the base model (+1.56 pp mean) with no catastrophic forgetting.
AI.conclusion: IndustryForge-27B serves as an effective common substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, providing a unified starting point for full-stack industrial agents spanning CAD design, industrial-software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

title: TriShield: Zero-Utility-Loss Defense Against Privacy Backdoors in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning via Orthogonal Gradient Projection and Optimizer State Entanglement
