summary: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) enables collaborative training without exposing raw data. However, a recent attack, NeuroImprint [1] (arXiv:2606.20553), demonstrates that a malicious parameter server can corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor: by assigning a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and ensuring each neuron updates at most once, the server can analytically reconstruct 59\%--79\% of client training data with high semantic fidelity. Existing defenses---including local differential privacy (LDP) [8] and gradient clipping---either fail against this attack or impose unacceptable utility degradation. We present \textbf{TriShield}, a three-layer deterministic defense that completely prevents NeuroImprint-style reconstruction with \textbf{zero model utility loss} and \textbf{no additional communication rounds}. TriShield consists of: (1) a \textbf{Parameter Artifact Detector} that identifies memory-neuron signatures in distributed model parameters before local training begins; (2) a \textbf{Stateful Virtual Iteration} mechanism that forces Adam/AdamW's momentum state to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, invalidating NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; and (3) a \textbf{Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection} operator that projects all local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace computed via SVD, physically eliminating any gradient components that carry private memorization. We prove theoretically that after Layers 2 and 3, the mutual information between the uploaded gradient and any individual training sample is zero. Experiments on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B verify that TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to \textbf{0\%} across all tested attack variants, while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with less than 5\% additional GPU computation overhead.

AI.tldr: TriShield is a three-layer deterministic defense that completely prevents NeuroImprint-style privacy attacks in federated LLM fine-tuning with zero utility loss and no extra communication rounds.
AI.motivation: The NeuroImprint attack shows malicious servers can corrupt PEFT adapters into privacy backdoors to reconstruct 59%-79% of client training data, while existing defenses like LDP and gradient clipping either fail or cause unacceptable utility degradation.
AI.method: TriShield uses: 1) Parameter Artifact Detector to identify memory-neuron signatures before training; 2) Stateful Virtual Iteration to entangle Adam/AdamW momentum states across virtual steps, breaking closed-form inversion; and 3) Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection to project gradients onto main-task semantic subspace via SVD, eliminating private memorization components.
AI.result: Theoretical proof shows zero mutual information between uploaded gradients and individual training samples. Experiments reduce NeuroImprint reconstruction to 0% across all attack variants while maintaining/improving training accuracy, with less than 5% GPU overhead.
AI.conclusion: TriShield provides a practical, provably secure defense against NeuroImprint attacks in federated LLM fine-tuning with no utility trade-off, addressing a critical vulnerability in collaborative training systems.

title: SemPIC: Learning Semantic Position-Independent KV Caches
summary: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse the same documents under changing instructions, histories, and document orders. Prefix caching cannot exploit this reuse, while position-independent caching (PIC) remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed. Our diagnostics show that a learned boundary-conditioned baseline sharply reduces attention deviation near reusable-block boundaries but leaves interior and task-level residuals, motivating adaptation of the document representation itself. We present \emph{SemPIC}, which trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation while retaining the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. We further introduce KV Gradient Checkpointing, which reduces peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs. Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.

AI.tldr: SemPIC is a method that trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KV states through behavioral distillation, enabling efficient reuse of document representations in long-context retrieval and agentic workloads while maintaining the standard decoder interface.
AI.motivation: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse the same documents under changing instructions, histories, and document orders. Existing caching methods are insufficient: prefix caching cannot exploit this reuse, while position-independent caching (PIC) remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed.
AI.method: SemPIC trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation while retaining the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. The method also introduces KV Gradient Checkpointing to reduce peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs.
AI.result: Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62. The learned boundary-conditioned baseline sharply reduces attention deviation near reusable-block boundaries, but SemPIC addresses interior and task-level residuals by adapting the document representation itself.
AI.conclusion: SemPIC effectively addresses the limitations of existing caching methods for long-context workloads by enabling semantic position-independent caching through distilled document representations, achieving performance close to full recomputation while maintaining efficient caching and standard interfaces.

title: AutoPref: Automatic Discovery of Task-Specific Preference Objectives for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
summary: Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) underpin many real-world decisions, but their exponentially large search spaces make high-quality solutions costly to obtain. Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) learns fast construction policies, typically with reinforcement learning (RL), while preference-based NCO improves sample efficiency by learning from relative solution quality. However, existing preference objectives combine two distinct design choices in manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations: what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. We present AutoPref, the first LLM-guided framework for automated preference-objective discovery in NCO. AutoPref factorizes the objective into a pairwise loss program, which defines the learning signal, and a set-aware weighting program, which determines each pair's relative contribution. Their composition forms a unified programmatic objective space containing existing preference objectives as special cases. To make its search tractable, we introduce a staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates that filter inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation. Across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across problem scales, demonstrating the benefits and scalability of automated objective discovery for NCO.

AI.tldr: AutoPref: An LLM-guided framework that automatically discovers preference objectives for neural combinatorial optimization by factorizing them into pairwise loss programs and set-aware weighting programs, outperforming hand-designed baselines across multiple optimization problems.
AI.motivation: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) learns fast construction policies, but existing preference-based approaches use manually specified, one-size-fits-all objectives that combine two distinct design choices in fixed formulations. This limits sample efficiency and optimal performance.
AI.method: AutoPref factorizes preference objectives into two components: pairwise loss programs (defining learning signal from solution pairs) and set-aware weighting programs (determining each pair's relative contribution). The framework uses a staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates to filter inadmissible programs before evaluation, making search tractable.
AI.result: Across Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), Flexible Flow Shop Problem (FFSP), and Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP), AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across different problem scales.
AI.conclusion: Automated objective discovery through AutoPref demonstrates significant benefits and scalability for neural combinatorial optimization, showing that LLM-guided framework design can effectively replace manual objective engineering while improving performance across diverse combinatorial problems.

title: Echoverse: Deep, Evolving Environments for Training Computer-Use Agents at Scale
summary: Computer-use agents learn from what their actions change, so training one needs applications it can act on, break and reset. The applications that matter most are login-gated and stateful, so synthetic environments stand in for them. Recent pipelines generate such environments in bulk, which moves the bottleneck from how many exist to what is inside each one. The returns, we find, come from three properties: how much behavioural depth an environment carries, whether it targets the interaction an agent actually fails, and whether it improves alongside the model. We present Echoverse, which compiles specifications into stateful applications whose tasks are graded against the application's own database, and a co-evolution loop that reads every graded rollout twice: as repairs to the environment, its tasks and its verifier, and as training signal for the model. Trained on twelve such environments, a 9B model improves from $36.5\%$ to $67.1\%$ across fourteen evaluation splits, within fourteen points of the much larger frontier model that taught it. We examine each property in turn. On the same domains, shallow environments push live-site accuracy below the base model ($80.0 \to 75.0$) while deep ones raise it ($80.0 \to 85.0$ and $48.0 \to 65.0$); drilling one interface control across many renderings transfers to held-out widget families and to the open web; and repairing a single environment lifts the model trained on it from $16.2\%$ to $38.5\%$. The same worlds serve as reinforcement-learning environments, where a reward combining the grounded verifier with a dense per-step judge raises held-out score from $58.8\%$ to $68.0\%$. We release four environments as a benchmark, with their applications, seed data and grounded graders. Code: https://aka.ms/echoverse

AI.tldr: Echoverse creates stateful applications from specifications with graded tasks and uses a co-evolution loop to simultaneously improve both environments and AI agents, significantly boosting a 9B model's performance on real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents need real applications to learn from, but login-gated and stateful applications are hard to access for training. Synthetic environments can substitute, but existing bulk generation approaches create shallow environments that don't effectively target agent weaknesses or improve alongside the model.
AI.method: Echoverse compiles specifications into stateful applications with tasks graded against the application's database. It uses a co-evolution loop that reads graded rollouts twice: 1) as repairs to improve environments, tasks, and verifiers, and 2) as training signal for the model. The system focuses on creating deep environments that target specific interaction failures.
AI.result: A 9B model trained on twelve Echoverse environments improved from 36.5% to 67.1% across fourteen evaluation splits, coming within 14 points of the larger frontier model that taught it. Deep environments raised performance significantly (80.0→85.0, 48.0→65.0), while shallow ones degraded it. Environment repair lifted model performance from 16.2% to 38.5%. In RL settings, combining grounded verifier with dense per-step rewards raised held-out scores from 58.8% to 68.0%.
AI.conclusion: The success of computer-use agent training depends on three key environment properties: behavioral depth, targeting of agent failures, and co-evolution with the model. Echoverse demonstrates that generating deep, adaptive environments with grounded task grading enables significant performance improvements, closing the gap with much larger models while providing a framework for future agent training.

title: What Makes Graph Unified? Principles and Generative Sliding-Window Transformer for Graph Foundation Models
summary: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose graph learning, aiming to learn reusable knowledge that generalizes across diverse graph domains and downstream tasks, reducing the need for specific model development. Achieving this goal requires reconciling the substantial heterogeneity in node features, graph structures, and semantic information across domains. Among them, heterogeneous node features constitute a fundamental input-level barrier, as their dimensionality and semantics vary substantially across datasets. Existing studies typically project or map heterogeneous node features into a fixed-dimensional space, often implicitly equating dimensional uniformity with effective feature unification. Yet dimensional consistency alone does not ensure that the unified features preserve informative semantics and capture transferable patterns that can support cross-domain knowledge transfer. To bridge this conceptual gap, we distill four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility. Guided by these principles, we propose SliGFM, a graph foundation model built upon topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction. SliGFM orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness and scans the reordered features with a shared sliding-window feature encoder, transforming heterogeneous features into a common space of ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. This formulation enables a smoothness-aware transformer to capture transferable relational patterns among feature tokens within each node, while the generative reconstruction objective encourages preservation of the original feature information.

AI.tldr: SliGFM is a graph foundation model that addresses heterogeneous node features across domains through topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction, enabling better cross-domain knowledge transfer.
AI.motivation: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) aim for general-purpose graph learning across diverse domains, but face challenges with heterogeneous node features that vary in dimensionality and semantics. Current approaches that simply project features into fixed-dimensional spaces don't ensure preservation of informative semantics or cross-domain transferability.
AI.method: SliGFM uses topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding: it orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness, scans reordered features with a shared sliding-window encoder to transform heterogeneous features into ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens, and employs a smoothness-aware transformer with generative reconstruction to capture transferable patterns.
AI.result: The method transforms heterogeneous node features into a common space while preserving semantic information and enabling cross-domain knowledge transfer through four key principles: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility.
AI.conclusion: SliGFM provides a principled approach to cross-domain graph feature unification that goes beyond simple dimensional alignment to ensure meaningful knowledge transfer in Graph Foundation Models, addressing the fundamental input-level barrier of heterogeneous node features.

title: Group-Reflective Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is effective for training large language model agents. However, terminal rewards provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, leaving successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices entangled in the same outcome signal. Existing agentic self-distillation methods enrich sparse supervision with natural-language skills, but skills retrieved externally or extracted from a single trajectory by stronger models may mismatch current experience, exceed the policy's capability, or remain path-specific. We propose Group-Reflective Self-Distillation (GRSD), which derives capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts. For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group, and a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts the resulting reflections from successful and failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance. Conditioned on this guidance, a self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction. Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales demonstrate that GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

AI.tldr: Group-Reflective Self-Distillation (GRSD) improves reinforcement learning for language agents by having policies reflect on their own verified rollouts to create better guidance, outperforming existing methods and generalizing better to new tasks.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides only coarse trajectory-level supervision, failing to distinguish between successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices. Existing self-distillation methods use skills that may mismatch current experience, exceed policy capability, or remain path-specific.
AI.method: GRSD derives guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts. For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group. A stop-gradient snapshot contrasts successful vs. failed rollout reflections to construct group-level privileged guidance. A self-teacher then refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving verifier-determined learning direction.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales show GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: GRSD provides an effective approach for enhancing RLVR by enabling policies to learn from their own experiences through reflective self-distillation, creating capability-aligned guidance that improves learning and generalization.

title: Beyond Binary Rewards: A Comparative Study of Reward Design for Reinforcement Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning seeks to selectively remove specific knowledge from trained language models without full retraining, a growing necessity under privacy regulations such as GDPR and the EU AI Act. Recent work has reformulated unlearning as a Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) problem, where models are optimized against verifiable rewards computed directly from their outputs. However, existing methods rely on sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided, and limiting convergence speed. In this paper, we study how reward design affects unlearning efficiency within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. We introduce a principled reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity, and propose two new reward functions: an exponential reward that provides graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and a PageRank inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance. We conduct experiments on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark, demonstrating that both rewards consistently outperform the binary setting, while reaching similar forgetting performance up to $3\times$ faster and preserving general model utility. Our results show that reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

AI.tldr: Reward design significantly impacts machine unlearning efficiency - proposed exponential and PageRank-based reward functions achieve similar forgetting performance 3x faster than binary rewards.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning is essential for privacy compliance (GDPR, EU AI Act). Existing RL-based unlearning methods use sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, limiting convergence speed and efficiency.
AI.method: Introduces a principled reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity. Proposes two new reward functions: 1) exponential reward with graded penalties based on forbidden-concept occurrence count, and 2) PageRank-inspired reward weighting penalties by semantic importance.
AI.result: Both proposed rewards outperform binary baselines on Real World Knowledge Unlearning benchmark, achieving similar forgetting performance up to 3x faster while preserving general model utility. PageRank reward provides additional semantic weighting benefits.
AI.conclusion: Reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency, offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning by improving learning signal quality without compromising verifiability.

title: Distilling Answer Set Programming Theories from Large Language Models
summary: Writing Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories from scratch is a difficult and time-consuming task. We take a neurosymbolic approach to study whether a model can distill complete and correct theories, given a fixed agent harness with the solver in the loop. The protocol is dataset-agnostic: with a single prompt and an empty file as the starting point the model is given a 1-hour time limit to derive a complete theory. We chose VQA as the application domain, three benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER), as these are publicly available and non-trivial. In order to study the model scale required for solving this task we nine different models: four frontier (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5, DeepSeek V4 Pro), two mid-tier (DeepSeek V4 Flash, gpt-oss-120b), and three open-weights (qwen3.6-27b, gpt-oss-20b, qwen3.5-9b). Three of four frontier models reach 100% on CLEVR and 92.8%-98.8% on GQA; on CLEVRER, Sonnet, Opus, DeepSeek V4 Pro score 92.7%-95.3%. GPT-5 reaches 98.7% on CLEVR but drops to 41.8% on GQA and to 86.7% on CLEVRER. Adding handwritten reference theories from other datasets moves the other three frontier models by at most +/-3.4 pp but reduces GPT-5's accuracy by 3-19 pp. We release the code, prompts, and theories distilled.

AI.tldr: A neurosymbolic approach where large language models distill complete ASP theories from scratch for VQA tasks, achieving near-perfect accuracy on CLEVR and high scores on GQA/CLEVRER with frontier models.
AI.motivation: Writing Answer Set Programming theories from scratch is difficult and time-consuming. The study explores whether models can automatically distill complete and correct theories using a neurosymbolic approach with the solver in the loop.
AI.method: Dataset-agnostic protocol: single prompt + empty file start, 1-hour time limit. Applied to VQA domain with three benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER). Tested nine models: four frontier, two mid-tier, three open-weights.
AI.result: Three of four frontier models achieved 100% on CLEVR, 92.8%-98.8% on GQA, and 92.7%-95.3% on CLEVRER. GPT-5 had inconsistent performance (98.7% CLEVR, 41.8% GQA, 86.7% CLEVRER). Adding reference theories minimally affected others but hurt GPT-5.
AI.conclusion: Frontier LLMs can successfully distill complete ASP theories for VQA tasks, though performance varies by model. The neurosymbolic approach with solver in loop shows promise for automating ASP theory generation.

title: TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents
summary: Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial paradigm for the post-training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. However, existing methods predominantly rely on sparse task rewards for policy optimization, failing to fully exploit another class of inherently dense supervisory signals naturally present during online interaction: environmental feedback following action execution. Recent theoretical studies suggest that generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks hinges on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Inspired by this, we propose TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents, a unified training framework that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, TAPO repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model. This approach enhances the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while concurrently optimizing the policy. It serves as a computationally lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement module for existing agent RL algorithms, requiring no additional expert data, extra sampling costs, or inference-time overhead. We conduct systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, integrating foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms. Empirical results demonstrate that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

AI.tldr: TAPO is a reinforcement learning framework for LLM agents that combines policy optimization with action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision, improving performance without extra data or inference overhead.
AI.motivation: Current RL methods for LLM agents rely mainly on sparse task rewards and fail to leverage dense environmental feedback signals available during online interactions. Theoretical studies show that generalization in multi-step tasks depends on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences, which existing methods don't fully exploit.
AI.method: TAPO (Transition-Aware Policy Optimization) alternates between standard policy optimization and transition supervision. It repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model, enhancing the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics while optimizing the policy. It's a lightweight, plug-and-play module requiring no additional expert data or sampling costs.
AI.result: Experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld with foundation models of various scales and different policy optimization algorithms show that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.
AI.conclusion: TAPO effectively combines policy optimization with transition supervision to enhance LLM agents' environmental understanding and task performance, providing a computationally efficient enhancement for existing agent RL algorithms without requiring additional resources.

title: Diversifying Personalized Research Ideation against AI-Induced Homogenization
summary: AI-assisted research ideation has emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating scientific discovery, with systems now capable of generating research directions conditioned on papers, topics, or lightweight researcher contexts. Yet current systems largely optimize individual suggestions in isolation. This leaves two blind spots. First, coarse researcher representations may elicit mainstream directions that appear broadly feasible, but lack sufficient researcher-specific grounding. Second, independent recommendations can concentrate a community's portfolio around recurring high-probability themes. To address these blind spots, we propose DivAlign, a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization. DivAlign extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, scores them along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential), and surfaces researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio. On a benchmark we construct from 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared with coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared with the independent top-choice variant, DivAlign reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ruixxxx/DivAlign.

AI.tldr: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline that generates personalized AI research ideas while reducing community redundancy by extracting fine-grained researcher profiles and scoring ideas along alignment dimensions.
AI.motivation: Current AI-assisted research ideation systems optimize individual suggestions in isolation, leading to two problems: 1) coarse researcher representations produce mainstream but insufficiently grounded directions, and 2) independent recommendations cause community portfolio concentration around recurring themes.
AI.method: Four-stage pipeline: 1) extract fine-grained researcher profiles, 2) generate profile-conditioned candidate directions, 3) score them along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, Growth Potential), 4) surface researcher-local directions while reducing community redundancy.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduced average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608 compared to coarse single-shot ideation. Compared to independent top-choice variant, it reduced nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of researcher-direction fit.
AI.conclusion: DivAlign successfully addresses the blind spots in current research ideation systems by providing more personalized, researcher-grounded suggestions while simultaneously reducing community-level redundancy, offering a better balance between individual relevance and portfolio diversity.

title: Generalization Bounds on Optimal Control for Transformer Training and Wasserstein Distributional Robustness
summary: We derive finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions. Building on the doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, we view data sets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures, allowing us to interpret the training problem as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. We then analyze a quantized model, derived by quantizing the state, action, and measure-state spaces, and derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces together with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. These bounds are transferred to the base model at the cost of an explicit approximation error. Finally, we show that the same machinery yields a distributionally robust control formulation of the training problem, connecting Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

AI.tldr: Finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming, using measure-valued formulation and Markovian control interpretation, with connections to distributionally robust optimization.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to provide rigorous finite-sample generalization guarantees for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions. Current understanding of Transformer generalization properties lacks finite-sample theoretical bounds. The motivation is to bridge this gap by developing a mathematical framework that connects Transformer training to control theory and distributionally robust optimization.
AI.method: Uses a doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics to interpret data sets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures. This reformulates training as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. Then analyzes a quantized model by discretizing state, action, and measure-state spaces. Applies concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces combined with Lipschitz stability estimates for the value function.
AI.result: Derives explicit finite-sample generalization bounds for the quantized Transformer model, which are then transferred to the original model with explicit approximation error. Also shows that the same framework yields a distributionally robust control formulation connecting Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a novel theoretical framework for analyzing Transformer generalization through the lens of control theory and measure-valued dynamics. It establishes concrete finite-sample generalization bounds and reveals fundamental connections between Transformer training and distributionally robust optimization, offering new theoretical tools for understanding neural network generalization.

title: PerturbMap: Cross-Context Transfer of Single-Cell Perturbation Responses
summary: Single-cell perturbation atlases rarely measure every intervention in every cellular context: a query perturbation is often observed in one or more source contexts but missing in the recipient context where its effect is needed. Ignoring those measured responses discards query-specific experimental evidence, whereas copying or weakly calibrating them across contexts risks transferring the wrong signal. We propose PerturbMap, which predicts a missing recipient-context effect by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with accepted proposals that transport the same perturbation's measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge experts fit on paired training perturbations, with proposal weights determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors. On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1\% over a recipient-local low-rank base and achieves lower MSE than FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It remains within $2.82\times10^{-6}$ MSE of our centralized token-matched pooled reference, which uses a stronger training interface. A condition-mean specificity diagnostic shows the same direction: same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine increases from 74.5\% for the low-rank base to 80.5\% for PerturbMap.

AI.tldr: PerturbMap is a method that predicts missing perturbation effects in single-cell atlases by combining local context information with transport of measured source responses, improving accuracy over existing approaches.
AI.motivation: Single-cell perturbation atlases often have missing data where specific interventions aren't measured in certain cellular contexts, creating gaps in understanding perturbation effects. Current approaches either discard valuable query-specific evidence or risk transferring incorrect signals when copying/calibrating across contexts.
AI.method: PerturbMap predicts missing recipient-context effects by combining: 1) a recipient-local low-rank base, 2) transport of measured source responses through ridge experts trained on paired perturbations, and 3) weighted proposals based on route reliability estimated on validation anchors.
AI.result: On Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improved full-effect MSE by 4.1% over local low-rank base, outperformed FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls, and remained close to centralized pooled reference. Condition-mean specificity increased from 74.5% to 80.5% for same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval.
AI.conclusion: PerturbMap effectively addresses the missing data problem in single-cell perturbation atlases by intelligently combining local and transported information, providing more accurate predictions of perturbation effects across different cellular contexts.

title: It's All Just Vectorization: einx, a Universal Notation for Tensor Operations
summary:
Tensor operations represent a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. However, the Numpy-like notation adopted by predominant tensor frameworks is often difficult to read and write and prone to so-called shape errors, i.a., due to following inconsistent rules across a large, complex collection of operations. Alternatives like einsum and einops have gained popularity, but are inherently restricted to few operations and lack the generality required for a universal model of tensor programming.
  To derive a better paradigm, we revisit vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, and use it to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations, and conceptually decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations and their vectorization.
  Building on the universal nature of vectorization, we introduce einx, a universal notation for tensor operations. It uses declarative, pointful expressions that are defined by analogy with loop notation and represent the vectorization of tensor operations. The notation reduces the large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables a clean, readable and writable representation in code. We provide an implementation of einx that is embedded in Python and integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks: https://github.com/fferflo/einx

AI.tldr: einx is a new universal tensor notation that uses declarative, pointful expressions based on vectorization to provide a cleaner, more consistent alternative to existing tensor operation notations like Numpy, einsum, and einops.
AI.motivation: Existing tensor operation notations (Numpy-like, einsum, einops) are difficult to read/write, prone to shape errors due to inconsistent rules, and lack generality. There's a need for a universal model of tensor programming that addresses these limitations.
AI.method: Revisit vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations - using it to lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations and decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations. Introduce einx, a universal notation using declarative, pointful expressions defined by analogy with loop notation that represent vectorization of tensor operations.
AI.result: einx reduces large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables clean, readable, and writable code representation. The authors provide a Python implementation that integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks.
AI.conclusion: einx offers a better paradigm for tensor programming by leveraging the universal nature of vectorization to create a more consistent, readable, and general-purpose tensor operation notation that addresses the limitations of current approaches.

title: An Instrument to Evaluate Governance Proposals: AI Policy Analysis at Scale
summary:
This paper introduces a policy analysis framework for systematic, transparent assessment of AI governance proposals in an evolving and contested regulatory landscape. AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. The framework structures policy analysis around multiple policy attributes, allowing users to surface priorities and tensions without prescribing outcomes. We use a mixed-methods approach that integrates qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to inform the design of policy attribute rubrics. This quantifies the relative emphasis of different policy objectives and presents them through comparative visualizations that support interpretability and cross-policy comparison. The paper also examines the use of commercial LLMs for rubric-based policy analysis, benchmarking their outputs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicitly defined analytical assumptions. Rather than assessing policy effectiveness or desirability, the framework focuses on relevance and alignment across attributes. By making analytical assumptions explicit, including attribute selection, rubric construction, and weighting schemes, the framework enables users to evaluate whether its embedded priorities align with the users' own normative commitments. The approach is jurisdiction-agnostic and intended to support policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance environments.
  Contributions: (1) multidimensional policy assessment through empirically grounded rubrics that surface tradeoffs rather than resolving them; (2) a transparent hybrid methodology combining feedback from subject-matter experts with computational validation; and (3) use of domain-trained rubric-calibrated models as a benchmark for comparing different general-purpose large language models.

AI.tldr: A framework for systematic, transparent AI policy analysis that uses multidimensional rubrics to surface tradeoffs without prescribing outcomes, combining expert insights with computational methods and benchmarking LLMs against domain-trained models.
AI.motivation: AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions, making systematic assessment difficult in an evolving, contested regulatory landscape where transparency about analytical priorities is needed.
AI.method: Mixed-methods approach integrating qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to design policy attribute rubrics; uses comparative visualizations; benchmarks commercial LLMs against domain-trained rubric-calibrated models with explicit analytical assumptions.
AI.result: Developed a jurisdiction-agnostic policy analysis framework that quantifies relative emphasis of policy objectives through rubrics, enables cross-policy comparison via visualizations, and provides transparent benchmarking of LLM performance for policy analysis tasks.
AI.conclusion: The framework focuses on relevance and alignment across policy attributes rather than assessing effectiveness, making analytical assumptions explicit to allow users to evaluate whether embedded priorities align with their own normative commitments, supporting policymakers in complex AI governance environments.

title: Building a User Foundation Model for the Open Web
summary: User foundation models have demonstrated strong results in e-commerce and social recommendation, but most industrial deployments assume environments where user identity is stable and persistent. Open-web real-time bidding (RTB) operates on a structurally different data distribution: user identity is fragmented and non-persistent across browsing sessions, and the availability of browsing history depends on user privacy choices. Consequently, a significant portion of traffic carries no historical data, and available records often consist of relatively short, disjointed sessions. As a result, historical signals in this domain are typically represented as aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving the sequential structure unexploited. To address this limitation, we present a user foundation model that applies self-supervised learning on user browsing histories and show that the learned representation improves multiple downstream production tasks, demonstrating the viability of this approach on the open web. We pre-train a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective, then fine-tune it on the click prediction task. We optimize the encoder's pre-training pipeline with an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting. The same encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker; a 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excluding zero on both metrics).

AI.tldr: A user foundation model using self-supervised learning on fragmented RTB user browsing histories improves multiple downstream production tasks in open-web advertising, demonstrating viability despite non-persistent user identity challenges.
AI.motivation: Open-web RTB environments differ from traditional recommendation systems because user identity is fragmented and non-persistent, with significant traffic having no historical data and available records consisting of short, disjointed sessions. Current approaches only use aggregated counters and recency buckets, failing to exploit sequential structure in browsing histories.
AI.method: Pre-train a Transformer encoder using masked language modeling and sequence-level contrastive learning on user browsing histories, then fine-tune on click prediction. Use an LLM-in-the-loop search to optimize the pre-training pipeline by reviewing code-level edits (lifters) from a curated catalog, implementing LLM-as-optimizer paradigm.
AI.result: The learned representation improves multiple downstream tasks: +1.197% RIG on production bid win-rate model, +1.354% RIG on production CTR ranker. A 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR and -1.13% eCPC, with 80% confidence intervals excluding zero for both metrics.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised learning on fragmented user browsing histories can effectively create user foundation models that improve open-web RTB advertising performance, demonstrating the viability of this approach despite challenges with non-persistent user identity.

title: SciDataSailor: Deep Scientific Data Exploring
summary: Scientific datasets are commonly organized as hierarchical repositories containing heterogeneous and interdependent files, making their inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and reliant on domain expertise. Although large language model (LLM) agents have advanced substantially in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. We introduce Deep Scientific Data Exploration, an agentic task paradigm in which agents navigate repositories, interpret heterogeneous files and schemas, execute analyses, integrate cross-file evidence, and produce conclusions grounded in executed observations. To operationalize this paradigm, we present SciDataSailor, a framework for synthesizing tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation. SciDataSailor instantiates trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching. Using this framework, we construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, with the latter comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning the life, earth, and physical sciences.

AI.tldr: SciDataSailor enables LLM agents to autonomously explore and analyze complex scientific datasets through executable environments using Monte Carlo Tree Search with specialized mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Scientific datasets are organized as hierarchical repositories with heterogeneous, interdependent files, making inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and dependent on domain expertise. Existing LLM agent research has overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data through executable environments.
AI.method: SciDataSailor framework synthesizes tool-interactive trajectories using Monte Carlo Tree Search with four mechanisms: 1) difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, 2) dual-feedback first-play urgency, 3) hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and 4) entropy-guided branching. The framework is applied to create SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation.
AI.result: Created evaluation benchmarks with 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning life, earth, and physical sciences. Operationalized the Deep Scientific Data Exploration paradigm for agents to navigate repositories, interpret files, execute analyses, and integrate cross-file evidence.
AI.conclusion: SciDataSailor represents a significant advancement in enabling LLM agents to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments, addressing the gap in existing research and providing a robust framework for scientific data exploration and analysis.

title: Flux-OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Evolving Contexts
summary: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts can convey such preferences, yet provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision results in an unstable distillation target and conflicting distributions, requiring mechanisms to stabilize target and downweight conflicts. In this paper, we analyze the effect of contexts through a decomposition of the reverse KL objective, revealing two findings: the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and the objective contains a conflict term that measures conflicts among these teachers. Based on this decomposition, we propose Flux-OPD, an OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains. Flux-OPD treats the differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights their correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator. Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential to combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

AI.tldr: Flux-OPD is a new online preference distillation method that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains, outperforming existing OPD approaches by stabilizing context distillation through contextual corrections weighted by teacher conflicts.
AI.motivation: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize. While contexts can convey preferences, they provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, necessitating evolving contexts that adapt with student performance.
AI.method: The authors propose Flux-OPD, which treats differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals. These signals are injected as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, with their correction strength weighted using a conflict term (derived from reverse KL decomposition) that measures conflicts among context-conditioned teachers.
AI.result: Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms. The method successfully combines teacher supervision with evolving contexts to capture task preferences in open-ended domains.
AI.conclusion: Flux-OPD demonstrates the potential to effectively combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts for preference distillation in open-ended domains, addressing challenges of unstable distillation targets and conflicting distributions when using evolving contexts as in-training supervision.

title: MIND: Lightweight and Effective Memory Injection Defense for LLM Agents via Intent-Aware Information Bottleneck
summary: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks: Agents may retrieve poisoned memory from attackers, which diverts their behavior from initial user intent and finally causes task failure. However, existing defense mechanisms either incur high computational cost or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts. To address these challenges, we propose Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising(MIND), a lightweight defense framework for memory injection attack. Our preliminary analysis reveals that benign and poisoned trajectories exhibit distinguishable relationships between the initial user intent and subsequent behavior. Building on this observation, MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck(IB) to extract compact intent--behavior representations from the initial intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information, and a lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from the resulting representations. As such, MIND mitigates information redundancy in multi-turn contexts while avoiding the overhead of repeated LLM auditing. Extensive experiments show that MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. Notably, on ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3%, respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.

AI.tldr: MIND is a lightweight defense framework using intent-aware Information Bottleneck to detect and filter poisoned memories in LLM-based agents, reducing attack success rates while maintaining efficiency.
AI.motivation: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks that divert their behavior from user intent. Existing defenses have high computational costs or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts.
AI.method: Proposes Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising (MIND) framework. Uses intent-aware Information Bottleneck to extract compact intent-behavior representations from initial intent and turn-level behavior, preserving attack signals while filtering irrelevant/repetitive information. A lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from these representations.
AI.result: MIND significantly reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. On ReAct-StrategyQA, reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3% respectively, while matching undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.
AI.conclusion: MIND provides an effective lightweight defense against memory injection attacks that addresses computational cost and information redundancy issues of existing approaches, making LLM-based agents more secure and efficient.

title: Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation
summary: Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) or On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). While OPSD provides dense, logit-level supervision, it inherently suffers from exposure bias due to the privileged information of the self-teacher. In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and the loss of clear optimization directions. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO), which reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective. By leveraging predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), CRPO conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals. Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

AI.tldr: CRPO reformulates agentic On-Policy Self-Distillation from a contrastive learning perspective to address exposure bias and reasoning convergence in multi-turn LLM agent training.
AI.motivation: Existing On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) methods for LLMs suffer from exposure bias due to privileged information of self-teachers, leading to reasoning route convergence and loss of clear optimization directions in multi-turn agentic settings.
AI.method: Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO) reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective. It uses predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), conducting group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.
AI.conclusion: CRPO provides an effective solution to exposure bias in OPSD for multi-turn agentic LLMs by leveraging contrastive learning principles, resulting in improved optimization signals, training stability, and generalization performance.

title: Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training
summary: Synthetic textbook data has improved language model pre-training, but prior work largely treats the benefit as a property of generated content or local rewriting style. We study a different factor: whether related content is organized into coherent book-level documents. We contribute both a scalable synthesis pipeline and controlled evidence that this organization matters. The pipeline retrieves source material from a pre-training corpus, clusters it into topical units, plans hierarchical tables of contents, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books (our Full setting), yielding 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines. Replacing natural books in a mid-training mix with this corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Controlled comparisons then disentangle the relevant design factors. A content-matched Split condition holds generated text and tokens fixed but treats each section as an independent document; Full's +1.02 mean gain isolates document packaging. A length-matched RandomConcat control that joins sections from different books remains below Full, ruling out document length alone. A retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase condition independently rewrites individual retrieved documents under the same audience-by-style scheme, without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly; Full's +1.17 gain demonstrates the value of structured synthesis. On Llama3-8B, Full likewise outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books, supporting book-level organization as a useful axis for synthetic pre-training data design.

AI.tldr: Synthetic textbooks organized into coherent book-level documents outperform both natural books and unstructured synthetic content in language model pre-training, demonstrating that document organization matters more than just content quality.
AI.motivation: Prior work on synthetic textbook data focuses on content quality or local rewriting style, but doesn't investigate whether organizing related content into coherent book-level documents provides additional benefits for language model pre-training.
AI.method: Developed a scalable synthesis pipeline that retrieves source material, clusters it into topical units, plans hierarchical tables of contents, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books. Conducted controlled experiments comparing: 1) Full (complete books), 2) Split (same content as independent documents), 3) RandomConcat (mixed sections), and 4) Rephrase (individually rewritten documents).
AI.result: Full organization (+1.09 improvement) outperforms natural books. Document packaging contributes +1.02 gain (Full vs Split). Structured synthesis contributes +1.17 gain (Full vs Rephrase). Full also outperforms RandomConcat, ruling out document length effects. Results generalize to Llama3-8B.
AI.conclusion: Book-level organization is a crucial factor in synthetic pre-training data design that provides substantial performance benefits beyond content quality, demonstrating that coherent document structure matters for language model learning.

title: Enhancing Irregular Time Series Forecasting with Continuous-Time Modeling Framework
summary: Irregular multivariate time series are widely encountered in applications such as healthcare monitoring, human activity recognition, and environmental sensing. Their core challenges stem from asynchronous observations, non-uniform sampling intervals, and the fact that temporal patterns themselves carry critical dynamic information. Existing approaches either rely on discretization-based preprocessing (e.g., interpolation, imputation, or aggregation), which disrupts the underlying continuous-time semantics, or adopt continuous-time modeling via ODE-based frameworks, which typically require specialized architectures and incur substantial computational overhead due to numerical solvers. To address these limitations, we propose WrapFlow, a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting. On the input side, WrapFlow introduces Continuous-Time Tokenization, which directly encodes raw observation events and explicitly models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens. The resulting continuous-time tokens are then processed by a standard Transformer backbone to capture long-range temporal dependencies. On the output side, we develop a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions while avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training. This design enables high-quality continuous forecasting using only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: WrapFlow: A continuous-time modeling framework for irregular multivariate time series forecasting that avoids ODE numerical solvers via continuous-time tokenization and simulation-free flow matching.
AI.motivation: Irregular multivariate time series (common in healthcare, activity recognition, sensing) have challenges with asynchronous observations, non-uniform sampling, and temporal patterns carrying critical dynamic information. Existing methods either use discretization-based preprocessing (which disrupts continuous-time semantics) or ODE-based frameworks (which require specialized architectures and heavy computational overhead from numerical solvers).
AI.method: 1) Continuous-Time Tokenization: Directly encodes raw observation events and models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens. 2) Standard Transformer backbone processes these tokens for long-range dependencies. 3) Simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching: learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions without numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training, enabling continuous forecasting with few fixed rollout steps at inference.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: WrapFlow provides an effective continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting that avoids the computational burdens of ODE-based methods while maintaining continuous-time semantics and achieving superior performance.

title: BlueprintRepair: Typed Local Edits for Failed Lean Proof Blueprints
summary: LLM-based Lean proving systems increasingly organize a proof as a blueprint: a dependency graph of formal statements. We introduce BlueprintRepair, a repair interface that lets a model change this graph through ten schema-checked local operations. An operation names the node it edits, so the target theorem cannot be changed. Lean checks every applied change, and an accepted repair must declare every blueprint lemma its proof uses. We also construct BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with complete accepted and rejected repair trajectories. We compare typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, one episode per state and interface. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the three interfaces solve almost the same number of the benchmark's localized failures. Typed repair is the cheapest per solved state (patching is 1.30x as expensive, rewriting 2.06x), and within 10,000 completion tokens per task it reaches almost all of its final coverage, while both free-form interfaces are well behind. A second model, Qwen3.6-Flash, solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest, puts it ahead on the proof-authoring states, and repeats the localized pattern.

AI.tldr: BlueprintRepair introduces a repair interface for LLM-based Lean proving systems using ten schema-checked operations on proof blueprints, with typed edits proving most efficient and cost-effective for fixing failures.
AI.motivation: LLM-based Lean proving systems organize proofs as dependency graphs (blueprints), but there's a need for efficient repair mechanisms when these proofs fail. Current approaches may be inefficient or lack proper structure for targeted fixes.
AI.method: BlueprintRepair provides ten schema-checked local operations that allow models to edit proof dependency graphs while maintaining structure. The system includes Lean verification for every change and requires declaration of blueprint lemmas used. They also created BlueprintTrace benchmark with 142 controlled failures and compared typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under controlled conditions.
AI.result: With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, all three interfaces solved similar numbers of localized failures, but typed repair was cheapest (patching 1.30x more expensive, rewriting 2.06x). Typed repair reached near-maximal coverage within 10,000 tokens, outperforming free-form interfaces. Qwen3.6-Flash solved fewer states but maintained typed repair as cheapest and superior for proof-authoring states.
AI.conclusion: Typed repair operations on proof blueprints are the most cost-effective approach for fixing failures in LLM-based Lean proving systems, offering better efficiency and coverage than patch-based or rewrite-based approaches while maintaining structural integrity of proofs.

title: Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers
summary: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

AI.tldr: A two-stage Newton initial guess strategy that learns from parameter-space sampling to predict better starting points, reducing Newton iterations and computational time for nonlinear PDE problems.
AI.motivation: Newton's method converges faster with better initial guesses, but finding good starting points for large-scale nonlinear problems is challenging. The paper aims to reduce the number of Newton iterations and overall CPU time by improving initial guesses through machine learning.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) Learn from parameter-space sampling and precomputed solutions to create two reduced spaces - solution feature space from converged states and corrective search direction feature space from Newton increments. Use regression to predict surrogate solutions for new parameters. (2) Apply residual-minimizing correction using GMRES-based approach to refine the prediction, then use as initial guess for high-fidelity Newton method.
AI.result: The strategy significantly reduces Newton iterations and overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared to standalone surrogate initialization, with computationally inexpensive corrective steps requiring only residual evaluations and small least-squares problems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed weakly intrusive methodology successfully accelerates Newton convergence through intelligent initial guess generation, is applicable to broad classes of large-scale nonlinear problems, and demonstrates practical computational benefits through reduced iteration counts and faster solution times.

title: ConMem: Contribution-Aware Memory for Long-Horizon Manufacturing Inspection Logs
summary: Long-horizon steel-equipment inspection requires reasoning over heterogeneous records accumulated across repeated inspection cycles. Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems treat historical logs as a static corpus and retain records without estimating their diagnostic value, failing to report early risk. To this end, we propose ConMem, a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted equipment inspection, supporting a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system. Specifically, our ConMem first segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, then estimates each memory unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis through a Shapley-style estimation, and finally retains high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget. In experiments, we evaluate ConMem on real-world dataset and ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, exceeding the strongest directly comparable baseline. Relative to the naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces the average number of input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablation studies also show that the functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation are helping prioritize weak degradation signals for targeted field inspection. Practical deployments further confirm that ConMem retains the weak early signal across three inspection cycles, providing an early-stage seal-wear alert targeted for on-site inspectors.

AI.tldr: ConMem is a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted steel equipment inspection that intelligently selects and retains high-value historical inspection evidence under memory constraints to enable early risk detection.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems for equipment inspection treat historical logs as static corpora without assessing diagnostic value, which prevents them from identifying early risk signals across repeated inspection cycles.
AI.method: ConMem segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, estimates each memory unit's diagnostic contribution using Shapley-style estimation, and selectively retains high-value evidence under constrained memory budgets.
AI.result: ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy on real-world datasets, exceeding comparable baselines. It reduces input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6% compared to naive 8K-context LLM baselines, successfully retaining weak degradation signals across inspection cycles.
AI.conclusion: ConMem's contribution-aware memory framework enables effective early-risk screening for equipment inspection by intelligently selecting diagnostic evidence, as demonstrated by practical deployments that successfully detected early-stage seal-wear alerts.

title: ClawTrack: Towards Trace-Level Evaluation and Improvement of Real-World Autonomous Agents
summary:
As LLM-based agents are deployed in complex, multi-step workflows, a critical evaluation gap has emerged: most existing benchmarks judge only final outcomes, unable to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies, hindering attribution in long-horizon tasks.
  In this work, we present ClawTrack, a dual-assessment benchmark that simultaneously measures what an agent achieves (Task Score) and how it achieves it (Process Score). ClawTrack comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification), anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, we find that: (1) process scores effectively attribute success and failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary, with result verification as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; and (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

AI.tldr: ClawTrack is a benchmark that evaluates LLM-based agents on both task outcomes (Task Score) and reasoning process quality (Process Score) across 320 multi-step tasks to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky successes.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks only judge final outcomes in complex, multi-step workflows, making it impossible to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies in long-horizon tasks.
AI.method: ClawTrack uses dual assessment: Task Score (what agents achieve) and Process Score (how they achieve it). It includes 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, result verification) using 12,541 task-specific rubric items.
AI.result: Evaluation of 21 models over 16,000+ trials shows: (1) process scores effectively attribute success/failure to specific reasoning dimensions and filter lucky passes; (2) the four dimensions are complementary with result verification as systematic bottleneck; (3) framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.
AI.conclusion: ClawTrack provides a comprehensive benchmark that enables fine-grained evaluation of LLM agent reasoning processes, addressing critical gaps in current evaluation methods for complex workflows and offering actionable insights for improving agent reliability and attribution in long-horizon tasks.

title: AgenticASR: Refining Speech Recognition in Real-World Scenarios via an Agentic Approach
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has achieved substantial gains in transcription accuracy, yet verbatim transcription does not necessarily produce readily usable text. It retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that increase reading effort, obscure the speaker's final intent, and propagate unresolved or abandoned content to downstream tasks. Existing spoken-to-written methods process completed audio or transcripts but cannot revise emitted text when later speech changes how preceding content should be interpreted. We therefore formulate Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), an audio-to-clean-text task that removes disfluencies, resolves self-corrections, and normalizes written form while preserving the speaker's final intent. AgenticASR implements this task through an ASR--Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces its corresponding output span as audio arrives. This enables continual emission and revision over streams of arbitrary duration. We also introduce AASR-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with fine-grained atomic rubrics. Across multiple ASR front ends, AgenticASR attains the highest AASR-Bench scores among evaluated systems. A human--AI agreement study shows that rubric-based judgments align with independent expert assessments. Ablations characterize Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality--latency trade-off between online and offline inference. Together, these results establish AgenticASR as a practical framework for intent-preserving clean transcription during ongoing speech. Code, AASR-Bench, and a demo will be released at https://github.com/AnXMuy/AgenticASR.

AI.tldr: Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticASR) is a new audio-to-clean-text framework that produces readable transcripts by removing disfluencies and resolving self-corrections in real-time, outperforming existing systems on a new benchmark.
AI.motivation: While ASR achieves high accuracy, verbatim transcription retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that increase reading effort, obscure speaker intent, and create problems for downstream tasks. Existing methods cannot revise emitted text when later speech changes how preceding content should be interpreted.
AI.method: Proposes AgenticASR with ASR-Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms bounded active context and replaces corresponding output spans as audio arrives, enabling continual emission and revision over arbitrary audio streams. Also introduces AASR-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with fine-grained atomic rubrics.
AI.result: AgenticASR achieves highest AASR-Bench scores across multiple ASR front ends. Human-AI agreement study shows rubric-based judgments align with expert assessments. Ablations characterize Refiner capacity, context length, and quality-latency trade-off between online/offline inference.
