summary: Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses data heterogeneity in federated settings by grouping clients with similar data distributions to enable effective training. Existing methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. We formalize this as the CFL trilemma, according to which improving two of these dimensions comes at the expense of the third. A prominent paradigm relies on metadata (i.e., low-dimensional representations of client datasets shared with the server) to enable communication- and computation-efficient clustering. However, such approaches are not compatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. To address this limitation, we propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This design enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes. We conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios. Results show that FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models. It enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

AI.tldr: FLAMECHE proposes a new federated learning approach that enables metadata-based clustering while maintaining compatibility with privacy-preserving encryption schemes, addressing the trade-off between privacy, communication cost, and computational efficiency in clustered federated learning.
AI.motivation: Existing clustered federated learning methods face a trilemma between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. Metadata-based approaches enable efficient clustering but are incompatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms.
AI.method: Reformulates metadata-based clustered federated learning as a distributed Expectation-Maximization procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios show that FLAMECHE improves client model effectiveness and enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering.
AI.conclusion: FLAMECHE successfully addresses the CFL trilemma by enabling metadata-based clustering that is compatible with privacy-preserving encryption, improving the positioning of metadata approaches within the trade-off between privacy, communication, and computational efficiency.

title: HyperClaim: Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Hypergraph Reasoning for Video Misinformation Detection
summary: Video misinformation detection is often approached through global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning. Both paradigms can under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Because such interactions are inherently higher-order, pairwise graph formulations are insufficient to capture multi-way cross-modal dependencies, whereas hypergraphs offer a suitable representation for these relations. We propose HyperClaim, a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for sample-level authenticity classification. Using the title or benchmark-provided paired text as a claim-like query, HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout. Without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten. Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, it achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV, respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights further reveal token- and frame-level structure.

AI.tldr: HyperClaim: A temporal hypergraph framework for video misinformation detection that captures fine-grained cross-modal interactions between query phrases, text evidence, and video frames.
AI.motivation: Existing video misinformation detection methods (global multimodal fusion or free-form reasoning) under-represent localized authenticity cues from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Pairwise graph formulations are insufficient for multi-way cross-modal dependencies.
AI.method: HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through discrepancy-aware readout.
AI.result: Achieves 83.7% accuracy on FakeSV, 82.0% on FakeTT, and 87.3% on FakeVV under the FactGuard temporal protocol, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. The model preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure.
AI.conclusion: Hypergraph representations are effective for capturing multi-way cross-modal dependencies in video misinformation detection, preserving fine-grained structure that global fusion approaches flatten. The framework demonstrates strong performance without needing generated rationales or external tool calls.

title: LEDGERMIND: Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger
summary: Multimodal agents for visual question answering increasingly operate as multi-step trajectories that interleave perception, retrieval, and reasoning, yet evaluation still largely reduces to final-answer accuracy. This aggregate signal cannot tell whether a correct answer was reached through grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. We propose to treat a multimodal agent trajectory as a provenance-constrained state machine: tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger that serves as the trajectory state, downstream reasoning and decision claims may cite only active ledger entries, grounding is checked at the entity and numeric level, and repair is realized as typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. We instantiate this design as LedgerMind (Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger), augmented by a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher that matches reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee. We use LedgerMind to target four recurring failure patterns that final-answer accuracy tends to obscure: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs show that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness.

AI.tldr: LedgerMind introduces a provenance-constrained state machine approach for evaluating multimodal agents, using a Structured Evidence Ledger to ensure grounding in evidence rather than language priors or error cancellation.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of multimodal agents focuses only on final-answer accuracy, which cannot distinguish whether correct answers come from grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. This obscures important failure patterns.
AI.method: Treat multimodal agent trajectories as provenance-constrained state machines with: 1) Structured Evidence Ledger that normalizes tool outputs, 2) citation requirement that downstream reasoning can only cite active ledger entries, 3) grounding checks at entity/numeric level, and 4) typed state transitions that prevent content introduction without tool-produced provenance. Additional components include Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher, and Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine.
AI.result: LedgerMind targets four failure patterns that final-answer accuracy obscures: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. Experiments across multimodal reasoning benchmarks show improvements in both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: The provenance-constrained approach with Structured Evidence Ledger provides a more rigorous evaluation framework that improves both the accuracy and faithfulness of multimodal agents by ensuring proper grounding in evidence throughout reasoning trajectories.

title: When Specifications Conflict: A Symmetry-Based Framework for Measuring LLM Preferences
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly required to integrate multiple sources of information that may be inconsistent or conflicting. However, there is still a lack of controllable and attributable methods for analyzing how models resolve conflicts between competing specifications. We propose a controlled experimental framework for studying model preferences under conflicting specifications. By constructing specifications with explicit conflicts, the framework enables model choices between competing specifications to be directly observed and analyzed. A symmetry-based design further reduces confounding factors, allowing preferences across representation types to be compared systematically.
  We evaluate the framework on an executable mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances spanning 11 function families, comparing four representation types: pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input--output examples. Results show systematic preference patterns rather than random behavior, with a consistent ordering: $ \text{Formal} \approx \text{Naturalized Formal} > \text{Pure Natural Language} > \text{Input--Output Examples} $. Example effects further depend on model capability and function family.
  We extend the framework to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and the clinical domain, demonstrating its applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms. The framework provides a unified approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information.

AI.tldr: A framework for studying how LLMs resolve conflicting information sources, showing systematic preferences for formal representations over natural language and examples.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of controllable and attributable methods for analyzing how LLMs resolve conflicts between inconsistent or competing information sources, especially when specifications conflict.
AI.method: Proposes a controlled experimental framework with explicit conflict construction, symmetry-based design to reduce confounding factors, and systematic comparison across four representation types: pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input-output examples.
AI.result: Systematic preference patterns emerged rather than random behavior, with consistent ordering: Formal ≈ Naturalized Formal > Pure Natural Language > Input-Output Examples. Example effects depend on model capability and function family.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a unified approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing information sources, demonstrating applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms in Boolean algebra, code generation, and clinical domains.

title: Hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo for Order-Optimal Neural Actor-Critic in Average-Reward CMDPs
summary: Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) provide a natural framework for reinforcement learning in safety-critical applications, where agents maximize long-term reward while satisfying long-term constraints. Although primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained open. The main challenge is a fundamental bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation: under Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis, reducing critic bias substantially increases critic optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework. We resolve this bottleneck by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization. The resulting estimator attains the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, we develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$. This establishes the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, while eliminating the need to know the underlying mixing time. Our results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo neural critic that achieves order-optimal convergence for average-reward constrained MDPs with neural function approximation, overcoming bias-cost trade-off limitations.
AI.motivation: CMDPs provide important framework for safety-critical RL applications, but extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained an open problem due to a fundamental bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation.
AI.method: Introduces hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization, achieving low bias with only logarithmic sample cost. Develops primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm building on this estimator.
AI.result: Achieves both optimality gap and constraint violation of order Õ(T^{-1/2}), establishing first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, without needing to know mixing time.
AI.conclusion: Resolves bottleneck in neural critic estimation for CMDPs by introducing hierarchical MLMC approach that overcomes bias-cost trade-off, enabling order-optimal convergence with neural function approximation even in the unconstrained setting.

title: GLM-RAG: Graph Language Models for Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs requires retrievers that can effectively capture both graph structure and semantic information. Recent approaches have explored graph neural network (GNN)-based retrievers to model graph topology in multi-hop reasoning tasks. In parallel, graph language models (GLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm that integrates graph reasoning and the semantic capabilities of language models. In this work, we introduce a GLM-based retriever and investigate the comparative strengths of GLM-based, GNN-based, and traditional vector-search-based retrievers in single- and multi-hop RAG settings, and with a particular focus on transferability to unseen domains. Our findings suggest that finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out of domain, achieving SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets they remain comparable to prior work, with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with an efficient training setup, whereas the vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.

AI.tldr: GLM-based retrievers outperform GNN-based and vector-search methods in multi-hop RAG tasks, showing better out-of-domain generalization while achieving state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG approaches over knowledge graphs need retrievers that effectively capture both structural and semantic information. While GNN-based retrievers model graph topology well and GLMs integrate graph reasoning with language model capabilities, there's a need to compare their effectiveness in single- and multi-hop RAG settings with focus on transferability to unseen domains.
AI.method: Introduce a GLM-based retriever and conduct comparative evaluation of three approaches: GLM-based retrievers, GNN-based retrievers, and traditional vector-search-based retrievers. Evaluation covers single- and multi-hop RAG settings with particular attention to transferability to unseen domains.
AI.result: Finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out-of-domain, achieving state-of-the-art on two multi-hop benchmarks. For in-domain multi-hop QA datasets, GLM retrievers remain comparable to prior work with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with efficient training, while vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.
AI.conclusion: GLM-based retrievers offer superior out-of-domain generalization for multi-hop RAG tasks over knowledge graphs, suggesting they represent a promising direction for retrieval-augmented generation systems that need to handle unseen domains effectively.

title: Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees
summary: Computer-use agents often fail on transient GUI events because they produce the correct action only after the relevant window has already closed. We identify the main cause as expensive autoregressive decoding on the decision-time critical path. We propose Adaptive Anticipatory Policy Trees (AAPT), which eliminates this delay without modifying the underlying model. During idle screen periods, the same frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. The tree is sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without generating new text. In paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests, AAPT improves the success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within a contested decision window ($p=1.8\times10^{-3}$), while producing no incorrect actions. Both open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines achieve zero success because they still decode during execution. A preparation-time sweep shows that the gain emerges where the latency-based tree-sizing rule predicts, and ablations reveal three key requirements: fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing. A pre-registered oracle probe rejects our initial hypothesis and instead points to branch routing as the causal bottleneck. We further reproduce the effect on an independent general-purpose multimodal model over 126 paired trials ($p=4.9\times10^{-13}$). On an external benchmark, AAPT matches the overall performance of a reactive baseline, although the two methods exhibit complementary strengths. Together, these results suggest that AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, whereas reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot.

AI.tldr: AAPT pre-computes conditional policy trees during idle periods to eliminate decision latency, enabling instant action execution when GUI events occur, significantly improving success rates in time-sensitive scenarios.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents fail on transient GUI events due to expensive autoregressive decoding delays that cause actions to be produced after relevant windows have already closed.
AI.method: AAPT constructs bounded conditional policy trees with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines during idle periods using a frozen multimodal model. When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to prepared branches and executes corresponding actions immediately without generating new text.
AI.result: In paired trials, AAPT improved success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within contested decision windows (p=1.8×10⁻³) with no incorrect actions, while open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines achieved zero success. The method was also validated on an independent multimodal model over 126 paired trials (p=4.9×10⁻¹³).
AI.conclusion: AAPT effectively eliminates decision latency by pre-computing conditional policies during idle periods, performing best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, while reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot.

title: QuantWAMs: Calibrating at the Right Granularity for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, but their iterative denoising and closed-loop execution make efficient deployment costly. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are poorly suited to WAMs because they rely on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that do not reflect deployment. We present QuantWAMs, a PTQ framework that aligns quantization decisions with the calibration context defined by model structure, rollout distribution, and task objective. QuantWAMs introduces three strategies: shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; co-training-objective saliency, which computes empirical-Fisher scores from the joint video--action gradient and assigns weight precision at a calibration-stable layer granularity; and fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing the precision budget. We evaluate QuantWAMs on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation with an AgiBot G2. Under a W4A4-dominant setting, the reported simulation means differ from FP16 by 0.2--0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials further establish deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. For the targeted video and action blocks, QuantWAMs reduces peak weight-and-activation memory to about 29\% of FP16 and provides 1.4--1.6$\times$ block-level speedups.

AI.tldr: QuantWAMs is a post-training quantization framework for World Action Models that enables efficient deployment through specialized calibration strategies aligned with WAM structure, rollout distribution, and task objectives.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training quantization methods are poorly suited for World Action Models due to their reliance on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that don't reflect actual deployment contexts. WAMs have iterative denoising and closed-loop execution that make efficient deployment costly.
AI.method: QuantWAMs introduces three key strategies: 1) shared-basis outlier calibration that pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules, 2) co-training-objective saliency that computes empirical-Fisher scores from joint video-action gradients and assigns weight precision at calibration-stable layer granularity, and 3) fixed-intervention rollout auditing that revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing precision budget.
AI.result: Under W4A4-dominant quantization, the method achieves simulation means differing from FP16 by only 0.2-0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials establish deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. QuantWAMs reduces peak weight-and-activation memory to about 29% of FP16 and provides 1.4-1.6× block-level speedups.
AI.conclusion: QuantWAMs provides an effective PTQ framework for World Action Models that aligns quantization decisions with the specific calibration context of WAMs, enabling efficient deployment with minimal performance degradation while significantly reducing memory requirements and improving inference speed.

title: On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning for Large Action Spaces
summary: This thesis studies policy learning in interactive systems where an agent observes a context, selects an action from a very large set, and receives partial feedback. The main framework is contextual bandits, with two paradigms: on-policy learning, where the agent interacts sequentially with the environment and minimizes regret, and off-policy learning, where it learns from logged data collected by a logging policy. In large action spaces, both settings face major challenges: inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. The first part develops structured Bayesian methods for on-policy learning. We introduce meTS, a mixed-effect extension of Thompson sampling, and dTS, which leverages diffusion-inspired priors to model dependencies between actions. These methods share information across actions and yield regret guarantees depending on an effective number of actions. The second part addresses off-policy learning. We propose sDM, a structured direct method based on latent variables, show that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces, and introduce concave, efficiently optimizable policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives. Finally, we develop differentiable pessimistic methods based on exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control the bias-variance trade-off of regularized importance-sampling estimators.

AI.tldr: Thesis develops structured Bayesian and direct methods for contextual bandits with large action spaces, addressing exploration challenges in on-policy learning and bias-variance trade-offs in off-policy learning.
AI.motivation: Policy learning in interactive systems with large action spaces faces major challenges including inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes.
AI.method: Two-part approach: 1) For on-policy learning: structured Bayesian methods including mixed-effect Thompson sampling (meTS) and diffusion-inspired prior methods (dTS). 2) For off-policy learning: structured direct methods (sDM) with latent variables, concave policy-weighted objectives, and differentiable pessimistic methods with PAC-Bayesian bounds.
AI.result: Developed methods that share information across actions with regret guarantees depending on effective number of actions; showed optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces; introduced concave, efficiently optimizable objectives; and developed methods to control bias-variance trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Structured approaches to contextual bandits with large action spaces can effectively address exploration challenges and bias-variance trade-offs through Bayesian sharing of information, latent variable modeling, and regularization techniques with theoretical guarantees.

title: WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning
summary: Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of LLMs. Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly and can deliver practical throughput gains, but their input-agnostic computation allocation often causes substantial accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity. Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality retention by adapting computation to individual inputs, yet they remain largely limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and their practical acceleration under real-world inference scenarios remains challenging. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework designed for both prefill and decode scenarios. WIDE enables fine-grained computation allocation by allowing each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning beyond layer-level decisions to neuron-block-level granularity. Through a two-stage training pipeline, WIDE learns effective token-wise sparse execution patterns and achieves substantially better quality retention than existing approaches. To make such fine-grained dynamic pruning practical, we further propose a pruning--kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across different granularities. At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost when compared to the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning/tree/main/WIDE.

AI.tldr: WIDE is a novel differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework for LLMs that achieves fine-grained computation allocation by allowing each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, with a co-designed pruning-kernel framework for practical acceleration.
AI.motivation: Existing static structured pruning methods cause substantial accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity due to input-agnostic computation allocation, while dynamic sparsity methods remain limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and face practical acceleration challenges in real-world inference scenarios.
AI.method: WIDE introduces an end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework with: 1) fine-grained computation allocation via token-wise selection of attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, 2) a two-stage training pipeline to learn effective sparse execution patterns, and 3) a pruning-kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping.
AI.result: At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost compared to state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. For prefill and decoding workloads, it achieves kernel-level speedups up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, with 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration respectively.
AI.conclusion: WIDE successfully addresses the limitations of existing pruning methods by enabling fine-grained dynamic pruning at neuron-block-level granularity while maintaining practical acceleration through hardware-aware optimization, making it a promising approach for efficient LLM inference.

title: QQWorld: Quantile-Quantile Matching for World Model Regularization
summary: Latent world models enable efficient planning by predicting future states in a compact representation space, but their performance depends critically on the quality of the learned latent distribution. LeWorldModel (LeWM) regularizes its latents toward an isotropic Gaussian using the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective. We show that the corrective gradients of EP rapidly vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled. To address this limitation, we propose QQWorld, which replaces EP with a quantile-quantile matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, thereby maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. We further develop cross-batch QQ, which enlarges the effective ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, and characterize its bias-variance trade-off. Across four control environments, QQWorld effectively improves the average planning success rate of LeWM, while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.

AI.tldr: QQWorld improves upon LeWM's latent world models by replacing Epps-Pulley regularization with quantile-quantile matching, achieving better latent distribution alignment and planning performance.
AI.motivation: The paper identifies a limitation in LeWorldModel (LeWM), where the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective fails to adequately regularize heavy-tailed deviations in latent distributions because its corrective gradients vanish for isolated tail samples.
AI.method: Proposes QQWorld which uses quantile-quantile matching to align projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles. Also introduces cross-batch QQ that enlarges the effective ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, with analysis of its bias-variance trade-off.
AI.result: QQWorld improves average planning success rate over LeWM across four control environments, consistently yields better Gaussian alignment, and produces thinner latent tails.
AI.conclusion: Quantile-quantile matching provides more effective regularization for latent world models than EP objective by maintaining corrective gradients in the tails, leading to improved planning performance through better latent distribution alignment.

title: When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence
comment: 25 pages, including references and supplementary material; 3 figures and 19 tables. Code: https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead
summary: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. We define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as the failure in which a downstream LLM assigns such a measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or uses it outside its valid scope. Using physiological sensing as a case study, D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG, whereas D2 tests rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history. ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference construction but is never shown to the LLM. Five estimands quantify this chain: conflict over-trust rate (COTR) and context-induced error rate (CIR) characterize D1/D2; correct repair rate (CRR) measures frozen-error repair; evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasts matched and patient-disjoint shuffled evidence; and utility harm rate (UHR) measures unnecessary verification among HIGH-reliability cases used without verification at baseline. The framework does not depend on a particular reliability generator. We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference. On a protocol-locked 187-patient test, the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero; UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7). DFOT provides a common evaluation target for stronger mitigation methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead.

AI.tldr: Researchers define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as LLMs wrongly treating derived measurements as direct facts, propose a framework to quantify this issue using physiological sensing case studies, and demonstrate mitigation improvements.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly rely on derived measurements as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity, creating risks when these measurements are used outside their valid scope or treated as ground truth.
AI.method: Defined DFOT framework with five estimands to quantify: conflict over-trust rate (COTR), context-induced error rate (CIR), correct repair rate (CRR), evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM), and utility harm rate (UHR). Used physiological sensing (PPG vs ECG) as case study with 50,000 paired records and ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as baseline.
AI.result: On 187-patient test, baseline improved four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points with all confidence intervals excluding zero; UHR increased by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7). Framework successfully quantified DFOT issues and mitigation improvements.
AI.conclusion: DFOT provides a standardized evaluation target for mitigating LLMs' over-trust in derived measurements, with demonstrated effectiveness in physiological sensing applications, though some utility trade-offs exist. The framework is adaptable to various reliability generation methods.

title: QAdapt: A Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding Framework for Quantum Error Correction
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) relies on quantum error correction to suppress physical errors and preserve logical information at scale. In practice, however, performance is constrained not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing rapidly generated syndrome data. This challenge is exacerbated by hardware noise that is strong, heterogeneous, and nonstationary, as well as by the simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that can substantially degrade fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces the logical error rate relative to the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves reductions of up to 5.79 percent in logical error rate and 9.32 percent in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome. These results demonstrate that QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

AI.tldr: QAdapt is a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction that captures local spatiotemporal correlations, adapts to evolving noise conditions, and reduces both logical error rates and decoding latency.
AI.motivation: The performance of fault-tolerant quantum computing is constrained not only by physical noise but also by classical decoder latency, which is exacerbated by strong, heterogeneous, nonstationary hardware noise and the simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that degrades fixed neural decoders.
AI.method: QAdapt is a neural pre-decoding framework that captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder.
AI.result: QAdapt consistently reduces logical error rates across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations. On Google's Willow benchmark data without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves reductions of up to 5.79% in logical error rate and 9.32% in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome.
AI.conclusion: QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

title: A foundation model of numerical intelligence with cross-disciplinary generalization
summary: Intelligence is commonly understood as the ability to acquire and apply knowledge, adapt to unfamiliar situations and solve new problems. Large language models exhibit this capacity by inferring task-relevant knowledge from textual context and applying it to new tasks. Yet intelligence need not be confined to language. For scientific and social systems, we need models that acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context-an ability we call numerical intelligence. Here we introduce UNified In-Context Operator Networks (UNICON), a foundation model that exhibits numerical intelligence across disciplines. Using graph-based examples from a system as context, UNICON infers the predictive relation shared across them and applies it to queries from the same system. Across scientific and social systems, including those from disciplines absent from training, the same model approaches specialist performance without retraining. Combining UNICON with language-model agents yields further gains, enabling it to surpass state-of-the-art specialists in a discipline unseen in training. We further show that training-corpus diversity improves generalization to unseen disciplines. Together, these results establish UNICON as a foundation model of numerical intelligence and position it as a building block for a broader ecosystem of artificial intelligence.

AI.tldr: UNICON is a foundation model that learns numerical intelligence from graph-based examples to make predictions across scientific and social systems, achieving near-specialist performance even on unseen disciplines when combined with language models.
AI.motivation: While large language models demonstrate intelligence through textual context, scientific and social systems need models that can acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context - what the authors call "numerical intelligence." Current models lack this capability for inference from numerical data across disciplines.
AI.method: UNICON (UNified In-Context Operator Networks) is a graph-based foundation model that learns predictive relations from system examples as context. It infers relationships shared across examples and applies them to queries from the same system, enabling generalization across disciplines without retraining.
AI.result: UNICON approaches specialist performance across scientific and social systems, including those from disciplines absent from training. When combined with language-model agents, it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists in unseen disciplines. Training with diverse corpora improves generalization to unseen disciplines.
AI.conclusion: UNICON establishes itself as a foundation model for numerical intelligence and serves as a building block for broader AI ecosystems, demonstrating that numerical intelligence can be achieved through unified models that learn from diverse disciplinary data.

title: Kohn-Sham Spectral Embedding on Sparse Graphs at the Nishimori Temperature for Image Classification
comment: 42 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables, was presented at the 10th International Conference 'Deep Learning on Computational Physics (DLCP2026)', under review for the Moscow University Physics Bulletin, Physics series
summary: We introduce Kohn--Sham Spectral Embedding (KSSE), a physics-inspired energy-based model replacing dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding evaluated at the Nishimori temperature of an associated Random-Bond Ising Model. By mapping pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check graphs and constructing a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn--Sham Hamiltonian, we solve $D$ independent channel spectral problems in $\mathcal{O}(N\log N + k^2_{\text{mode}} N)$ time via FFT on circulant blocks (leveraging Pontryagin self-duality of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$) and low-order Rayleigh refinement. Graph topology is optimized using \emph{star-domain surgery}: rather than destroying information-carrying codewords by removing frustrated cycles, we construct edge shifts creating local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration to $ρ(B_γ)\leq 1+δ$. Multi-scale fractal analysis ($D_2$ spectrum) and fractal learning-rate landscape certifies a landscape transition from rough regimes ($D_2>3$) to star-domain basins ($D_2<1$), enabling Rayleigh refinement with $k_{\text{mode}}=5$ modes. We prove six theoretical results: a generalized Ihara--Bass identity linking belief propagation to the Laplacian; trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence; additive channel separability with an explicit exchange-correlation bound; a surgery theorem bounding frustration with attractor width $Ω(1/\sqrt{d_{\min}})$; a quasi-stationarity perturbation bound; and a fixed-point convergence theorem. In a transductive protocol on ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features ($D=1792$), KSSE achieves \textbf{88.93\%} Top-1 accuracy using $\approx 21.24$M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4--87.3\%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0--89.5\%) under standard inductive setups, while reducing model footprint by $10\times$ and $30\times$, respectively.

AI.tldr: KSSE replaces CNN classifiers with sparse-graph spectral embedding using quasi-cyclic parity-check graphs, achieving ImageNet-1000 accuracy competitive with large vision transformers while being 10-30x smaller.
AI.motivation: Current vision models like Swin Transformers and Vision Transformers require huge parameter counts. KSSE aims to achieve similar accuracy with significantly smaller models by replacing dense CNN classifiers with physics-inspired sparse graph spectral embeddings.
AI.method: Maps pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check graphs, constructs a regularized Laplacian as Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian, solves spectral problems via FFT on circulant blocks, optimizes graph topology with star-domain surgery to bound frustration, and uses multi-scale fractal analysis to certify landscape transitions.
AI.result: Achieves 88.93% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1000 with only ≈21.24M parameters using frozen EfficientNet-B4 features, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4-87.3%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0-89.5%) while being 10-30x smaller.
AI.conclusion: KSSE demonstrates that physics-inspired sparse graph spectral embeddings can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy with dramatically reduced parameter counts, providing an efficient alternative to large vision transformer architectures.

title: Metaphor Tracer: A Theory-Informed Analysis of Hidden States
summary:
What do a language model's hidden states say about the organization of a single text? From one forward pass, without training, we score every token position on two properties. The *aggregator* measures whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration. The *differentiator*, whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace as the model reads: metaphor in its root sense, transport. Constants were frozen on one discovery text; every other is confirmatory.
  The aggregator is not, in the classic sense, an information measure, nor a measure of salience. Across three unrelated models, as a signifier repeats, its surprisal and its attention drain while its aggregator score holds: the channel marks a token's place in the text. That this tracks a reading rests on independent ground truth: an engineered register the aggregator follows across its boundaries (6/6 cells), and a psychoanalyst's marking of clinical transcripts, fixed before the instrument existed, in 34/36 cells, with a graded increment above lexical controls and dissociations no type-level measure reproduces. A transfer test gives the result its shape: the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads the singular discourse worst, and in a matched base/instruct pair tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer. Structural value is a property of a token's place in *this* text, not of its vector alone: a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states, operationalizing theory that predated the instrument.

AI.tldr: Hidden states can identify text positions as 'aggregators' (stabilizing whole text) and 'differentiators' (drawing other tokens into their subspace), revealing structural properties beyond lexical type.
AI.motivation: To understand what language model hidden states reveal about the organization of individual texts, moving beyond lexical-level analysis to examine structural properties at specific token positions.
AI.method: From a single forward pass without training, score every token position on aggregator (consolidates text into stable configuration) and differentiator (draws other tokens into its subspace). Frozen constants on discovery text, validation on others.
AI.result: Aggregator marks token's place in text, distinct from surprisal/attention. Validated on engineered register (6/6 cells) and psychoanalyst transcripts (34/36 cells). Transfer test shows structural value is relational (text-specific) rather than essentialist (lexical type).
AI.conclusion: Language model hidden states reveal text-specific structural properties, supporting a relational rather than essentialist reading that operationalizes theory predating the instrument. Structural value depends on token's place in specific text, not vector alone.

title: Oracle-Budgeted Molecular Optimization with Short-Term Graph Memory
summary: Molecular optimization is commonly performed under a limited oracle budget, which makes deciding what to evaluate as important as deciding what to generate. We introduce short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that preserves the generator architecture and native update rule while learning from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize subsequent oracle queries. The module maintains an online graph neural surrogate that pre-screens each round's candidate pool, so the fixed oracle budget is spent on molecules with higher predicted utility. Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard molecular optimization benchmark, it improves the mean top-10 score at no extra oracle cost and never falls behind the base on any oracle; the gain extends to all four generators we tested at a tight budget of one thousand calls. We then analyze how surrogate-guided selection interacts with the exploration and exploitation behavior of different generators. Its benefit at larger budgets is consistent with two properties of the backbone: how broadly it searches, and how effectively its native search already exploits oracle feedback. We provide a simple way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, and evidence on which generators benefit from it.

AI.tldr: A plug-in graph memory module improves molecular optimization by pre-screening candidates with a GNN surrogate, spending limited oracle budget more selectively on higher-predicted-utility molecules.
AI.motivation: Molecular optimization faces limited oracle budgets, making evaluation decisions as crucial as generation decisions. Current approaches may waste oracle calls on low-utility candidates.
AI.method: Introduces short-term graph memory, a plug-in module with online graph neural surrogate that pre-screens candidate pools. Maintains generator architecture while learning from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize subsequent oracle queries.
AI.result: Improves mean top-10 score at no extra oracle cost across four generators, never falls behind base performance. Gain particularly strong at tight budgets (1000 calls). Benefit at larger budgets depends on generator's exploration breadth and existing feedback exploitation effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Provides effective method for selective oracle budget spending, with evidence showing which generator types benefit most from surrogate-guided selection based on their exploration-exploitation characteristics.

title: SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute
summary: Scaling test-time computation can improve language-model reasoning, but uniform budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. We introduce Self-Verifying Refinement (SVR), an oracle-free multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy. At each turn, the model produces a solution together with a discrete correctness verdict and a confidence score; it retains the current answer only when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, and otherwise continues refinement using its own self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to construct training rewards and is never exposed to the policy through refinement prompts or required at inference. SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories using rewards that promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states; adaptive stopping is activated only at inference. On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 inference turns on average. In the evaluated complete-system comparison, it exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference. These results demonstrate that learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

AI.tldr: SVR is an oracle-free reinforcement learning framework where language models learn to use self-verification to control test-time computation, adaptively refining solutions only when needed.
AI.motivation: Current approaches have limitations: uniform computation budgets waste resources on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement requires external feedback. There's a need for more efficient, self-contained adaptive computation methods.
AI.method: SVR uses multi-turn reinforcement learning (GRPO) where the model produces solutions with correctness verdicts and confidence scores. It retains answers only when verdict is "Correct" and confidence exceeds threshold, otherwise continues refinement. Training uses fixed-horizon trajectories with rewards for correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states.
AI.result: On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves 0.563 macro-average accuracy with only 2.99 average inference turns. It outperforms standard GRPO, multi-turn baselines, and oracle-guided approaches while using substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference.
AI.conclusion: Learned self-verification can effectively serve as an internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation, demonstrating the potential for efficient, self-contained refinement strategies.

title: Cybersecurity Detection Classification with Reasoning-enabled Language Models
summary: A major issue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) is alert fatigue, as the number of detections reported is more than staff can triage in a given day. Prior work prompts or fine-tunes large language models (LLMs) to emit a triage label directly, but does not train them to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat. We train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections by combining automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. We find that CoT reasoning also degrades the label-token probabilities that automated triage relies on, so we separately train a calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace and estimates the probability that the verdict is correct. Our system reaches 82.6% test accuracy and, at the high-confidence operating point that governs automated triage, improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. We further show that the trained calibrator is necessary - an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero - and that a finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, motivating targeted training over scale.

AI.tldr: A novel LLM-based triage system combining chain-of-thought reasoning, automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning achieves 82.6% test accuracy for Windows endpoint detections, significantly improving recall over direct-label approaches.
AI.motivation: Address alert fatigue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) where the volume of detections exceeds human triage capacity. Previous LLM approaches directly output triage labels without reasoning about whether detections are genuine threats, lacking explainability and reliability.
AI.method: Train a chain-of-thought reasoning-enabled triage classifier using: 1) automated prompt optimization, 2) self-training, and 3) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on real human-labeled Windows endpoint detections. Address CoT's degradation of label-token probabilities by training a separate calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace to estimate verdict correctness probability.
AI.result: System achieves 82.6% test accuracy. At high-confidence operating points for automated triage: improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over direct-label LLM classifier. Calibrator is essential - untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero. Fine-tuned 30B model outperforms frontier general-purpose models, showing targeted training beats scale.
AI.conclusion: Combining CoT reasoning with specialized training techniques creates an effective SOC triage system. The trained calibrator is critical for reliable confidence estimation. Targeted training of smaller models outperforms using larger general-purpose models, demonstrating the value of domain-specific optimization over pure scale.

title: LeanCSP: A Framework for Certifying Constraint Reformulation and Solving in Lean
summary: Constraint programming is a core technology for solving complex combinatorial problems in scheduling, planning, configuration, and verification. Trusting its results therefore demands guarantees at two levels: that reformulations applied beforehand are semantics-preserving, and that solvers produce correct answers. In this work, we introduce a framework that addresses both verification levels in the Lean theorem prover: it can be used to prove formulation-level properties, such as equivalence, equisatisfiability, and the correctness of symmetry-breaking constraints, parametrically for entire problem families; and to check solver-produced certificates for individual instances via translation backends to external formats such as MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB. Combining both levels yields an end-to-end workflow that establishes the satisfiability or unsatisfiability of a constraint problem without trusting the external solver. Experimental results show that our framework's verified symmetry breaking also pays off in practice: a single parametric proof per problem family, reused across all instance sizes, reduces solver search effort by a factor of up to 2x10^7, while the entire in-Lean certification stays affordable, taking at most a few minutes for our largest instances.

AI.tldr: Verified constraint programming framework in Lean that proves formulation properties for problem families and checks solver certificates, enabling end-to-end trust without external solver trust.
AI.motivation: Constraint programming requires trust guarantees at two levels: semantics-preserving reformulations and correct solver outputs. Current approaches lack integrated verification for both formulation-level properties and solver certificates.
AI.method: A framework in Lean theorem prover that: 1) proves parametric formulation-level properties (equivalence, equisatisfiability, symmetry-breaking correctness) for entire problem families, and 2) checks solver-produced certificates via translation backends to external formats (MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, OPB).
AI.result: Verified symmetry breaking reduces solver search effort by up to 2×10^7 factor; in-Lean certification stays affordable (minutes for largest instances). End-to-end workflow establishes satisfiability/unsatisfiability without trusting external solver.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully addresses both verification levels, enabling trustworthy constraint programming with practical performance benefits. Verified symmetry breaking shows significant search reduction while maintaining affordable certification costs.

title: Stage-Replay Divergence Follows the KV Cache: Fixed-Prefix Precision Controls and Bidirectional Cache Transplantation
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Reproducibility artifacts (frozen manifests, token IDs, per-item scores, analysis harnesses) described in Section 3.9
summary: Stage-replay diagnostics reconstruct intermediate token prefixes and treat fresh-prefill continuation as continuation from the decoder state that originally reached the prefix. We audit that assumption at a whole reasoning-stage boundary in a Qwen2.5-derived system. A matched 200-item experiment compares retained live cache with one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens and places an exact replica on both sides. In BF16, replicas remain exact while the constructions differ on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels; the accuracy difference is only one point (paired 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). A fixed-prefix 2x2 holds all 200 token states constant while crossing construction and precision. The BF16 disagreements recur, whereas FP32 produces no decoded disagreement (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). A prospective bridge makes token-by-token incremental and retained live caches bit-exact on 12/12 rows; an all-200 saved-ledger audit reproduces every retained trajectory and comparison fingerprint. Bidirectional transplantation of all 48 key/value layers makes every tested divergent continuation follow its cache donor, both on a selected set at the primary checkpoint (24/24) and an outcome-blind replication at a later checkpoint (43/43). Exact-token replay can therefore be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. On the tested states, boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of the divergent trajectory, while numerical precision moderates its behavioral expression.

AI.tldr: Stage-replay diagnostics assume fresh prefill is equivalent to continuation from original decoder state, but testing reveals boundary cache differences cause behavioral divergence in some contexts, though accuracy impact is minimal.
AI.motivation: To audit the assumption in stage-replay diagnostics that treating fresh-prefill continuation as continuation from the original decoder state is valid at whole reasoning-stage boundaries.
AI.method: Matched 200-item experiment comparing retained live cache with one-shot prefill of identical tokens; 2x2 design crossing construction (cache vs. prefill) and precision (BF16 vs. FP32); token-by-token incremental and saved-ledger audits; bidirectional transplantation of K/V layers.
AI.result: BF16 replicas remained exact but constructions differed on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels (accuracy difference only 1 point, CI [-3.5, +5.5]); FP32 produced no decoded disagreement; K/V layer transplantation made all divergent continuations follow cache donor; boundary K/V cache is causally sufficient for divergent trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Exact-token replay can be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity; boundary K/V cache carries sufficient causal information for divergent trajectories, with numerical precision moderating behavioral expression.

title: A report-grounded vision-language foundation model for colonoscopy from 280000 routine reports
summary: Vision-language models remain underused in colonoscopy despite the rich expert descriptions recorded in routine reports. These reports document lesion appearance, size and location but summarise entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings only weakly linked to the corresponding images. Here we develop EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs progressively recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. Across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks, EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings. On benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approaches the performance of expert readers in a blinded study involving 12 endoscopists. These results suggest that recovering finding-to-frame correspondence can transform routine documentation into scalable supervision, enabling clinical targets to be specified in language rather than separately annotated for each task.

AI.tldr: EndoCLIP is a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on lesion-level image-text pairs recovered from routine colonoscopy reports, enabling superior performance on clinical tasks by establishing finding-to-frame correspondence.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models are underutilized in colonoscopy despite rich expert descriptions in routine reports. Current reports summarize entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings weakly linked to corresponding images, creating a gap between documentation and visual data.
AI.method: Developed EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs progressively recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. Used a vision-language approach to establish direct correspondence between clinical findings and endoscopic images.
AI.result: EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation, and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings. On benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approaches expert reader performance in a blinded study with 12 endoscopists.
AI.conclusion: Recovering finding-to-frame correspondence can transform routine clinical documentation into scalable supervision, enabling clinical targets to be specified in natural language rather than requiring separate annotation for each task, potentially revolutionizing clinical AI development in colonoscopy.

title: The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse
summary:
Algorithmic recourse aims to provide individuals with actionable changes to improve their predicted outcomes in high-stakes classification settings, such as loan and mortgage applications. However, most existing approaches focus only on flipping a model's prediction, without accounting for whether the recommended changes lead to genuine improvement in an individual's true qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming of the classifier. Consequently, deployed recourse policies can induce behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and become ineffective after model retraining.
  In this work, we formalize this failure mode through a causal performative framework for recourse. We model how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model, capturing interactions among features as well as their effect on the true label. These causal responses induce a non-convex optimization problem, even under standard convex losses. We characterize conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and can be efficiently computed via simple iterative dynamics. Our analysis reveals that recourse policies that ignore causal structure can induce large, misaligned behavioral responses, whereas causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce incentives for gaming. Experiments on both semi-synthetic and real credit datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining to accommodate distribution shifts caused by strategic agent behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a causal performative framework for algorithmic recourse that accounts for how recommended changes affect true qualifications rather than just gaming classifiers, ensuring more stable and effective recommendations.
AI.motivation: Current algorithmic recourse methods focus on flipping model predictions without considering whether recommended changes genuinely improve true qualifications or just enable gaming the classifier. This leads to behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and make recourse ineffective after model retraining.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem through a causal performative framework for recourse, modeling how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model that captures feature interactions and their effects on true labels. They characterize conditions for performatively stable solutions and develop efficient iterative algorithms.
AI.result: The framework shows that causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce gaming incentives, while standard approaches induce misaligned behavioral responses. Experiments on semi-synthetic and real credit datasets demonstrate superior performance over standard empirical risk minimization and reduced need for frequent retraining.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating causal structure into algorithmic recourse is essential for creating stable and effective recommendation systems that genuinely improve individual qualifications rather than enabling strategic gaming, leading to more sustainable and reliable decision-making systems.

title: Towards Autonomous Aircraft Surveillance from Nanosatellites through On-Board Inference and Generative Data Augmentation
summary: Airborne surveillance from low Earth orbit is hindered by two interconnected bottlenecks: nanosatellites have a limited downlink budget, yet the conventional approach still transmits terabytes of raw imagery to the ground for processing, and open satellite datasets for aircraft are scarce and severely class-imbalanced. These limitations either delay timely decision-making or prevent standard detectors from learning robust representations of rare aircraft classes. In this paper, a workflow that combines on-board inference with generative data augmentation is proposed to address both limitations jointly. Inference is executed on a 6U CubeSat equipped with a low-power edge tensor accelerator, while a diffusion model fine-tuned through low-rank adaptation generates synthetic minority-class imagery. This synthetic output is automatically annotated, pseudo-labelled, by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples. The results show that the balanced dataset increases global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, with the minority class rising from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811, and that the quantised detector fits the on-chip memory and projects 25-30 frames per second on orbit. This approach contrasts with the conventional bent-pipe architecture, in which the satellite acts as a passive data collector. Therefore, the computational tests support the proposed workflow as a decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites.

AI.tldr: On-board edge inference combined with generative data augmentation enables real-time aircraft detection from nanosatellites, addressing limited downlink bandwidth and class imbalance issues.
AI.motivation: Current nanosatellite surveillance faces two key bottlenecks: limited downlink bandwidth that prevents transmitting terabytes of raw imagery, and scarcity/class-imbalance in existing satellite aircraft datasets that hinders robust detection of rare aircraft classes.
AI.method: Proposes a workflow combining on-board inference on a 6U CubeSat with low-power edge tensor accelerator, and generative data augmentation using diffusion models fine-tuned via low-rank adaptation. Synthetic minority-class imagery is automatically annotated by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples.
AI.result: Balanced dataset increases global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, with minority class rising from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811. Quantized detector fits on-chip memory and projects 25-30 frames per second on orbit.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables real-time autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites, contrasting with conventional bent-pipe architecture, and serves as an effective decision-support tool for timely aerial surveillance operations.

title: Same Graph Cross-Task Transfer in GNNs: Protocols and Predictors
summary: Many real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks over the same underlying structure, creating an opportunity to reuse supervision across node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP). However, existing evaluations often rely on incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable. We formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. Across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), we find that transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC $\to$ LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP $\to$ NC is fragile and can even degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP $\to$ NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting that LP acts as structural pretraining. Finally, we introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility when a shared encoder must serve both tasks, and show that simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper examines cross-task transfer between node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP) on the same graph, finding directional transfer patterns: NC→LP benefits homophilic graphs, while LP→NC is fragile and mainly helps in structure-dominant regimes. The authors propose a leakage-free evaluation protocol and CoTask Score metric.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations for same-graph cross-task transfer between node classification and link prediction are unreliable due to incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and inconsistent negative sampling rules. There's a need for standardized evaluation to understand how supervision can be effectively reused across these tasks on the same underlying graph structure.
AI.method: The authors formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free evaluation protocol with fixed node/edge splits, a shared message-passing graph excluding evaluated edges, and fixed negatives for LP. They evaluate across three graph neural network backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS) and introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to measure joint NC+LP utility when using a shared encoder for both tasks.
AI.result: Transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC→LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP→NC is fragile and can degrade accuracy with naive representation reuse. LP→NC becomes reliably positive only in structure-dominant regimes where LP is easy but NC performance is unsaturated, suggesting LP acts as structural pretraining. Homophily is identified as a key dataset statistic guiding mechanism choice.
AI.conclusion: Cross-task transfer between node classification and link prediction shows clear directional patterns, with homophily as a key predictor of successful transfer. The proposed CoTask Score and leakage-free evaluation protocol provide reliable tools for measuring and understanding joint task utility, helping avoid negative transfer in multi-task graph learning scenarios.

title: A Fuzzy Rule-based Neuro-Symbolic Approach for Pipe Severity Prediction in Sewer Networks
summary:
Standard automated sewer pipe severity assessment relies on direct image classification, creating a "black box" where the link between visual defects and final severity scores remains implicit. This study introduces a modular, fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by decoupling neural perception from symbolic reasoning. The perception module utilizes a Swin Transformer to predict 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees directly from images. For reasoning, a DT, specifically Weka's J48, algorithm is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, and its paths are converted into 19 fixed IF--THEN rules. Inference operates via fuzzy logic: t-norm activations from CODE conditions are weighted by rule confidence and combined with corresponding s-norms to produce interpretable class evidence. We assessed Product, Łukasiewicz, and Hamacher operator pairs using a dataset of 3,244 images spanning five highly imbalanced severity classes. Ground-truth labels were robustly generated via consensus from five independent large language models analyzing original inspector notes. Our results show an improvement of accuracy, balanced accuracy, Macro F1 and MCC by 17.9%, 12.2%, 23.0%, and 17.3%, respectively, over image-only based classification.
  Overall, the framework combines competitive class-balanced performance with traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a neuro-symbolic framework that combines neural perception with symbolic reasoning for interpretable sewer pipe severity assessment, improving performance metrics by 12-23% over image-only classification.
AI.motivation: Standard automated sewer pipe severity assessment methods create "black box" systems where the relationship between visual defects and final severity scores is not transparent or interpretable. There's a need for methods that bridge the gap between neural perception and symbolic reasoning to make the assessment process more explainable.
AI.method: The framework uses a modular approach: (1) A perception module with Swin Transformer predicts 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees from images, (2) A symbolic reasoning module trains a DT (J48) algorithm on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, converting decision paths into 19 fixed IF-THEN rules, (3) Inference uses fuzzy logic with t-norm activations from CODE conditions weighted by rule confidence and combined with s-norms to produce interpretable class evidence. The system evaluates Product, Łukasiewicz, and Hamacher operator pairs on 3,244 images across five imbalanced severity classes.
AI.result: The framework shows significant improvements over image-only classification: accuracy (+17.9%), balanced accuracy (+12.2%), Macro F1 (+23.0%), and MCC (+17.3%). Ground-truth labels were generated via consensus from five independent large language models analyzing original inspector notes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed neuro-symbolic framework successfully combines competitive class-balanced performance with traceable reasoning, providing interpretable severity assessments that link predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence, addressing the black box problem in automated sewer pipe inspection.

title: SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination
summary: Can supply-chain AI move beyond isolated decision modules toward unified operational planning? A complete replenishment plan specifies which products each location carries, which upstream facility supplies it, how often it is replenished, and how deliveries are routed.
