These decisions are operationally coupled: the selected assortment changes the demand and load passed to later stages; source assignment and replenishment frequency reshape the delivery requests; and route feasibility and cost, in turn, determine the system value of the earlier choices. Yet in modern supply chains, these decisions are often handled by separate departments and optimized through separate systems, which can lead to stockouts, inventory exposure, and avoidable transportation. We propose SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination, a composite policy model that represents supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to the corresponding decision interface. Each decision builds on the partial plan formed by earlier decisions while the completed plan is evaluated using a shared system-level utility. We instantiate this framework in urban fresh-retail replenishment, where service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing interact strongly, and evaluate it on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com, two large-scale supply chains operating at different replenishment echelons. Across both settings, SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage separately, as well as practice-oriented baselines commonly used in supply-chain operations. These results show that learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings lead to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions.

AI.tldr: SCOPE is a unified AI framework for supply chain operations that coordinates traditionally separate decisions (assortment, sourcing, frequency, routing) through token-based representation and shared utility optimization, outperforming isolated decision systems.
AI.motivation: Modern supply chains handle replenishment decisions (assortment, sourcing, frequency, routing) through separate departments and systems, leading to inefficiencies like stockouts, inventory exposure, and avoidable transportation due to lack of coordination between operationally coupled decisions.
AI.method: SCOPE: Composite policy model representing supply-chain entities as tokens with shared operational representation, mapping each token type to corresponding decision interfaces. Decisions build incrementally on partial plans while evaluating completed plans using shared system-level utility function.
AI.result: Evaluated on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com (urban fresh-retail replenishment), SCOPE consistently outperformed both isolated decision optimization methods and practice-oriented baselines across different replenishment echelons.
AI.conclusion: Learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings leads to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions, demonstrating the value of unified AI planning over isolated optimization modules.

title: $β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to improve reasoning language models, but it remains brittle in practice: making it work reliably often requires substantial engineering effort. We identify a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is precisely the $β=1$ member of a broader policy-optimization family, where $β$ weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. This equivalence turns $β$ from an implicit value fixed at one into a controllable regularization parameter, yielding a more general formulation that trades off proximity to a reference policy against privileged teacher guidance. We introduce $β$-OPSD and derive its optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Directly optimizing this objective with reinforcement learning, however, would be costly and high-variance. Rather than optimize the RL objective directly, we turn its closed-form solution into a distillation target. Each value of $β$ selects a target along the reference-to-teacher path, which we implement efficiently by mixing their token-level logits. In this way, inexpensive distillation approximates the solution of expensive policy optimization. Return-to-go credit assignment further aligns token updates with the sequence-level objective while retaining the simplicity of OPSD. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that $β$-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance. Our results provide a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

AI.tldr: β-OPSD generalizes on-policy self-distillation by introducing a tunable KL penalty parameter β, creating a geometric interpolation between reference policy and privileged teacher, approximated efficiently via logit mixing rather than expensive RL optimization.
AI.motivation: Vanilla on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is brittle in practice and requires substantial engineering effort to work reliably. The authors identify that vanilla OPSD corresponds to β=1 in a broader policy optimization family, but this fixed parameter limits flexibility.
AI.method: Introduce β-OPSD as a generalization where β weights the KL penalty between student and reference policy. Derive optimal policy as geometric interpolation between reference policy and privileged teacher. Instead of expensive RL optimization, use the closed-form solution as distillation target by mixing token-level logits. Use return-to-go credit assignment for sequence-level alignment.
AI.result: β-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, improving both optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance. Provides principled connection between self-distillation and policy optimization while maintaining efficiency.
AI.conclusion: β-OPSD offers a principled generalization of self-distillation that transforms implicit design choices into tunable regularization parameters, achieving better performance while maintaining the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

title: InfoOps Bench: A live information operations safety benchmark
summary:
In this paper we present an active, constantly updated AI benchmark which measures the integrity of frontier language models against being co-opted for state-backed information operations. We draw on over 2,100 information operations from a live monitoring pipeline which tracks Russian, Chinese and Iranian state-backed information assets. Alongside this paper, we release a companion website that tracks the most prominent claims spread by state-backed media outlets, updated weekly, available from: pattrn.ai/research/infoopsbench. The dynamic nature of the benchmark makes it resistant to saturation.
  In the benchmark, we test 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings. We find that most models can be co-opted for information operations. Integrity scores, defined as the percentage of refused requests, range from 8.8% to 94.5%, an 85.7-percentage-point spread not explained by model size. Model choice also changes the character of the resulting operation. Some models fabricate details and produce output more harmful than the source material, others defuse claims even while complying, and fact-checking rates vary from 2.9% to 72.9%.
  Integrity against information operations is at least partly related to refusal to produce content even for benign claims, illustrating the challenge of balancing model usability with safety. With one exception (Z.ai's GLM 5.2), the Chinese-developed models sharply cut compliance on factually grounded but China-critical claims, dropping 48-70 percentage points relative to matched benign claims.

AI.tldr: Active AI benchmark measures frontier language models' vulnerability to being co-opted for state-backed information operations, finding most models can be manipulated with integrity scores ranging from 8.8% to 94.5%.
AI.motivation: To measure the integrity of frontier language models against being exploited for state-backed information operations, addressing concerns about AI systems being manipulated for propaganda and disinformation campaigns by hostile state actors.
AI.method: Created a dynamic, constantly updated benchmark using over 2,100 information operations from live monitoring of Russian, Chinese, and Iranian state-backed assets. Tested 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings, tracking model responses to information operation content.
AI.result: Most models can be co-opted for information operations with integrity scores (refusal rates) ranging from 8.8% to 94.5%. Chinese-developed models (except GLM 5.2) sharply reduce compliance on China-critical claims. Some models fabricate harmful details, others defuse claims while complying, and fact-checking rates vary widely (2.9% to 72.9%).
AI.conclusion: Language models are vulnerable to exploitation for information operations, presenting challenges in balancing usability with safety. The dynamic benchmark provides ongoing monitoring of this security threat as models and information operations evolve.

title: KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models
summary: Clinical risk models routinely achieve strong aggregate performance while producing materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines have been proposed to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested, so it is unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions. We present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring, evaluated to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Four findings follow. (i) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect: rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) across the 15 axes is rho = 0.56, rising to rho = 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling -- the better calibrator -- behaves as a coin flip on EOD (19 of 48 runs improved, 95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with mean effect near zero, so what an audit should report is the variance, not the average. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal that it failed. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease: at the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p = 0.002), so a threshold tuned on one cohort fails to transfer. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity. Code, artifacts, and scripts reproducing every number are released.

AI.tldr: KAISEN is a five-phase audit pipeline for evaluating clinical risk models that tests each component to failure using synthetic benchmarks, revealing critical limitations in current audit practices including misalignment between significance and actual disparities, inconsistent post-hoc mitigation effectiveness, diagnostic failures under proxy misspecification, and poor transferability of drift detection thresholds.
AI.motivation: Clinical risk models often show strong aggregate performance but materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Existing audit pipelines are rarely stress-tested, making it unclear which audit components can be trusted and under what conditions.
AI.method: The authors present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering: subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring. They evaluate it to the point of failure using synthetic benchmarks of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect (rank correlation improves from ρ=0.56 to 0.78 when standardizing by floor). (2) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in all 48 runs, while Platt scaling shows coin-flip performance on EOD improvement. (3) Mechanism diagnostic correctly classifies all 144 controlled cases but fails on all 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification. (4) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization more than disease, showing poor threshold transferability across cohorts.
AI.conclusion: Current audit components have critical limitations: significance testing is misaligned with actual disparities, post-hoc mitigation shows inconsistent effectiveness, diagnostics fail silently under proxy misspecification, and drift thresholds don't transfer between cohorts. The synthetic benchmark approach reveals these failure modes that would be undetectable with real data lacking ground truth.

title: Selective Credibility-Limited Belief Update
summary: Belief update concerns changes in an agent's beliefs induced by changes in the underlying world. Standard Katsuno-Mendelzon update assumes that an epistemic input can be incorporated from every initially possible world, whereas credibility-limited belief update restricts, for each source world, the successor worlds regarded as credible or reachable. Nevertheless, existing credibility-limited approaches treat the epistemic input as an indivisible whole, and therefore cannot represent cases in which only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. We introduce selective credibility-limited belief update, in which the epistemic input is transformed, relative to each source world, into a weaker proxy before the credibility-limited transition is performed. We provide semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting class of update operators. We then identify two well-behaved sub-classes; namely, consistency-preserving update operators, which require every transformed epistemic input to be credible from its source world whenever the original epistemic input is consistent, and maximal consistency-preserving update operators, which additionally require the selected proxy to be maximally informative among the credible consequences of the original epistemic input. Finally, we establish the generality of the proposed framework by showing that credibility-limited belief update is recovered as a special case, while Katsuno--Mendelzon belief update emerges when credibility restrictions are removed and the transformation functions are taken to be identities. These results demonstrate that the framework provides a unified and strictly more expressive account of belief update, encompassing established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance.

AI.tldr: Introduces selective credibility-limited belief update, which allows partial acceptance of compound epistemic inputs by transforming them into weaker proxies before credibility-limited transitions, providing a more expressive framework that encompasses existing update approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing credibility-limited belief update approaches treat epistemic inputs as indivisible wholes, making them unable to represent cases where only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. This limitation prevents modeling scenarios where agents can selectively accept parts of incoming information based on credibility.
AI.method: Proposes selective credibility-limited belief update where epistemic inputs are transformed, relative to each source world, into weaker proxies before performing credibility-limited transitions. Provides semantic and axiomatic characterizations, identifies two well-behaved sub-classes: consistency-preserving and maximal consistency-preserving update operators.
AI.result: Develops a unified framework showing that credibility-limited belief update emerges as a special case when transformation functions are taken as identities, and Katsuno-Mendelzon belief update emerges when credibility restrictions are removed and transformations are identity functions. Demonstrates that the framework supports source-dependent selective acceptance while being strictly more expressive than existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The selective credibility-limited belief update framework provides a unified and strictly more expressive account of belief update that encompasses established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance of epistemic inputs.

title: MANTA: Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation for Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model-based multi-agent systems improve complex problem solving through task decomposition, agent specialization, information exchange, and intermediate validation. However, existing systems typically treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or an offline optimization target. We introduce MANTA, a framework for Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation that enables communication structures to self-evolve at inference time. Before execution, MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience. During deployment, it monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates when the current organization becomes insufficient. These updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and agent budget. We evaluate MANTA against representative single-agent and multi-agent baselines on five benchmarks spanning information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning. MANTA achieves the highest average score of 74.0, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft. These results show that inference-time self-improvement can extend to the architecture of collaboration itself.

AI.tldr: MANTA enables LLM-based multi-agent systems to dynamically adapt their communication topologies during inference, outperforming static systems by 5.8% across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent systems treat communication topology as fixed or offline-optimized, which limits their ability to adapt to changing task demands during execution.
AI.method: MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior experience, then monitors collaboration traces during deployment and applies bounded structural updates (agent roles, communication links, execution order, info visibility, validation pathways) when needed.
AI.result: MANTA achieves highest average score of 74.0 across five benchmarks (information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, mathematical reasoning), outperforming strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining best result on PlanCraft.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time self-improvement can extend to the architecture of collaboration itself, demonstrating that dynamic topology adaptation significantly enhances multi-agent system performance.

title: Rethinking Inference-Time Scaling in Local Computer-Use Agents: Failure Modes and Compute Tradeoffs
summary: Deploying autonomous computer-use agents (CUAs) locally is increasingly important for privacy, cost efficiency, and practical usability, yet improving their performance under strict hardware constraints remains challenging. While recent studies show that inference-time scaling can improve frontier computer-use agents through additional computation during execution, its effectiveness for resource-constrained local models remains poorly understood. We present a systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling in local CUAs across contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel dimensions. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B on the OSWorld benchmark. Our results show that additional computation often yields diminishing returns while changing failure modes. Contextual scaling provides historical grounding that improves trajectory stability and task accuracy, but its gains saturate as token cost increases and failures shift from repetitive or stalled trajectories toward premature false successes. Temporal scaling similarly reduces max-step stalls, yet does not substantially improve task success, indicating that longer horizons often extend erroneous trajectories rather than correct them. We further find that structural decomposition can introduce planning and formatting overhead in local two-stage agents, while parallel scaling partially mitigates these failures at a substantial computational cost. Overall, our findings suggest that efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation, failure-aware control mechanisms, and agentic frameworks designed around the capabilities and limitations of local models.

AI.tldr: Inference-time scaling (additional computation during execution) has limited effectiveness for improving resource-constrained local computer-use agents, with contextual and temporal scaling showing diminishing returns and changing failure modes rather than improving task success.
AI.motivation: Local deployment of autonomous computer-use agents is important for privacy, cost efficiency, and practical usability, but improving their performance under strict hardware constraints remains challenging. While inference-time scaling helps frontier models, its effectiveness for resource-constrained local models is poorly understood.
AI.method: Systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling in local CUAs across four dimensions: contextual (historical grounding), temporal (longer horizons), structural (decomposition), and parallel scaling. Evaluated Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B on the OSWorld benchmark.
AI.result: Additional computation often yields diminishing returns while changing failure modes. Contextual scaling improves trajectory stability but gains saturate with token cost increases. Temporal scaling reduces max-step stalls but doesn't improve task success. Structural decomposition introduces planning/formatting overhead, while parallel scaling partially mitigates failures at high computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Efficient local computer-use agents require selective compute allocation, failure-aware control mechanisms, and agentic frameworks specifically designed around the capabilities and limitations of local models, rather than simply applying more computational resources.

title: DualG-MRAG: Decoupling Macro-Reasoning and Micro-Matching for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026). 12 pages
summary: While Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MM-RAG) has shown promising results, it still struggles with complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. Existing methods primarily focus on independent instance-level matching, which often fails to capture explicit relationships across modalities and documents. Although Graph-enhanced methods introduce structural modeling, they face a fundamental challenge in multimodal scenarios: incorporating fine-grained visual features leads to rapid graph expansion and retrieval noise, whereas coarse-grained representations cause the discarding of critical local evidence. To address this dilemma, we propose DualG-MRAG, a Dual-tier framework that introduces a decoupled architecture comprising Macro-reasoning and Micro-matching Graphs for Multimodal RAG. Specifically, to suppress retrieval noise by isolating global structural reasoning from fine-grained evidence matching, we construct a Macro Graph for global topological routing and a Micro Graph for precise local verification. Subsequently, to enable dynamic relevance propagation across heterogeneous evidence sources, we formulate retrieval as a query-driven message passing process via a GNN Retriever. Furthermore, to provide the generative model with coherent structural guidance, we introduce a dynamic programming decoding mechanism that extracts explicit reasoning paths directly from the GNN's forward pass, replacing the standard input of isolated document chunks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DualG-MRAG outperforms baselines in both evidence recall and complex QA accuracy.

AI.tldr: DualG-MRAG: A dual-tier graph framework for multimodal RAG that separates global reasoning from local verification to improve complex multi-hop reasoning without noise from fine-grained visual features.
AI.motivation: Current MM-RAG methods struggle with complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. Existing approaches have two main issues: 1) Independent instance-level matching fails to capture explicit cross-modal/document relationships, and 2) Graph-enhanced methods face a fundamental dilemma - fine-grained visual features cause graph expansion and retrieval noise, while coarse-grained representations discard critical local evidence.
AI.method: Proposes DualG-MRAG, a dual-tier framework with a decoupled architecture containing: 1) Macro Graph for global topological routing, 2) Micro Graph for precise local verification. Retrieval is formulated as query-driven message passing via a GNN Retriever. A dynamic programming decoding mechanism extracts explicit reasoning paths directly from GNN's forward pass instead of using isolated document chunks.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DualG-MRAG outperforms baselines in both evidence recall and complex QA accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The dual-tier graph approach successfully addresses the fundamental dilemma in multimodal RAG by isolating global structural reasoning from fine-grained evidence matching, enabling better complex multi-hop reasoning through explicit relationship modeling across modalities and documents.

title: OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models
summary: Computer-using agents (CUAs) are advancing rapidly across the digital world. A CUA trajectory records the agent's actions, states, and reasoning. Verifying whether it fulfilled the task instruction is central to CUA evaluation, data curation, and reinforcement learning. Neither human-written verifiers nor human annotators can provide such verification at scale, so the field increasingly turns to vision-language models (VLMs) as judges of CUA trajectories. But a fundamental question has long gone unexamined: are these VLM judges reliable enough? To study it systematically, we introduce OSReward, a realistic, high-quality benchmark that evaluates VLM judges on CUA trajectories. The trajectories come from diverse agent backbones executing human-verified instructions across platforms, then rigorously labeled with ground-truth verdicts through multi-stage human annotation. Building on it, we derive OSReward-Hard, a challenge set concentrating genuinely hard cases, and OSReward-Multi for fine-grained efficiency and alignment scoring. The most comprehensive evaluation of VLM judges to date finds even state-of-the-art models fall short of an ideal judge, sharing a systematic leniency bias that mislabels failed runs as successes. The few reliable enough to trust are too expensive to run at scale, while affordable open models trail far behind. To close this gap, we construct and release OS-Shepherd-100K, an open corpus of reasoning-annotated trajectory judgments for the CUA community. On it, we train OS-Shepherd (9B and 35B), open reward models that supply low-cost, stable, and reliable reward signals, matching commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost than the frontier. Extensive analyses further inform the design of reliable CUA reward at scale. Our code, benchmark, dataset, and model checkpoints are available at https://os-copilot.github.io/OSReward-Home/.

AI.tldr: OSReward is a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models as judges of computer-using agent trajectories, revealing systematic biases in current VLM judges and introducing OS-Shepherd reward models as more reliable, cost-effective alternatives.
AI.motivation: As computer-using agents become more prevalent, verifying whether they fulfill task instructions is crucial for evaluation, data curation, and reinforcement learning. Current approaches using human-written verifiers or human annotators don't scale, so the field increasingly uses VLMs as judges, but their reliability remains unexamined.
AI.method: 1) Introduced OSReward benchmark with realistic, high-quality trajectories from diverse agent backbones executing human-verified instructions. 2) Used multi-stage human annotation for ground-truth verdicts. 3) Built OSReward-Hard (challenge set) and OSReward-Multi (fine-grained scoring). 4) Conducted comprehensive evaluation of VLM judges. 5) Created OS-Shepherd-100K dataset with reasoning-annotated judgments. 6) Trained OS-Shepherd reward models (9B and 35B parameters).
AI.result: State-of-the-art VLM judges fall short of ideal judges, showing systematic leniency bias that mislabels failed runs as successes. The few reliable judges are too expensive to scale, while affordable open models perform poorly. OS-Shepherd models provide low-cost, stable, and reliable reward signals, matching commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost.
AI.conclusion: Current VLM judges for computer-using agent trajectories are unreliable and biased, creating a need for better evaluation benchmarks and reward models. The OSReward benchmark and OS-Shepherd reward models address this gap by providing reliable, cost-effective solutions for CUA trajectory evaluation at scale.

title: AISPA: User-Centric System Prompt Auditing for Large Language Model Applications
summary: System prompts are instructions configured by developers to govern the behaviors of foundation models in AI applications. They are used throughout commercial AI products, but are rarely disclosed to the public or regulators, creating a serious trust and accountability gap in the wide deployment of AI systems. In this paper, we introduce Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance (AISPA), a user-centric framework for systematically auditing system prompts in AI systems. AISPA examines specific parts of a system prompt and evaluates them along eight dimensions that matter to users. We then use this framework to review 3,249 instructions from system prompts in 88 commercial AI products, classifying each instruction as either protective (of users) or problematic. Our audit surfaces four core findings. First, system prompt design varies substantially across products and developers, with some organizations averaging over 60 protective instructions per product while others average fewer than 5. Second, protective instructions are widely adopted but shallow in scope: 98.9% of products contain at least one, yet only 24% cover all eight dimensions of the AISPA taxonomy. Third, system prompts have grown steadily longer and more protective of users, suggesting that user protection is becoming a more visible concern in commercial prompt design. Fourth, despite this progress, problematic instructions remain pervasive: roughly 40% of products contain at least one instruction that works against user interests, and protective and problematic instructions frequently coexist within the same prompt. Our findings highlight the need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight for system prompts in commercial AI products.

AI.tldr: AISPA is a user-centric framework for auditing system prompts in AI systems, revealing significant variation in prompt design across 88 commercial products and widespread coexistence of both protective and problematic instructions.
AI.motivation: System prompts in commercial AI products are rarely disclosed publicly or to regulators, creating a serious trust and accountability gap in AI system deployment. There's a need for transparency and oversight in how these foundational instructions are designed.
AI.method: Developed Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance (AISPA) framework that examines specific parts of system prompts and evaluates them along eight dimensions that matter to users. Used this framework to audit 3,249 instructions from system prompts in 88 commercial AI products.
AI.result: Four core findings: 1) Substantial variation in prompt design across products/developers (some averaging over 60 protective instructions, others fewer than 5); 2) Protective instructions are widely adopted but shallow in scope (98.9% have at least one, but only 24% cover all eight dimensions); 3) System prompts have grown steadily longer and more protective over time; 4) Problematic instructions remain pervasive (40% of products contain at least one anti-user instruction).
AI.conclusion: Findings highlight the need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight for system prompts in commercial AI products. There's a coexistence of both protective and problematic instructions within the same systems, indicating current practices are insufficient.
